author: Saurav Das
text:
From the second strip, each bucket holds 11 pounds of corn, but you fill only eight. You carry heavier buckets back from that strip and end up with 88 pounds of grain. Interactive figure · Move the sliders

### Can heavier buckets add up to less grain?

Two strips of corn, the same size. Strip A filled 10 buckets at 10 lb each. Set what came off Strip B.

Weight of one full bucket11 lb

Works like test weight: one fixed container, weighed full.

Buckets filled8

Every bucket added up is where yield starts.

**Strip A**stays fixed

**100** lb

10 buckets × 10 lb each

**Strip B**yours to change

**88** lb

8 buckets × 11 lb each

*Strip A*

Heavier buckets, smaller harvest.

Each Strip B bucket weighs 1 lb more, but the strip filled 2 fewer buckets. That is 88 lb against Strip A’s 100 lb: 12 lb less grain from the same area.

At 11 lb a bucket, Strip B matches Strip A’s 100 lb at 9.1 buckets.

The grain tester works on the same principle as the bucket. A **test weight** of 61 lb/bu means a standard bushel of volume, about 1.24 cubic feet, holds 61 pounds of that corn. The size, shape, condition and moisture of the kernels affect how tightly they pack. ⁠[[2]](#source-2)⁠[[3]](#source-3)

A **market bushel** is how corn is counted when it’s sold or reported as yield. For shelled corn, that’s 56 pounds. To get the market bushels for a load, start with its scale weight, apply the moisture adjustment under the buyer’s terms and divide by 56. ⁠[[3]](#source-3)⁠[[4]](#source-4)

To measure test weight, a USDA grain inspector lets corn flow from a hopper into a calibrated cup called a kettle. Once the cup overflows, the inspector levels the grain at the rim and weighs it. A scale or conversion table gives the result in pounds per bushel. The cup is filled the same way each time because a shake or a tap can change how the kernels settle. ⁠[[2]](#source-2)

A scale or conversion table gives the result in pounds per bushel. The cup is filled the same way each time because a shake or a tap can change how the kernels settle. ⁠[[2]](#source-2) Interactive figure · Three steps

### Follow the sample through the test

A test-weight reading comes from one fixed cup of grain. Step through how the cup is filled, levelled and weighed.

Step 1 of 3

Fill the kettle

Release a representative sample from the hopper so the calibrated kettle overflows. Let the grain settle as it falls.

Diagram follows the USDA hopper-and-kettle method, drawn as a cutaway. The display uses the test weight in Joe’s newsletter as an example.

## What happened after pollination in Wisconsin

Heading into pollination, Joe thought the crop had the best setup he’d seen in his career. The plants had set their kernel rows with little stress, and pollination went smoothly. “Then the water shut off,” he wrote. ⁠[[1]](#source-1)

Water stress early in grain fill can cause kernels near the tip of the ear to stop developing. Later in grain fill, stress can limit how much dry matter the surviving kernels put on. Joe suspects some tip kernels were lost and more of the crop’s available starch went to kernels in the middle and at the base of the ear. Fewer kernels can leave less grain to harvest even when the remaining ones fill well. ⁠[[1]](#source-1)⁠[[6]](#source-6)

Disease pressure stayed low through grain fill. After black layer, when the kernels had finished filling, warm weather and little rewetting helped the crop dry quickly in the field. Near the junction of Polk, St. Croix, Barron and Dunn counties, Joe reported about 2,500 growing degree units from May 1 to October 1, compared with about 2,200 in an average year. ⁠[[1]](#source-1)

Joe points to that quick dry-down as a reason for the high test weights. As sound kernels dry, they shrink and can pack more tightly. By Purdue’s estimate, sound corn that tests 52 lb/bu at 25% moisture could reach about 58.9 lb/bu when dried to 15%. Severe stress can leave kernels poorly filled and lower the test weight. ⁠[[1]](#source-1)⁠[[3]](#source-3)⁠[[6]](#source-6)

## How test weight and yield compared in Kansas

The two numbers also told different stories in a 2011 Kansas State trial at Scandia, where 60 hybrids grew side by side under irrigation. The corn with the highest test weight, 62 lb/bu, had the lowest yield at 162 bushels per acre. The top-yielding hybrid made 241 bushels per acre and tested at 58 lb/bu. ⁠[[8]](#source-8)

Interactive figure · Real trial data

### Did the heaviest corn yield the most?

Every dot is one hybrid, grown side by side under irrigation in Kansas in 2011. Pick a test weight to see what those hybrids yielded.

One hybrid · Top yield · Trial average, 209 bu/a

The heaviest corn was not the best yielder.

At Scandia, the heaviest test weight was 62 lb/bu, and that entry yielded 162 bu/a. The top yield, 241 bu/a, came from corn that tested 58 lb/bu.

At 62 lb/bu: 1 hybrid, 162 bu/a, 47 bu/a below the trial average. Yield gaps under 18 bu/a were within this trial’s margin of error (LSD 0.05).

Source: Kansas State University, 2011 Kansas Performance Tests with Corn Hybrids (SRP1055), Table 3, Scandia, Republic County. Test weight measured at harvest moisture. Maturity-check entries are left out.

Twenty-eight of those hybrids also grew at Manhattan, Kansas. Hybrids with higher test weights at one site tended to test higher at the other, while yields lined up less closely between sites. Purdue agronomist Bob Nielsen found a weak relationship between test weight and yield in Kansas and Ohio trials. ⁠[[3]](#source-3)⁠[[8]](#source-8)

When choosing hybrids, Joe looks for staygreen, the ability to keep leaves green late in the season. Leaf disease can cut photosynthesis during grain fill and hurt both yield and test weight. ⁠[[1]](#source-1)⁠[[3]](#source-3)

At 62 lb/bu: 1 hybrid, 162 bu/a, 47 bu/a below the trial average. Yield gaps under 18 bu/a were within this trial’s margin of error (LSD 0.05).

Source: Kansas State University, 2011 Kansas Performance Tests with Corn Hybrids (SRP1055), Table 3, Scandia, Republic County. Test weight measured at harvest moisture. Maturity-check entries are left out.

Twenty-eight of those hybrids also grew at Manhattan, Kansas. Hybrids with higher test weights at one site tended to test higher at the other, while yields lined up less closely between sites. Purdue agronomist Bob Nielsen found a weak relationship between test weight and yield in Kansas and Ohio trials. ⁠[[3]](#source-3)⁠[[8]](#source-8)

When choosing hybrids, Joe looks for staygreen, the ability to keep leaves green late in the season. Leaf disease can cut photosynthesis during grain fill and hurt both yield and test weight. ⁠[[1]](#source-1)⁠[[3]](#source-3)

## How weight and moisture shape your scale ticket

The grade can affect the price per bushel. To figure out how many bushels are on the ticket, start with the load’s weight and moisture. Take a 56,000-pound load that comes in at 20% moisture. It contains 44,800 pounds of dry matter. On a 15.5% moisture basis, that works out to about 53,018 pounds, or 947 market bushels. ⁠[[3]](#source-3)⁠[[4]](#source-4)

That calculation accounts for the weight of water removed. Purdue’s drying guide reports on-farm handling losses of 0.22% to 1.71%, and the shrink factor in your buyer’s contract may include an allowance for those losses. ⁠[[4]](#source-4)

Joe’s sample was already drier than the 15.5% basis in that example. At 14.8% moisture, the same amount of dry matter weighs about 0.8% less than it would at 15.5%. That weight difference is equivalent to about eight market bushels per 1,000. Ask your buyer how they handle deliveries below their base moisture. ⁠[[4]](#source-4)

## Check the yield monitor against a scale

A reliable scale also gives you a way to check your yield monitor as grain conditions change. In Joe’s experience, a well-calibrated mass-flow monitor usually handles a test-weight change of about 5 lb/bu. He estimates that a monitor calibrated on corn at 23% moisture and 52 lb/bu could read 10% to 15% low on corn at 16% moisture and 61 lb/bu. That’s why he recalibrates during harvest when moisture and test weight change. ⁠[[1]](#source-1)

Weigh a calibration load on a reliable grain cart scale, weigh wagon or truck scale and compare it with the monitor reading. Follow the manufacturer’s procedure. If it calls for several loads, run them at different grain flow rates. Check moisture with a separate tester while you’re at it. ⁠[[7]](#source-7)

# What Does a Cover Crop Need to Earn Back?

**Author:** Saurav Das
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0004
**Published:** 2026-04-12T17:23:33.036Z

An acre of rye can start with a $54.40 bill for seed, drilling and spring termination. What happens next depends on the job. You might be buying winter cover, trying to replace a weed pass, or growing feed the cattle can reach. Start with what the cover has to earn back on that acre.

## Run one acre before you price the whole field

This example puts overwintering cereal rye ahead of soybeans. Use $18/ac for seed, $19.05 for custom drilling, $9.35 for a separate spray pass and $8 for herbicide materials. The total is $54.40/ac. Drilling and spraying use 2026 Iowa survey averages. Seed, herbicide and the payment and forage below are examples. [Iowa State custom rates, pp. 2–3](https://www.extension.iastate.edu/agdm/crops/pdf/a3-10.pdf).

title: What Does a Cover Crop Need to Earn Back?
author: Saurav Das
text:
[Iowa State custom rates, pp. 2–3](https://www.extension.iastate.edu/agdm/crops/pdf/a3-10.pdf).

#### Same field, three budgets

| Scenario | Change vs. no cover |
| --- | --- |
| Cover only | −$54.40/ac |
| Cover with a hypothetical $25/ac net payment | −$29.40/ac |
| Same payment and $35/ac additional net forage | +$5.60/ac |

Change in dollars per acre compared with no cover. Soybean yield stays flat in all three scenarios.

The example with a payment and no forage needs another $29.40 per acre. At $11 per net bushel of soybeans, that gap takes 2.7 additional bu/ac to close through crop sales alone. If forage adds $35 after supplements, fencing, water and moves, the example crosses zero at flat yield. Use that combination where grazing fits the field and the payment agreement. [Purdue cover crop decision tool](https://ag.purdue.edu/commercialag/home/resource/2020/12/cover-crop-decision-making-tool/).

### How much yield risk can the payment cover?

At $11 per bushel after the expenses that change with yield, 3 bu/ac moves the soybean budget by $33/ac. The table holds the $54.40 rye cost fixed, assumes zero added forage, and compares the same soybean field with no cover crop. Margins and example payments are in dollars per acre.

author: Saurav Das
text:
The table holds the $54.40 rye cost fixed, assumes zero added forage, and compares the same soybean field with no cover crop. Margins and example payments are in dollars per acre.

#### Rye margin by soybean yield change and net payment

| Yield change | No payment | $25 | $55 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| −3 bu/ac | −$87.40 | −$62.40 | −$32.40 |
| Flat yield | −$54.40 | −$29.40 | +$0.60 |
| +3 bu/ac | −$21.40 | +$3.60 | +$33.60 |

The $25 payment and $35 net grazing value in the earlier example leave $5.60/ac at flat yield. That margin covers only about **half a bushel** of soybean loss. Take away the payment and keep the forage, and the field still needs **$19.40/ac** in extra crop sales or avoided purchases. Run the year after the contract ends before you use the payment to justify a permanent change in the rotation.

[Run this acre with your seed bill, forage value and soybean price](/learn/regenerative-economics#cover-crops).

| −3 bu/ac | −$87.40 | −$62.40 | −$32.40 |
| Flat yield | −$54.40 | −$29.40 | +$0.60 |
| +3 bu/ac | −$21.40 | +$3.60 | +$33.60 |

The $25 payment and $35 net grazing value in the earlier example leave $5.60/ac at flat yield. That margin covers only about **half a bushel** of soybean loss. Take away the payment and keep the forage, and the field still needs **$19.40/ac** in extra crop sales or avoided purchases. Run the year after the contract ends before you use the payment to justify a permanent change in the rotation.

##### Write down when the cash moves

Date the seed and custom bills, then date the payment. When a stand fails or the grazing window closes, budget the replacement feed or rescue work, and check which payment terms still apply.

Adoption is growing, although cover crops still occupy a small share of U.S. cropland. The 2022 Census of Agriculture recorded 17.99 million cover-crop acres, which was 17% more than in 2017 and equal to 4.7% of total cropland. Adoption differs substantially by region because climate, soils, cropping systems, and public programs affect whether a cover crop fits. [USDA Economic Research Service](https://ers.usda.gov/data-products/charts-of-note/chart-detail?chartId=108950).

The economic question begins with the difference between a biological benefit and a cash return. Erosion control, nutrient retention, improved trafficability, forage, and cash-crop yield can all affect value, but the farm may receive them in different years. Costs also vary widely with species, seeding rate, establishment method, termination, and end use.

## What the farm ledgers show after labor and management

EDF and University of Minnesota partners tracked 41 Minnesota farms that reported in all three years from 2022 through 2024. On Southern Minnesota acres, the combined corn-and-cover enterprise came in **$7.77 to $21.89/ac above** regional corn without cover after labor and management. The comparable soybean margins were **$28.06 to $144.39/ac below** regional soybeans without cover. Each annual comparison used 12 to 16 covered enterprises for the crop, alongside a much larger regional benchmark. [EDF and University of Minnesota partners, Tables 6 and 7](https://library.edf.org/AssetLink/6s6awk47yxg1gxrf6f6voqc4e886n332.pdf)

### Southern Minnesota farm margins with cover crops

| Comparison | −$150 · $0 · $150 | $/acre |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2022 corn | · | +$8.20 |
| 2022 soybeans | · | −$144.39 |
| 2023 corn | · | +$7.77 |
| 2023 soybeans | · | −$28.06 |
| 2024 corn | · | +$21.89 |
| 2024 soybeans | · | −$66.32 |

Combined cover and cash-crop net return after labor and management, minus the same crop’s regional average without cover. Land costs, yields and other expenses differed between groups. EDF and University of Minnesota partners, Tables 6 and 7. [[44]](#source-44)

In 2024, the combined corn-and-cover enterprise still lost $34.09/ac after labor and management. The regional corn benchmark lost $55.98/ac, so the comparison was positive despite a loss in both budgets. The cover-crop corn group had lower grain yield and gross receipts. Its combined direct and overhead expenses were about $66/ac lower, with about $78/ac less in land costs. Keep rent and crop insurance receipts on the ledger when comparing two farms. To assess a change on one field, use the same land cost in both budgets. [EDF and University of Minnesota partners, Table 6](https://library.edf.org/AssetLink/6s6awk47yxg1gxrf6f6voqc4e886n332.pdf)

### The benchmark changes the 2025 comparison

The fourth year of data included 144 farms in Minnesota, South Dakota and Wisconsin. The researchers added a benchmark from fields without cover within the participating cohort. On rented land in Northern Minnesota, corn plus cover came in **$38/ac above the area benchmark** and **$8/ac below the cohort’s no-cover fields**, using the report’s rounded values. Those averages cover 13 corn enterprises with cover, 25 without cover in the cohort, and 338 without cover in the area group. [2025 Upper Midwest farm records, Table 4B](https://library.edf.org/AssetLink/rv4h125322o6ib12cxnsh13b2mv3w4b4.pdf)

#### 2025 net returns per acre after labor and management

| Enterprise and land tenure | With cover | Cohort, no cover | Area, no cover |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Southern group, owned corn | −$7 | $85 | $39 |
| Northern Minnesota, rented corn | $13 | $21 | −$25 |
| Southern group, rented soybeans | −$52 | $3 | $20 |

The southern group includes Southern Minnesota, South Dakota and Wisconsin. The 2025 tables group fields by crop, region and tenure. Each group still contains different fields and management histories. A side-by-side comparison on the same farm can hold more of those costs in place. [2025 Upper Midwest farm records, Tables 1B, 4B and 8B](https://library.edf.org/AssetLink/rv4h125322o6ib12cxnsh13b2mv3w4b4.pdf)

In a three-year Minnesota cohort, 41 farms provided financial records every year from 2022 to 2024. Direct cover-crop costs ranged from $14 to $277 per acre, with a $42 median. Intended use matters. The records include covers for soil protection, forage, feed and seed. [EDF and University of Minnesota partners, 2025](https://library.edf.org/AssetLink/6s6awk47yxg1gxrf6f6voqc4e886n332.pdf).

Satellite estimates and farmer surveys give different views of yield. Two field-scale studies estimated small average corn and soybean losses after recent adoption. Some longer-term adopters reported increases. The comparisons below put the study population and years alongside each result.

tion, additional scouting and management, machinery ownership or rental, fencing and water for grazing, and any cash-crop revenue change associated with planting or termination timing. ## What the yield and profitability studies show

#### Why credible studies reach different results

| Source and evidence type | Main result | Important limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deines et al. 2023; satellite-based econometrics | Average yield effects of -5.5% for maize and -3.5% for soybean on fields with at least three years of recent cover-crop use | Study could not observe species, biomass, termination timing, or field-level nutrient management |
| Lobell et al. 2025; more than 100,000 fields | Average yield effects of about -3% for corn and -2% for soybean; planting was delayed 4 and 2.5 days, respectively | Average effects were heterogeneous across weather, soils, and management |
| SARE/CTIC 2015–2016 survey regression | Farmer-reported five-year yield differences of +3% for corn and +4.96% for soybean | Self-reported, self-selected survey data; not a randomized or nationally representative yield trial |
| USDA-ERS ERR-353; national farm survey analysis | No statistically significant aggregate productivity effect for cover crops alone; combined no-till and cover-crop use was associated with higher technical efficiency | Association at farm scale does not isolate the causal return from one practice |

Field estimates, farmer reports and whole-farm budgets measure different outcomes.

The 2025 study adds an important mechanism. It estimated that eliminating cash-crop planting delays would reduce the observed yield penalty by roughly 50% for corn and 90% for soybean. It also found that cover-cropped fields were about half as likely to experience prevented planting during the wet spring of 2019, while dry conditions increased downside risk. [Lobell et al. 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41893-025-01599-5).

##### Build a different budget for each year

Planting and termination costs arrive each year. Put forage, actual changes in purchases, cash-crop yield and any payment in the year they occur. Change the weather or price assumptions to see how the payback moves.

A 2026 study of 100 established reduced-tillage adopters found no statistically significant difference in net income between those who used cover crops and those who did not. A Purdue scenario analysis asks how changes in yield, fertilizer purchases, and incentive payments move the budget. Read them together when deciding what to measure on your own acres. [Pugel et al.](https://acsess.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/agj2.70287) · [Purdue Center for Commercial Agriculture](https://ag.purdue.edu/commercialag/home/resource/2026/06/cover-crop-net-returns-and-soil-health-improvements/).

## Regional evidence: strong signals and large gaps

### Corn Belt

Planting dates and spring soil conditions matter in the Corn Belt. The field-scale studies estimate small average yield penalties after recent adoption, while the farm ledgers show how land costs, forage and payments can move profit even when yield falls. In a field comparison, record when each strip was fit to plant, the cover termination date and the yield and grain moisture you harvested. That makes a delayed planting cost visible in the same budget as the seed bill.

In a field comparison, record when each strip was fit to plant, the cover termination date and the yield and grain moisture you harvested. That makes a delayed planting cost visible in the same budget as the seed bill.

### Great Plains and other water-limited systems

Water competition can dominate the economics. A Colorado Plateau study found an average 48% wheat-yield penalty after fall-planted cover crops and a $176/ha reduction in net returns, which is about $71/acre, in the studied rotations. When the authors assigned forage value to 50% of cover-crop biomass, returns improved enough to reverse the result in some fall-planted treatments. This supports grazing or forage as a potentially important value stream without implying that grazing is the only viable dryland system. [Eash et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecs2.70397).

### Southeast and eastern systems

Comparable multi-farm financial datasets are thinner in the Southeast, so precise regional cost and payback tables are not justified. Longer and wetter cool seasons can support much more legume biomass than colder or drier regions. The Nebraska hairy-vetch studies produced only 364–724 lb of biomass per acre, compared with 2,658–5,076 lb/acre in Maryland and 2,685–4,915 lb/acre in Michigan. The lower Nebraska biomass explains the lower total nitrogen in the crop. Biomass contained 12–29 lb N/acre in Nebraska, 93–160 lb N/acre in Maryland, and 89–161 lb N/acre in Michigan. [Nebraska Extension synthesis](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/2020/how-much-nitrogen-does-my-cover-crop-take-and-when-do-i-get-it-back/).

### Nitrogen available to the next crop

Legumes can add biologically fixed nitrogen, while cereal rye primarily captures soil nitrogen that might otherwise move below the root zone. The amount and timing available to the next crop depend on biomass, the share of legume N derived from fixation, carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, termination, soil moisture, and temperature. Nebraska Extension notes that not all biomass N becomes available to the subsequent crop; high-C:N rye residue can temporarily immobilize soil N. A flat dollar credit based on total biomass N therefore overstates short-term savings. [Nebraska Extension](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/2020/how-much-nitrogen-does-my-cover-crop-take-and-when-do-i-get-it-back/).

### Which pesticide purchases change?

American Farmland Trust analyzed 23 selected row-crop farms using one or more soil-health practices. Nine reduced pesticide costs by $3–$36/acre/year, ten reported no change, and four increased pesticide costs by $6–$29. The farms were selected as “soil health successful,” and many combined cover crops with nutrient management, crop rotation, and reduced tillage, so the results cannot be attributed to cover crops alone. [AFT case-study findings](https://farmland.org/soil-health-case-study-findings).

### Grazing and harvest can replace a feed bill

Iowa farmer Ben Albright measured how much mixed ration he delivered to finishing cattle with access to an adjoining 79-acre field of rye and oats. Across three seasons, Practical Farmers of Iowa estimated a grazing margin of **$15.56/ac without incentives** and **$45.56/ac with cost share and an insurance discount**. The case budget credits feed displaced and charges seed, establishment and additional termination. If your herd needs a new fence or a truck to reach the field, include those added costs. [Practical Farmers of Iowa, Albright feedlot case, Table 2](https://practicalfarmers.org/resources/research-reports/economic-and-soil-health-impacts-of-grazing-cover-crops-in-a-feedlot-system/)

When the alternative is grazing crop residue, charge the cover only for the extra feed it supplies. In a later Practical Farmers of Iowa comparison, estimated added grazing value minus cover costs was +$11.82/ac before soybeans and −$16.30/ac before corn, based on separate groups of reported fields. Fence, water, crop sales and payments sit outside that two-line comparison. [Practical Farmers of Iowa, 2025, Table 4](https://practicalfarmers.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/PFI2025_GrazingFactsheet_Flyer_FINAL-1.pdf).

##### Before adding two payments

Check eligible acres, timing, practice requirements and environmental attribute ownership with both sponsors.

## Two costs that economic summaries often miss

### Cash-crop timing and yield

A one- or two-percent cash-crop yield change can outweigh seed-cost differences. The 2025 field study links much of the average yield penalty to delayed corn and soybean planting. Any economic comparison that excludes cash-crop revenue change is incomplete.

### Herbicide carryover and feed restrictions

Residual herbicides can reduce cover-crop emergence and growth. Injury varies with chemistry, rate, rainfall, temperature, soil and the time between spraying and seeding. Check the product label for restrictions before grazing or harvesting the cover for feed. ## Two costs that economic summaries often miss

### Cash-crop timing and yield

A one- or two-percent cash-crop yield change can outweigh seed-cost differences. The 2025 field study links much of the average yield penalty to delayed corn and soybean planting. Any economic comparison that excludes cash-crop revenue change is incomplete.

### Herbicide carryover and feed restrictions

Residual herbicides can reduce cover-crop emergence and growth. Injury varies with chemistry, rate, rainfall, temperature, soil and the time between spraying and seeding. Check the product label for restrictions before grazing or harvesting the cover for feed. - Start with delivered seed, establishment and termination. Use comparable farm records to check the scale and local quotes to price the field.

# Why a Cover Crop Can Hold More Potassium Than Your Soil Test Shows

**Author:** Soil Health Exchange
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0065
**Published:** 2026-10-24T15:37:05.052Z

In an [October 21 Facebook post](https://www.facebook.com/share/p/16LbndhFxYq/), Joe Ailts of Ailts Agronomy shared a potassium puzzle from his northwest Wisconsin farm. He had seeded a fall mix of sunflower, barley, buckwheat, turnip, and medium red clover after sweet corn in the first week of August. A cover crop biomass test put the potassium in the aboveground growth at 291 lb K₂O per acre, the equivalent of about 485 lb of 0-0-60 potash. The field gets no phosphorus or potassium fertilizer; years of turkey litter built its soil test potassium to around 150 lb per acre.

As Joe put it, “How does that math math?” His post set that question aside to discuss brassica root fungi, which we take up in [What fungi do brassica roots partner with if not mycorrhizae?](https://soilhealthexchange.com/hub/brassica-root-fungi-without-mycorrhizae)

Both numbers can be right, because they count different things. A soil test reads a small, calibrated slice of the field’s potassium. A biomass test counts what the plants pulled from a much larger supply, and most of that potassium returns to the soil within weeks to months.

title: Why a Cover Crop Can Hold More Potassium Than Your Soil Test Shows
author: Soil Health Exchange
text:
A soil test reads a small, calibrated slice of the field’s potassium. A biomass test counts what the plants pulled from a much larger supply, and most of that potassium returns to the soil within weeks to months.

##### The short answer

A routine soil test is an index of plant-available potassium in the plow layer, calibrated to predict whether a crop will respond to potash. It is not an inventory: most soil potassium sits in forms the test does not read, and roots also feed below the sampling depth. A biomass test counts the potassium a cover crop took up, nearly all of it recycled from the field. Use the soil test, sampled consistently, for potash decisions. Use the biomass test to see how much potassium is cycling and what would leave if the cover were harvested.

### Get more field answers like this.

Get practical cover crop and nutrient guidance, plus funding deadlines, in the free Field Memo.

## Start with the units

Put both numbers in the same unit first. Fertilizer labels and most biomass reports use K₂O, the oxide form. Soil tests report elemental potassium (K). One pound of K₂O contains 0.83 lb of K, and muriate of potash is 0-0-60 to 0-0-62, about 60% K₂O ​[[1]](#source-1).

It is not an inventory: most soil potassium sits in forms the test does not read, and roots also feed below the sampling depth. A biomass test counts the potassium a cover crop took up, nearly all of it recycled from the field. Use the soil test, sampled consistently, for potash decisions. Use the biomass test to see how much potassium is cycling and what would leave if the cover were harvested.

## Start with the units

Put both numbers in the same unit first. Fertilizer labels and most biomass reports use K₂O, the oxide form. Soil tests report elemental potassium (K). One pound of K₂O contains 0.83 lb of K, and muriate of potash is 0-0-60 to 0-0-62, about 60% K₂O ​[[1]](#source-1).

## A soil test is a gauge, not an inventory

A routine soil test estimates the potassium in soil water and on the exchange sites of clay and organic matter, the forms a crop can draw on right away ​[[2]](#source-2). UW describes phosphorus and potassium tests as indexes of available nutrients. Their value comes from calibration: field trials tie each test range to the chance that a crop will respond to potash. In Wisconsin, a Very Low potassium test carries a better than 90% probability of a yield increase from added potassium, an Optimum test 30–60%, and a High test 5–30% ​[[1]](#source-1). UW Extension is updating its corn and soybean ranges for 2026, so check the current edition when you read a report ​[[17]](#source-17).

That design explains the gap. Most of a soil’s potassium is invisible to the test. Total potassium in many soils exceeds 20,000 ppm, about 40,000 lb per acre in the top 6 inches by the standard conversion, and 90–98% of it is held in minerals such as feldspars and micas ​[[3]](#source-3)​[[4]](#source-4). Between those minerals and the exchange sites sits a fixed, slowly available pool that routine tests do not measure. It stays in balance with the exchangeable pool and releases some potassium during the season, though a crop draws little of it in a single year ​[[3]](#source-3).

#### Where soil potassium sits

| Pool | Share of total soil K | Read by a routine soil test? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solution K | A small fraction; 1–3% of exchangeable K | Yes |
| Exchangeable K | 1–2% | Yes |
| Non-exchangeable (fixed) K | 1–2% | No; released slowly, little within one season |
| Mineral K | 90–98% | No; released over decades as minerals weather |

Wisconsin’s own guidelines show how much potassium slips out of the test’s view. Raising soil test potassium by 1 ppm takes about 5 to 7 lb K₂O per acre, depending on soil group ​[[1]](#source-1). On paper, 1 ppm in a 6-inch layer is only about 2.4 lb K₂O. Much of the rest moves into pools the test does not read.

Roots also feed below the sample. UW calibrations use samples taken to plow depth, at least 6 inches ​[[1]](#source-1). Across 34 German field trials, soil below 30 cm (12 inches) supplied an average of 34% of the potassium taken up by spring wheat, ranging from 9 to 70%, and the subsoil share was largest where topsoil potassium was lowest ​[[5]](#source-5).

## What a biomass test counts

A cover crop biomass test multiplies two measurements: dry matter per acre, from plants clipped inside a frame of known size ​[[6]](#source-6), and the potassium concentration of that tissue, from a lab analysis. The result is the potassium in the sampled growth on the day it was cut. Fast-growing fall species take up a lot of it. In a Swiss trial of 20 cover crops sown in early August and sampled 85 days later without fertilizer, shoots averaged 3.07% K and held the equivalent of about 192 lb K₂O per acre. Daikon radish shoots held about 285 lb K₂O-equivalent per acre, with about 160 more in the roots. Sunflower shoots held about 277, turnip rape (a leafy Brassica rapa) about 180, and buckwheat about 32 ​[[7]](#source-7). So 291 lb K₂O is a large result, but it sits within measured values for a vigorous, early-seeded stand. It equals about 242 lb K. By simple arithmetic, a stand of roughly 5,400 to 8,000 lb of dry matter per acre would hold that much at 3–4.5% K. Oat and brassica mixes planted from mid-August to early September in Nebraska produced 2,200 to 4,200 lb of dry matter per acre ​[[8]](#source-8), and forage turnip can yield 3 to 4 tons of dry matter about 90 days after planting ​[[9]](#source-9). Softball-size turnips point to a heavy stand. Crops such as alfalfa take up more potassium than they need when supply is high, a pattern called luxury consumption ​[[10]](#source-10). More broadly, high soil potassium raises potassium in vegetative tissue, so residue on well-supplied ground carries more potassium than average values suggest ​[[11]](#source-11). Two sampling details move the number.

## Where that potassium goes next

Potassium in plant tissue is not built into organic compounds; it stays dissolved in the plant’s water ​[[12]](#source-12). Once the turnips winter-kill and break down, rain and snowmelt wash it out. In field studies in Brazil and Iowa, up to 50–60% of the potassium in crop and cover crop straw washed out within about six weeks of termination ​[[11]](#source-11). In a Brazilian study, fodder radish residue released potassium faster than any other nutrient: 95% within 45 days, with release fastest around day 15 ​[[13]](#source-13). In Iowa, most of the potassium in corn and soybean residue left before December, little more left while the soil was frozen, and by early April the residue still held 31% of corn’s and 12% of soybean’s vegetative potassium ​[[14]](#source-14). Nearly all of that potassium lands back on the soil surface. Among the nutrients compared in more than 10,000 soil profiles worldwide, phosphorus and potassium were the most concentrated near the surface, which the researchers attribute to plants pulling them up and returning them in litter ​[[15]](#source-15). A deep-rooted cover crop can lift some potassium from below the sampling depth and from slowly available forms ​[[11]](#source-11). Unless the cover is hauled off as forage, nearly all of its potassium stays in the field, apart from some leaching on sandy soils ​[[2]](#source-2); the cover crop moves it. The soil test picks up part of that return, unevenly. In Iowa, the change in soil test potassium between harvest and early April tracked the potassium lost from crop residue, with wide scatter, and the researchers called early fall a very unstable time to sample ​[[14]](#source-14).

author: Soil Health Exchange
text:
In Iowa, the change in soil test potassium between harvest and early April tracked the potassium lost from crop residue, with wide scatter, and the researchers called early fall a very unstable time to sample [[14]](#source-14).

In a Wisconsin study, spring tests ran higher than fall at only one of five sites ​[[11]](#source-11). Sample at the same time of year, every time ​[[1]](#source-1). SHE’s [fall soil sampling guide](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/fall-soil-sampling-what-to-test-when-to-sample-how-to-use-results) covers timing, depth, and consistency.

## What leaves the field

A farm’s potassium balance comes down to what comes in (litter and fertilizer) and what leaves (harvested crops, hay, and forage). UW figures sweet corn removal at 6 lb K₂O per ton of fresh harvest ​[[1]](#source-1), so every 5 tons hauled off removes about 30 lb K₂O. Grazing returns most of the potassium in a cover: grazing animals retain less than 15% of the phosphorus and potassium they eat, and most potassium leaves the animal in urine ​[[16]](#source-16). Chopping and hauling the cover as forage removes the potassium in the harvested growth.

Turkey litter built this field’s reserve. UW book values put turkey litter at 31 lb K₂O per ton, with 80% credited as available in the first year ​[[1]](#source-1). At book value, matching the 291 lb K₂O in the cover crop would take about 9 tons of litter per acre on a total-K₂O basis. Without new inputs, each harvest draws that reserve down a little. The cover crop does not change the direction; it changes where the potassium sits for a few months.

## Back to the field

The math works. The turnips and their companions pulled close to 300 lb K₂O into their aboveground growth, drawing on exchangeable potassium, the slowly released reserve, and soil below the probe. The soil test gave a calibrated reading of the small pool it was built to measure. Each number is useful when it answers its own question.

For next season, keep four records together:

1. **The soil report:** confirm the units and extraction method, and sample at the same time and depth as before.
2. **The biomass sample:** note the frame size, number of frames, and whether turnip bulbs were included.
3. **The potassium ledger:** litter or fertilizer applied, and crops or forage hauled off.
4. **The trend:** compare each new soil test with the last two or three.

That ledger, more than either single number, tells you whether the field’s potassium bank is holding.

That ledger, more than either single number, tells you whether the field’s potassium bank is holding.

# What Makes Cover Crops Work? Lessons from 657 Farmers

**Author:** Soil Health Exchange
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0101
**Published:** 2026-09-04T16:17:38.100Z

##### The bottom line

The 657 submissions provide a detailed snapshot of engaged farmers rather than a single verdict on cover crops. Question-level sample sizes vary because respondents could skip items and incomplete surveys were retained when answers were usable. Within this group, cover-crop acres kept growing, mixtures were common, cereal rye dominated reported species acreage, yield differences were modest, and weather, timing, grazing, weed control, and economics shaped field-level decisions.

The most useful finding in the 2026 National Cover Crop Survey appears before any yield chart: cover crops are not a permanent yes-or-no identity. Farmers make the decision again for each field and season. A late harvest can close the planting window. A dry forecast can make a living cover feel too costly in water. Grazing can turn biomass into feed. A good rye stand can change the weed-control calculation. [1][[1]](#source-1)

So the headline number—657 participating farmers—is only the beginning. Of the 653 people who answered the use question, 68% planted cover crops every year, 16.4% used them in some years, 8% had used them previously, and 7.7% had never used them. Even among farmers currently planting cover crops, 60.8% said there were years when they left some fields without a cover crop. [1][[1]](#source-1)

The online survey ran from March 12 through April 4, 2026 and received 657 submissions from farmers in 46 states and Puerto Rico. Of those, 533 were complete and 120 were incomplete. That design explains the changing denominators. The report begins with 657 total submissions, uses n=655 for the farm-type profile, n=653 for the cover-crop-use and total-acreage questions, n=645 for age, n=640 for crops grown, and n=633 for location. These are not competing totals; each n is the number of usable answers for that question. Click to expand

The respondent pool crossed several kinds of agriculture. About two-thirds included commodity crops in their farm description, while specialty-crop and livestock operations were also well represented. That mix is useful because the value of a cover crop can show up differently—as row-crop residue and nutrient capture, vegetable-system rotation, livestock feed, or some combination of those jobs. [1][[1]](#source-1)

The survey was promoted through the organizers’ contact lists, agricultural media, associations, press releases, and social media. The resulting group leaned Midwestern and was more conservation-oriented than the general farm population: 44.4% reported continuous no-till, while 45.9% reported rotational no-till, reduced tillage, strip-till, or vertical tillage. That respondent profile is part of the context for interpreting the experience reported here. [1][[1]](#source-1)

##### How to read the evidence

The yield, weed-control, moisture, and profit figures are farmer-reported comparisons. They capture the experience of the respondents, but they do not isolate the effect of cover crops from soils, weather, rotation, fertility, planting date, termination, or management skill. The report is strongest as a description of this respondent group and the decisions they faced; national prevalence and causal effects require different study designs.

Editorially, the percentages are most useful as prompts for a field decision: Which benefits matter here? Which constraints are likely to decide the outcome? What would we measure before expanding the practice?

## Experienced farmers were expanding their cover-crop acres

Nearly half of the farmers who answered the experience question had planted cover crops for at least 10 years. Within this experienced and self-selected group, average cover-crop acreage rose from 313 acres in 2021 to 397 acres in 2025. Respondents anticipated an average of 416 acres in fall 2026. ## Mixtures were mainstream, but cereal rye dominated the acreage

Among 489 farmers currently planting cover crops who answered the mix question, 25.9% planted only single-species covers, 32.3% planted only mixes, and 41.7% used both approaches in different situations. Put another way, 74% used a mixture at least sometimes. The report also found a practical seasonal distinction: cool-season mixes generally contained two or three species, while warm-season mixes often contained four or more. [1][[1]](#source-1)

Cereal rye remained the workhorse. Among 439 farmers reporting species acres for fall 2025, rye appeared on 110,778 acres—more than three times the 33,042 acres reported for radishes. Oats, rapeseed or canola, turnips, winter wheat, crimson clover, and hairy vetch formed the next tier. [1][[1]](#source-1)

##### Take-home message

The practice described here was flexible: a single species on one field, a mix on another, more acres over time, but not every field every year. Cereal rye was the dominant workhorse, while mixtures let farmers combine jobs or adapt to a different planting window. That is a more useful picture than treating cover crops as one uniform practice.

Cereal rye remained the workhorse. Among 439 farmers reporting species acres for fall 2025, rye appeared on 110,778 acres—more than three times the 33,042 acres reported for radishes. Oats, rapeseed or canola, turnips, winter wheat, crimson clover, and hairy vetch formed the next tier. [1][[1]](#source-1)

##### Take-home message

The practice described here was flexible: a single species on one field, a mix on another, more acres over time, but not every field every year. Cereal rye was the dominant workhorse, while mixtures let farmers combine jobs or adapt to a different planting window. That is a more useful picture than treating cover crops as one uniform practice.

## Reported yield gains were positive, but small

Farmers compared 2025 cash-crop yields on similar land with and without a cover crop in 2024. Corn respondents reported a mean of 200 bushels per acre after a cover crop and 196.5 without one—a 3.5-bushel or 1.8% difference. A separate challenges question pointed in the same direction. Weather led at 57%, followed by timing conflicts at 42.4%, stand establishment at 38.2%, and unfavorable economics at 28% among 453 respondents. Those are management and fit constraints, not simply attitude.

A field skipped after a late harvest is different from a practice rejected on principle. Measure adoption by where a cover crop fits, what job it performs, and whether the farmer returns to it—not only by whether every acre was planted every year.

## Grazing changed the economic equation—but many could not price it

About 35% of 446 farmers currently planting cover crops reported grazing, harvesting the crop for forage, or doing both. Among 136 graziers, 84.6% selected lower feed costs as a benefit, 70.6% selected improved soil health, and 47.1% selected improved livestock performance. [1][[1]](#source-1)

Figure

author: Soil Health Exchange
text:
Among 136 graziers, 84.6% selected lower feed costs as a benefit, 70.6% selected improved soil health, and 47.1% selected improved livestock performance. [1][[1]](#source-1) Figure

#### Reported net-profit effect of grazing cover crops

Profit gain44.5 %

No impact11.7 %

Profit reduction1.5 %

Unable to quantify42.3 %

Calculated from the report’s counts for all respondents (n=137): 61 reported a gain, 16 no impact, 2 a reduction, and 58 were unsure. Source: 2026 National Cover Crop Survey, p. 54.

Click to expand

The report emphasizes that 77% of respondents who could quantify the result reported a gain: 61 of the 79 who chose gain, no impact, or reduction. But 42.3% of the full group was unsure. Both numbers matter. Grazing may create one of the clearest routes to near-term value, while fencing, water, labor, and incomplete records make that value hard to measure.

Infrastructure is the constraint behind the opportunity. Among farmers who used cover crops without grazing them and were interested or maybe interested in grazing, 81.6% said they would need fencing and 58.9% said they would need water infrastructure.

This is an intention, not a measured retention rate, and the survey cannot prove that payments caused continued use. Still, it supports a practical program-design idea: give farmers enough seasons to learn establishment and termination, observe benefits, and adapt the practice. The report recommends at least three years, flexible rules, and a smoother enrollment process.

Responses from farmers who had stopped planting cover crops add context. Only 21.6% of the 51 farmers in this group had ever received an incentive. All 10 who answered the follow-up said nothing about the incentive program caused them to stop. Their leading reasons were cash-crop yield concerns, unfavorable economics, weather, timing, and stand establishment.

## Most farmers who had never planted cover crops were open to trying them

The sample of farmers who had never planted cover crops was small, but it points toward a reachable group. Of 49 respondents who had never planted a cover crop, 18.4% said they would definitely consider trying one, 20.4% said probably, and 34.7% said maybe. Together, 73.5% were at least open to the idea. The goal is not to force a cover crop onto every field. It is to make the decision clear enough that you can repeat what worked—and diagnose what did not.

#### A field-level cover-crop fit check

| Decision | Signal from the survey | What to settle before seeding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can it establish? | Late harvest, weather, and poor stands drove many skipped acres | Realistic planting date, species, method, seed-to-soil contact, and fallback if the window closes |
| What job pays first? | Average yield gains were modest; weed control and forage created clearer near-term value for some | Primary goal, expected cost saving or revenue, and the record needed to verify it |
| What crop follows? | Results varied with rotation, moisture, nitrogen, and planting-green management | Cash-crop date, termination trigger, planter setup, nitrogen plan, and rescue option |
| Can livestock use it? | Feed savings were common, but fencing and water limited grazing | Animals, stocking plan, water, fencing, labor, pesticide restrictions, and how value will be recorded |
| Does cost share fit? | Most recipients intended to continue, while farmers who had never used cover crops wanted first-year risk reduced | Eligibility before planting, contract length, management flexibility, payment timing, and the post-payment plan |
| What would make us pause? | Intermittent use was common and often operational | A written no-plant threshold for date, moisture, labor, seed cost, or the following crop |

Use local Extension, NRCS, crop-insurance, and pesticide-label guidance to turn these questions into a field plan.

If you are trying cover crops, start with one job and one fair comparison. Record the planting date, seed and application cost, stand, termination, field operations, cash-crop yield, herbicide and fertility changes, and any forage value. Compare it with a genuinely similar field or strip. One season may reveal an establishment problem; several seasons are usually needed to judge resilience, soil change, and management learning.

##### Build the plan around the field

The Soil Health Exchange Cover Crop Lab can compare species and mixtures by location, planting window, rotation, goal, and termination preference. Use it to create a starting plan, then confirm rates, dates, herbicide restrictions, insurance rules, and termination guidance locally.

[Build a field-specific starting plan in the Cover Crop Lab](https://soilhealthexchange.com/tools/cover-crop-selector).

## What this report gives us

The survey does not settle whether cover crops pay everywhere. It offers something more useful: a clearer picture of the conditions under which farmers expand them, pause them, graze them, plant into them, or consider trying again.

title: Cover Crops in Dryland Systems: When the Water Trade-off Is Worth It and When It Isn't
author: Tushar Kumar, Ph.D.
text:
The honest decision is local: drive it off subsoil moisture and a termination trigger, not a blanket rule.

## The question dryland farmers actually ask

Nobody farming on 14 inches of rain needs to be convinced that water matters. So when cover crops started showing up in every extension newsletter and agronomist conversation over the past decade, the first question dryland producers asked was reasonable: where does that water go?

It goes into the cover crop. That is not a controversial claim. What is contested — and what the research has only recently started to sort out — is whether that loss is recoverable, manageable, or simply a cost that does not pencil out in dry country.

Site-specific dryland data remained thin and geographically patchy well into the 2010s. There were exceptions — USDA-ARS at Akron, Colorado published rigorous central Great Plains legume-fallow water and yield numbers back in 2005 [3][[3]](#source-3), and Kansas State ran dryland trials going back to 2006 [5][[5]](#source-5) — but for most of that window, what farmers were told came from humid-climate trials receiving 30 or 40 inches of annual rainfall, applied to regions getting less than half that. A 2022 meta-analysis of dryland cover-cropping went further, estimating that you need roughly 700 mm — about 27 inches — of annual precipitation before a cover crop reliably avoids a yield penalty in temperate drylands, and warning against universal promotion of the practice in low-rainfall areas [2][[2]](#source-2). These are not fringe findings. They are the current state of the evidence.

This article works through what that evidence actually says, where the management levers are, and what an honest decision looks like for a wheat-fallow producer in the Great Plains.

## What the water math looks like

A cover crop established after wheat harvest in a dryland system will use stored soil moisture from the moment it germinates. How much depends on species, stand density, and — most importantly — when you terminate it. The cleanest measured numbers come from USDA-ARS at Akron, Colorado, where spring legume green fallow reduced soil water at wheat planting by 55 mm (about 2.2 inches) with early termination and 104 mm (about 4.1 inches) with late termination, relative to conventional-till fallow [3][[3]](#source-3).

#### Table 1

| Termination timing | Measured soil water reduction at wheat planting vs fallow | Yield context | Source / site |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Early-terminated legume (early June) | 55 mm (~2.2 in) | Est. ~13 bu/ac loss if you apply the 5.94 bu/ac-per-inch slope from [6] — author calculation, not measured | Akron, CO — Weld silt loam [3]; MAP ~421 mm per LTAR site [11] |
| Late-terminated legume (late June–July) | 104 mm (~4.1 in) | Est. ~24 bu/ac on the same 5.94 slope — an upper-bound illustration only; can exceed realized dryland yields in dry years | Akron, CO [3]; slope from [6] |
| 6-yr avg, pea green fallow vs fallow | 84 mm lower (only 74% of fallow's available water retained) | Wheat yield reduced vs fallow in every comparison | Akron, CO [3] |
| Delay termination +32 days (Jun 12 → Jul 13) | Additional depletion | Additional ~12 bu/ac wheat loss (measured) | Nielsen & Vigil via UNL CropWatch [6] |
| Pulse/oilseed alternatives to fallow (Grant, NE) | 1.7 in (field pea) / 1.9 in (chickpea) / 2.2 in (soybean) | 6 / 16 / 36 bu/ac wheat loss; ~11.76 bu/ac per inch (measured) | Grant, NE — Kuma silt loam [6] |

Measured soil water depletion in dryland wheat systems, with yield context. The Akron legume rows give measured water reductions [[3]](#source-3); the ~13 and ~24 bu/ac figures in the legume rows are author calculations using the 5.94 bu/ac-per-inch slope reported by UNL CropWatch [[6]](#source-6), not measured penalties from [[3]](#source-3) — and [[3]](#source-3) explicitly found the yield-water relationship varies year to year, so treat them as illustrative. CropWatch [[6]](#source-6) in fact reports two Akron slopes (5.94 and 4.72 bu/ac/in). Akron MAP (~421 mm) is from the Akron LTAR climate record [[11]](#source-11), not [[3]](#source-3). The Grant, NE and +32-day rows are measured. Note: the Akron data is for spring legumes (pea, lentil, vetch), not cereal rye. Sources: Nielsen & Vigil 2005 [[3]](#source-3); UNL CropWatch [[6]](#source-6); Akron LTAR [[11]](#source-11). The early termination row is where most viable dryland cover crop management sits — but "a light rain event" undersells it. At Akron, even early-killed legumes cost 2.2 inches of stored water, closer to a substantial rain than a sprinkle [3][[3]](#source-3). A cover left to flower costs nearly double that, the equivalent of a significant portion of your entire stored profile. And the yield penalty per inch is not universal: UNL CropWatch reports it ran about 5.94 bu/ac per inch in the Akron regression — though CropWatch gives a second Akron slope of 4.72 bu/ac per inch as well — versus 11.76 bu/ac per inch at Grant, NE [6][[6]](#source-6).

##### For readers in India's rainfed belt

This trade-off is not a niche US concern. Rainfed farming covers roughly half of India's net sown area — about 70 of 140 million hectares — and produces nearly 90% of millets, 80% of oilseeds and pulses, and 60% of cereals (figures from a secondary government-summary source [[8]](#source-8)). On the semi-arid Deccan, the dominant Vertisols (black cotton soils) are often left fallow in the rainy kharif season because of waterlogging, and green-manure crops are studied there to lift soil carbon and moisture storage [[9]](#source-9). To my eye that is the inverse of the Great Plains stored-moisture problem — too much water at the wrong time rather than too little — but it lands on the same fallow-versus-cover decision; that framing is my own, not source [[9]](#source-9)'s. India's analogue to US extension dryland networks is ICAR's All India Coordinated Research Project on Dryland Agriculture, running since about 1970 [[10]](#source-10).

## The termination trigger approach

Several producers in central Kansas and western Nebraska have moved away from a fixed termination date toward a soil moisture threshold. The logic is simple: in a wet spring, the cover crop water cost is recoverable. In a dry spring, it is not. So the termination decision should be conditional on what the soil profile actually holds. The measured cost of getting this wrong is concrete — delaying termination 32 days at Akron added roughly 12 bu/ac of wheat loss [6][[6]](#source-6).

A workable rule reported by producers in on-farm network interviews: if April 1 soil moisture at 18–24 inch depth is below your site-specific field capacity threshold, terminate within the week regardless of cover crop growth stage. If moisture is adequate, allow another 2 to 3 weeks of growth before terminating. (This is a producer-reported heuristic, not a controlled-trial protocol — treat it as a starting point to calibrate, not a published recommendation.)

This is not a complicated system. It requires a soil probe and a threshold number calibrated to your field — typically developed after one or two seasons of measurement alongside yield data. The yield-versus-water relationship that makes it work is real and well documented: wheat yields at Akron tracked closely with available soil water, and the penalty scales with the water deficit at planting, anywhere from about 6 to 12 bu/ac per inch depending on site [3][[3]](#source-3)[6][[6]](#source-6). There is no clean binned-quartile yield chart to put behind that relationship in the dryland record I could locate, so take it as directional — the slope is real, but it is site- and year-variable, not a fixed set of quartile bars.

## Species selection for dry systems

Not all cover crops carry the same water cost. Winter annuals generally use less water than summer annuals in the same growth period, but summer annuals placed in the fallow year — rather than the cropping year — sidestep the competition problem entirely.

Several producers in central Kansas and western Nebraska have moved away from a fixed termination date toward a soil moisture threshold. The logic is simple: in a wet spring, the cover crop water cost is recoverable. In a dry spring, it is not. So the termination decision should be conditional on what the soil profile actually holds. The measured cost of getting this wrong is concrete — delaying termination 32 days at Akron added roughly 12 bu/ac of wheat loss [6][[6]](#source-6).

A workable rule reported by producers in on-farm network interviews: if April 1 soil moisture at 18–24 inch depth is below your site-specific field capacity threshold, terminate within the week regardless of cover crop growth stage. If moisture is adequate, allow another 2 to 3 weeks of growth before terminating. (This is a producer-reported heuristic, not a controlled-trial protocol — treat it as a starting point to calibrate, not a published recommendation.)

This is not a complicated system. It requires a soil probe and a threshold number calibrated to your field — typically developed after one or two seasons of measurement alongside yield data. The yield-versus-water relationship that makes it work is real and well documented: wheat yields at Akron tracked closely with available soil water, and the penalty scales with the water deficit at planting, anywhere from about 6 to 12 bu/ac per inch depending on site [3][[3]](#source-3)[6][[6]](#source-6). There is no clean binned-quartile yield chart to put behind that relationship in the dryland record I could locate, so take it as directional — the slope is real, but it is site- and year-variable, not a fixed set of quartile bars.

## Species selection for dry systems

Not all cover crops carry the same water cost. Winter annuals generally use less water than summer annuals in the same growth period, but summer annuals placed in the fallow year — rather than the cropping year — sidestep the competition problem entirely.

The 2–4 inch soil-water reduction is Kahl et al. 2022 (Idaho) and the <1.5 dry tons/ac over 8 years is Dagati & Miller 2020 (Montana) — two separate studies, both reported in the WSU-CSANR synthesis [[4]](#source-4), not a single Montana trial. Placing a summer annual in the fallow year means the cover is competing for summer rain that would otherwise be lost to evaporation from bare soil. Kansas State dryland trials have shown improved soil aggregate stability after dryland covers, though the clearest soil-health gains in that record come from grazed systems rather than from cover-fallow alone, and a standalone infiltration improvement is less firmly established [5][[5]](#source-5). ## Grazing changes the calculus

If livestock are part of the operation — or if a grazing agreement is available — the water cost of a cover crop becomes a revenue question rather than a pure loss.

A cereal rye cover grazed and then terminated returns roughly the same moisture profile as an early-terminated ungrazed stand, but the forage offsets the input cost. The Kansas State dryland work puts hard numbers on it: across years, growing a cover ahead of wheat cut yield from 51.9 bu/ac under chemical fallow to 41.8 bu/ac [5][[5]](#source-5), yet net returns rose between 26% and 240% when the cover was grazed or harvested for forage rather than left standing — a figure from the K-State extension reporting on that study [12][[12]](#source-12). In producer-reported on-farm networks across Kansas and Nebraska, this is the most consistently profitable cover crop model in dryland settings under 15 inches of rainfall — an anecdotal generalization, offered as such, not a controlled-trial result.

##### The grazing exception

Below 15 inches, grazing or forage is usually what flips a dryland cover crop from a water cost to a positive return. In the K-State western Kansas dryland study, wheat fell from 51.9 to 41.8 bu/ac when a cover preceded it [[5]](#source-5), yet net returns rose 26% to 240% when that cover was grazed or hayed rather than left standing [[12]](#source-12). Without cattle, the offset disappears and the decision reverts to the rainfall-zone table.

## What the multi-year data shows

Single-season yield comparisons miss the point of cover crops in dryland systems. The measurable benefits — soil organic matter, infiltration rate, surface crusting reduction — accumulate over years, not over one growing season.

The multi-year picture is cautiously encouraging only where the economics already work. In Kansas State's western dryland trials, grazed cover crops maintained soil-health gains while non-grazed covers more often carried a net water and yield cost [5][[5]](#source-5). A clean table of net outcomes binned by years of adoption — with, say, a 15-inch, five-year cutoff — would be useful, but no located dataset tabulates outcomes that way. The defensible statement is narrower: multi-year benefits in dryland concentrate where rainfall is higher or livestock are integrated, and the data below 15 inches remains too sparse for confident conclusions.

## Common mistakes

Three patterns show up consistently when dryland cover crops fail:

- Using humid-climate seeding rates. Higher seeding rates mean more biomass, more water use, and a bigger moisture deficit at termination. Dryland rates should be 30 to 50 percent below standard recommendations.
- Letting the cover run to maximize residue. Residue benefits are real, but they accumulate over years. A dense, late-terminated cover in a dry spring can cost more in yield than several years of residue benefit will recover — recall the jump from 2.2 to 4.1 inches of measured depletion between early and late kill at Akron [3][[3]](#source-3).
- Treating the first year as proof of concept. One good year does not validate the system; one bad year does not invalidate it. The decision needs at least three years of data and a management protocol that includes an exit rule for dry springs.

## Where the evidence gaps are

The western US dryland cover crop dataset is still thin enough that confident regional recommendations are not yet possible for many locations. A 2023 regional survey of 894 growers across 13 western states documented strong interest but persistent uncertainty about benefits and barriers under dryland conditions [7][[7]](#source-7). Soil texture, subsoil water-holding capacity, and local precipitation distribution all affect outcomes in ways that site-specific trial data has not yet captured.

Advice that works for a silty clay loam in central Kansas may not transfer to a sandy loam in western Nebraska receiving the same annual rainfall — the 5.94 versus 11.76 bu/ac-per-inch gap between Akron and Grant is exactly this problem made numeric [6][[6]](#source-6). The general principles in this article hold across the region, but the specific numbers — threshold moisture levels, biomass targets, yield expectations — need local calibration.

## An honest read

The water concern is legitimate. Anyone telling you otherwise has not farmed under 14 inches.

"Cover crops cost water" is not the same claim as "cover crops are not worth it in dryland," and running them together has pushed some farmers away from a practice that might have worked differently with modified management. For most operations under 13 inches, the answer is probably no — not without a grazing or forage component [5][[5]](#source-5)[12][[12]](#source-12). For operations between roughly 14 and 18 inches with flexibility in termination timing, the evidence is only beginning to supply the site-specific numbers needed to know, and the meta-analytic threshold to fully avoid a yield penalty sits higher still, near 700 mm — about 27 inches [2][[2]](#source-2). That ambiguity is uncomfortable, but it is honest.

# Crop Rotation Is a System, Not a List

**Author:** Soil Health Exchange
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0096
**Published:** 2026-08-31T05:01:27.333Z

##### The bottom line

A rotation is a timed management system, not a list of crop names. Strong rotations create deliberate contrasts in host status, planting and harvest dates, rooting, residue, nitrogen demand and supply, water use, and control tactics—while remaining marketable and operable. Research supports meaningful gains in yield resilience, weed suppression, soil carbon and microbial biomass, but the result depends on the baseline, crops, climate, rotation age, and management package. Evaluate the entire cycle per acre-year, identify the weakest transition, and test a candidate rotation with all phases represented before treating it as a recommendation.

Two rotations can each contain four crops and still behave very differently. One may alternate cool- and warm-season crops, grasses and broadleaves, shallow and deep roots, high- and low-residue phases, and several control windows. The other may repeat the same planting window, host family, herbicide pressure, rooting zone, and peak water demand under different crop names. The useful difference is the contrast each phase creates.

##### Begin with what each phase changes

Instead of stopping at “How many crops are in the rotation?”, ask: What problem does each phase solve? What new risk could it create? What conditions will it leave for the crop that follows?

## Why rotation design matters more than crop count

Crop richness is easy to count, so it often becomes a stand-in for rotation quality. But count ignores order, duration, crop function, timing, and management. A cereal followed by another cereal may carry a very different pathogen, weed, nitrogen, and residue legacy than a cereal followed by a pulse, forage, or non-host broadleaf. Reversing two crops can also change fall planting opportunity, soil-water carryover, herbicide plant-back, and the yield of the next crop.

Recent long-term evidence makes the same point statistically. Across 32 European and North American experiments, functional richness—the number of meaningfully different crop functional groups—was more consistently associated with climate resilience than species count alone. Yet a separate 16-year South Dakota experiment found that the most stabilizing weather niches did not map neatly onto familiar labels such as cool versus warm season or grass versus legume. Functional groups are therefore a better starting hypothesis than raw crop count, not a substitute for local performance data. ⁠[[2]](#source-2)⁠[[4]](#source-4)

#### Five different things often hidden inside the word diversity

| Dimension | What it measures | What it can miss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Species richness | Number of crop species in the cycle | Whether crops perform similar functions or occupy the same management window |
| Functional richness | Contrast among cereals, legumes, oilseeds, root crops, forages, covers, and other roles | Local weather response, marketability, and exact crop sequence |
| Temporal diversity | Variation in planting, canopy, harvest, and fallow periods | Whether the calendar is operationally realistic |
| Sequence diversity | Which crop follows which, and how long a host or control tactic is absent | Longer-term effects beyond the immediate next crop |
| Management diversity | Changes in fertility, tillage, herbicides, cultivation, grazing, manure, and harvest | Whether the benefit came from crop choice, management, or the combined system |

A defensible rotation description reports all five dimensions instead of reducing the design to one crop count.

## What long-term studies show

Rotation research uses different comparisons: monoculture versus any rotation, cereal-only versus functionally richer rotations, or a standard two-crop rotation versus a longer one. It also reports different outcomes: the yield of one crop, average output across a complete cycle, gross crop value, net return, or soil properties. “Rotation increased yield 20%” is incomplete. Which crop, following what crop, compared with what sequence, over how many years, under what nitrogen and water conditions? The denominator is part of the result.

## A rotation works by changing legacies

Every crop leaves more than residue. It changes water extraction, nitrogen supply and demand, the timing and depth of roots, pathogen and insect hosts, the weed cohorts that set seed, soil cover, traffic, tillage, and the dates available for the next operation. Those changes are crop legacies. Rotation design is the arrangement of legacies so that one phase prepares the next without creating an unacceptable problem later in the cycle.

title: Crop Rotation Is a System, Not a List
author: Soil Health Exchange
text:
Those changes are crop legacies. Rotation design is the arrangement of legacies so that one phase prepares the next without creating an unacceptable problem later in the cycle.

#### The legacy ledger: what each crop gives, takes, and shifts

| Legacy | Questions before placing a crop | What to verify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Host legacy | Does it host the same pathogen, nematode, insect, or volunteer problem as the next crop? | Crop- and pathogen-specific host range; required non-host interval; volunteer and weed hosts |
| Nitrogen legacy | Does it fix N, scavenge N, immobilize N, or demand early available N? | Biomass, residue C:N, termination or harvest timing, local N-credit guidance |
| Water legacy | How much water remains, and at what depth, for the next phase? | Stored soil water, rooting depth, fallow recharge, likely seasonal rainfall |
| Residue legacy | Will residue protect the surface, cool the seed zone, tie up N, or interfere with establishment? | Residue amount and distribution, planter capacity, row warming and seed placement |
| Weed legacy | Which emergence cohorts and control tactics does this phase select? | Planting-date shift, canopy timing, harvest date, survivors, seed return, herbicide sites of action |
| Soil-structure legacy | Does the phase add roots and cover, or require traffic and disturbance under vulnerable conditions? | Root architecture, harvest load, grazing pressure, compaction risk, erosion window |
| Operational legacy | Does this crop create or remove time for manure, drainage, lime, cover crops, or harvest? | Labor and machinery peaks, contractor availability, storage, drying, crop insurance and market dates |

The best previous crop is not automatically the crop with the largest average yield effect. It is the crop whose complete legacy fits the next phase and the farm.

| Water legacy | How much water remains, and at what depth, for the next phase? | Stored soil water, rooting depth, fallow recharge, likely seasonal rainfall |
| Residue legacy | Will residue protect the surface, cool the seed zone, tie up N, or interfere with establishment? | Residue amount and distribution, planter capacity, row warming and seed placement |
| Weed legacy | Which emergence cohorts and control tactics does this phase select? | Planting-date shift, canopy timing, harvest date, survivors, seed return, herbicide sites of action |
| Soil-structure legacy | Does the phase add roots and cover, or require traffic and disturbance under vulnerable conditions? | Root architecture, harvest load, grazing pressure, compaction risk, erosion window |
| Operational legacy | Does this crop create or remove time for manure, drainage, lime, cover crops, or harvest? | Labor and machinery peaks, contractor availability, storage, drying, crop insurance and market dates |

The best previous crop is not automatically the crop with the largest average yield effect. It is the crop whose complete legacy fits the next phase and the farm.

### 1. Break biological cycles—but identify the organism

### 2. Rotate calendars to make weeds solve a new problem

A crop planted at the same time each year repeatedly favors weeds that emerge in that window and survive its control program. Alternating fall-, early-spring-, and late-spring-planted crops changes seedbed timing, canopy development, herbicide options, cultivation windows, and harvest disturbance. The global weed meta-analysis found a 49% reduction in weed density under diversified rotations, while planting-date variance explained suppression better than crop species richness. ⁠[[7]](#source-7) That is direct evidence that calendar contrast can matter more than crop count.

This is not permission to assume a diverse rotation will manage weeds by itself. A crop that establishes slowly, has limited herbicide options, or is harvested after weed seed maturity can add to the seedbank. Score every phase for the weed cohorts it suppresses and the survivors it may allow to reproduce.

### 3. Treat legume effects as a measured legacy, not free nitrogen

The global 20% following-crop yield response to legume pre-crops is important, but it is not the same as an agronomic fertilizer credit. The meta-analysis compared following-crop yields after legume and non-legume pre-crops. It did not assign one transferable pounds-of-N value to every legume. Responses declined as fertilizer N increased and varied widely among continents and following crops. ⁠[[5]](#source-5) Use current regional guidance, stand or biomass information, harvest removal, termination timing, and soil or plant tests where locally calibrated.

More N can also be mistimed. In semi-arid Australian sequence experiments, crop effects of 0.6–0.9 t/ha persisted three to four years through water, nitrogen, and disease legacies, but appeared in one experimental phase and not another. Residual legume N could even contribute to haying-off when it drove early growth that later exceeded water supply. ⁠[[12]](#source-12) The useful question is not simply how much N a legume adds, but whether N release aligns with the next crop's water and uptake pattern.

### 4. Design root and water contrast for the climate

Deep and shallow roots, early and late water demand, and active versus fallow periods change where and when water is removed. In humid systems, longer living cover may increase infiltration and protect against excess water and erosion. In water-limited systems, a crop or cover can trade stored water for biomass and later benefits. The correct decision depends on soil profile, precipitation timing, crop rooting, termination, and the value of stored water to the following crop.

Long-term North American data support rotation as a resilience tool, not drought insurance. Bowles et al. found smaller maize losses during drought at many locations, but no average maize gain at the two most arid sites. ⁠[[1]](#source-1) Costa et al. found that one additional functional group could offset modeled warming losses under some conditions, while combined warming and precipitation decline required more functional groups. ⁠[[2]](#source-2) Rotation changes exposure and recovery; it does not eliminate the field water balance.

### 5. Build carbon through inputs and time—not labels

A rotation can change soil organic matter only if it changes carbon inputs, decomposition, erosion, or protection. King and Blesh found that cover-cropped and perennial-inclusive systems increased both estimated C inputs and SOC compared with grain-only systems. Within grain-only rotations, adding a grain legume reduced C input 16% and SOC 5.3% compared with cereal-only rotations; crop species richness alone had no SOC effect. ⁠[[9]](#source-9) A crop can improve nitrogen supply and still produce too little residue to build carbon in that comparison.

The broader 122-study meta-analysis found modest changes in total soil C and N but much larger changes in microbial biomass C and N. ⁠[[8]](#source-8) This is consistent with a system in which soil biology responds relatively quickly to altered roots and residue while total SOC changes more slowly and remains sensitive to sampling depth, equivalent soil mass, erosion, texture, and duration.

##### Perenniality is a design variable

A perennial forage, a well-established cover crop, or another phase that occupies an otherwise bare period can increase the duration of living roots and carbon input. But its value still depends on stand length, biomass, market or feed use, termination, water, and the crop that follows.

## The Marsden Farm lesson: sequence creates management options

The nine-year Marsden Farm experiment in Iowa compared a two-year corn–soybean system with three- and four-year systems that added small grain, red clover, and alfalfa. During 2003–2011, mean corn yield rose from 12.3 Mg/ha in the two-year system to 12.7 and 12.9 Mg/ha in the longer systems; soybean rose from 3.4 to 3.8 Mg/ha. From 2006–2011, net returns to land and management did not differ statistically among systems, while profit variability was lower in the diversified rotations. ⁠[[10]](#source-10)
