Its modest returns remain part of the calculation. So does the time it frees up. By the time corn comes around again, the value of that earlier harvest reaches beyond the grain that left the field.

## Becky keeps working on the next crop

For Becky, the next crop is always part of the cover crop decision.

Ahead of soybeans, cereal rye has found a useful place. The family plants soybeans into the living stand, then terminates the rye and leaves a thick mulch. Becky told Farm Journal that the mat of residue has helped suppress weeds in their fields.

Ahead of corn, the same vigorous growth has been harder to manage. Rye can compete with young corn for moisture and nutrients, she reported, leaving uneven emergence. A lighter mix of wheat, triticale, and camelina has been easier on corn in some fields. In others, it has left the soil too exposed to wind.

Click to expand

Protecting the soil and giving the next crop a strong start. Conceptual AI watercolor by Soil Health Exchange.

That is the problem Becky is working through: enough growth to hold and protect the soil, with room for corn to get a good start. One field can reveal a weakness that another did not. Success ahead of soybeans gives the family something to build on, while corn keeps asking for an adjustment.

By summer 2026, the family was testing mixtures and seeding methods, from drilling to an air cart pulled behind a vertical tillage tool. They also planned to try more aerial and broadcast seeding. Each approach offered another way to fit living roots into the crop calendar.

## Making the changes work in the yard, too

Back in the cattle yard, the resource that helps feed the crops brings work of its own. Manure must be stored, handled, and hauled. Heavy equipment can compact the very soil the family is trying to improve. They share GPS guidance lines with custom applicators so machinery follows recurring tracks through the fields.

Storage required a substantial investment. NRCS reported in 2024 that manure-handling improvements cost roughly $500,000, with EQIP assistance covering 90% of that project's costs.

Then an employee helped make more of the investment. The longtime feedlot foreman took responsibility for the storage site, checking temperatures and turning material on a schedule to develop the composting work. His experience became part of how the farm used its manure.

Click to expand

Cattle, manure, crops, and living roots connect across the farm. Conceptual AI watercolor by Soil Health Exchange.

The cattle business brings financial pressure as well. Shawn told Brooks that high cattle prices can still leave a feedlot squeezed by the cost of buying animals. Having lived through a group of cattle that lost heavily, he was prepared to leave space empty rather than repeat the experience.

That willingness to examine the business extends beyond the yard. The farm's [account of a 2024 Farm4Profit interview](https://www.feikemafarms.com/multimedia) describes Shawn pursuing agricultural executive education, the family hiring a fractional chief financial officer, and the start of monthly board meetings. As the field practices changed, they also made more room to look closely at the business supporting them.

## The people beyond the farm gate

When Shawn talks about the value of livestock, he also talks about the people who keep a farm running. Feed, parts, veterinary care: the needs recur through the year, and the spending reaches local businesses. Becky points to the people the farm employs and what those jobs mean to the community.

Those connections help explain why the family has opened its work to a wider audience. Through farm tours and the documentary [From the Heartland](https://www.fromtheheartlandfilm.com/about), they have shared the people and decisions behind the fields. The film follows the relationship between farms and rural communities through their experience; the family's [media page](https://www.feikemafarms.com/multimedia) offers a place to explore it.

Click to expand

A conversation beside farm equipment at Feikema Farms. Photograph from the gallery shared by Becky Feikema. ·  —  · Photo: Tami Carda Photography (@tamicardaphotography)

In the CHS interview, Shawn spoke about wanting people to understand that agriculture is carried on by families. The work of protecting soil belongs to that larger picture: people making a living, depending on one another, and trying to keep a place going.

## What they hope to pass on

“We don't want to do one thing 10% better. We want to do everything 5% better,” Shawn told Farm Journal.

That ambition takes shape in the work: soil tests that guide fertilizer placement, an earlier harvest that eases the fall workload, an employee's care for the compost, and Becky's next cover crop mix. Together, those decisions have reshaped the farm the family sat down to talk about in 2014.

Clarence began with dairy cattle and crops. His sons built a different operation. Shawn, Mike, Becky, and Staci are making their own changes now. What they hope to pass on is a farm with productive soil, a business that can support a family, and room for the next generation to make decisions of its own.

# FieldLog: A Working Memory for Every Field

**Author:** Soil Health Exchange
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0053
**Published:** 2026-10-04T16:09:37.125Z

*Updated November 14, 2026, with new screens from the redesigned app, what has changed since October, and a call for testers at the end.*

By the time a fall soil test comes back, the questions about a field are specific. When did the cereal rye go in, and at what rate? Were the cores pulled before or after the fall fertilizer? Which strips in the trial were the checks? The answers exist somewhere: in a pocket notebook, a text thread, a seed invoice, a spreadsheet on someone's laptop. They are rarely in one place, and rarely attached to the ground they describe.

[FieldLog](https://fieldlog.info/) keeps them together. It holds a farm's tasks, field work, inputs, soil samples, observations, yields, and trial layouts with the field each one belongs to, so a season can be read back as one account. FieldLog is one of the platforms the Soil Health Exchange team is building. When the conversation turns to soil, with an adviser, a certifier, or your own crew, it can start from the record instead of from memory.

The screens below follow a sample 2026 season on five fields: corn and soybeans, cereal rye seeded behind the combine, a four-treatment cover crop strip trial, and a small field in organic transition. They show the season as it stands in mid-November, with harvest finished and the rye up.

## What changed this fall

FieldLog was rebuilt in November around how a farmer uses a phone in the field. The record underneath is the same. What changed is how quickly you can reach it and add to it.

- **One menu.** Today, Fields, Log, Work, and More sit at the bottom of every phone screen and in a side menu on a computer. The tools under them follow your role, what you manage, and the programs you report to. Everything else stays one tap away under More tools.
- **Work, to do and done.** The plan and the finished work now share one screen. Tick a job when it is done, and undo the tick if you tapped the wrong one.
- **Longer voice notes.** Tap the microphone and say what you did, for up to 60 seconds. The audio stays on the phone if the signal drops, and you read the transcript before it fills in the log.
- **Photos that keep their time and place.** A photo attached to a log keeps when and where it was taken, even when it uploads hours later.
- **Units that fit the farm.** Each season is set to US or metric units, with its country and time zone, so rates and areas are entered the way the farm measures them. Grazing and the US program worksheets still use US units.
- **Grazing and perennial crops.** Grazing records herd moves and how long each pasture has rested. Log work now covers pruning, weeding, mulching, shade, and frost protection for tea, orchards, and other perennial crops.
- **Research beside the question.** Ask an expert opens from any field, and it can look up measured field-trial results for your county before you send.

## What changed this fall

FieldLog was rebuilt in November around how a farmer uses a phone in the field. The record underneath is the same. What changed is how quickly you can reach it and add to it.

- **One menu.** Today, Fields, Log, Work, and More sit at the bottom of every phone screen and in a side menu on a computer. The tools under them follow your role, what you manage, and the programs you report to. Everything else stays one tap away under More tools.
- **Work, to do and done.** The plan and the finished work now share one screen. Tick a job when it is done, and undo the tick if you tapped the wrong one.
- **Longer voice notes.** Tap the microphone and say what you did, for up to 60 seconds. The audio stays on the phone if the signal drops, and you read the transcript before it fills in the log.
- **Photos that keep their time and place.** A photo attached to a log keeps when and where it was taken, even when it uploads hours later.
- **Units that fit the farm.** Each season is set to US or metric units, with its country and time zone, so rates and areas are entered the way the farm measures them. Grazing and the US program worksheets still use US units.
- **Grazing and perennial crops.** Grazing records herd moves and how long each pasture has rested. Log work now covers pruning, weeding, mulching, shade, and frost protection for tea, orchards, and other perennial crops.
- **Research beside the question.** Ask an expert opens from any field, and it can look up measured field-trial results for your county before you send.

## Start with the plan you already have

The Today view opens on what needs attention. On November 14, that means fall soil samples on North 40 four days late, the sprayer to winterize today, and a biomass clip on the trial block and the 2027 seed order due Friday. The forecast beside the list comes with a spray check. At 47°F, it advises spraying with care.

A field can start as a name and a crop. Drawing its boundary on satellite imagery, or importing one as GeoJSON or KML, adds acreage, a map, and local weather. Plot outlines follow the boundary, so a crew can find a plot and its records while standing in it.

## Record work where it happens

In the field, a record has to fit on a phone and survive a weak signal. FieldLog's Log work sheet starts with one question: what did you do? Sprayed, fertilized, planted, harvested, tilled, scouted, or soil sample, with irrigation, cover crops, and other work under More. Choose the field and the day, then add a photo or a note. Or tap the microphone and **say what you did**: FieldLog turns up to 60 seconds of speech into the note and fills in the work and field it recognizes. You check the log before it saves. A log saved without signal waits on the phone and goes through, with its original date, when the connection returns.

Products, rates, and costs entered with the work become input records, so the cost of a pass reaches the field's totals without a second entry.

Other channels feed the same record. Each season has its own email address, so a forwarded note or photo lands in the work journal. WhatsApp messages routed through OpenClaw arrive the same way. Both wait for review, and on the Pro plan, messages that clearly match a field and task can post directly. A reply to a task notification becomes a comment on that task.

## Read a field's season in one place

Every task, log, input, and yield attached to a field appears on its page, newest first. Creek Field's reads like a season summary. Soybeans were planted May 12. Waterhemp escapes along the creek edge were spot-sprayed June 26. Harvest on September 28 averaged 63.1 bushels per acre. On October 1, the field was grid-sampled at 2.5 acres per composite, 0–6 inches deep, with a four-day CO₂ burst run on six zones. Cereal rye went in the next day at 60 pounds per acre for $666, with a note on why it went in early. By November 9 the rye stood 3 to 4 inches tall, and on November 11 the lab results came back.

That context shapes how results are read. Soil tests compare well from year to year when depth, timing, and lab stay consistent, as our [fall soil sampling guide](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/fall-soil-sampling-what-to-test-when-to-sample-how-to-use-results) explains. A [CO₂ burst result](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/soil-co2-respiration-burst-interpretation) means more when you know what was growing and what had just been applied. The timeline keeps those facts beside the number.

## Run on-farm trials with replication built in

A side-by-side comparison becomes evidence when treatments are replicated and randomized. The Plot & trial designer lays out a randomized complete block or split-plot design on a field's plot grid. It also accepts a design pasted from a spreadsheet or R output, or assigned plot by plot.

The trial shown here, CC-2026-01, compares four treatments in four blocks: a no-cover check, cereal rye at 60 pounds per acre, oats at 64 pounds per acre that winterkill, and rye with hairy vetch. Treatments are shuffled within each block, and the randomization seed is saved with the design. Observations are logged to individual plots, and fall stand counts are already on all 16. **Export plot data** writes a CSV with each plot's trial ID, treatment, replication, and harvest records, ready for R or JMP.

## Keep organic transition records in order

Land must go three years without prohibited substances before an organic crop is harvested from it ([7 CFR 205.202](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-7/subtitle-B/chapter-I/subchapter-M/part-205/subpart-C/section-205.202)). FieldLog counts that period from the field's last prohibited application. Pasture Field's was June 14, 2025, so its panel shows 17 of 36 months complete and an estimated eligibility date of June 14, 2028.

Products entered in Log work are checked by name against the USDA National List, and a possible prohibited match is flagged before the log saves. Confirming one on a transitioning field resets the clock. The organic inspection packet, under Reports & records, exports every input application for a chosen period, with its date, field, product, rate, supplier, and National List reading, oldest first, the way an application log is reviewed. Your certifier reviews the Organic System Plan and approves inputs; FieldLog keeps the records that review depends on. Our [organic certification guide](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/organic-certification-guide-farms-handlers) walks through the full process.

## Ask an expert with the record attached

When a decision needs a second opinion, **Ask an expert** sends the question to the Soil Health Exchange network of researchers, agronomists, and practitioners, who answer free of charge. It now opens from any field's page with that field, its crop, and its county already filled in, and you can type the question or say it. The field's recent activities, inputs, yields, and observations can travel with it, and you can preview exactly what is sent. The answer is published on the [Knowledge Hub](https://soilhealthexchange.com/hub), and FieldLog lets you know when it arrives.

Below the question, **What research says near you** looks up measured results from field trials in your county through [OpenAgData](https://open-ag-data.com/). Only the county, crop, and practice are sent. It is a limited public preview, so some counties return nothing yet. When it does find a result, you can add it to your question or save it to the field's notes.

The question from Creek Field asks when to terminate the rye ahead of 2027 soybeans. Our [cover crop termination guide](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/beyond-glyphosate-what-actually-works-for-terminating-cover-crops) works through the same decision.

## Where FieldLog is headed

FieldLog is built on one principle: ask the farmer only for the facts that create trust. Acres come from the boundary, weather from the date and location, and cost from the product, rate, and area. The app asks for what only the person in the field knows: which field or part of it, what went on, and how much. The next stages build on that principle:

- **Records for part of a field.** A pass on the west half or a spot spray along a waterway will be recorded as a mapped area instead of the whole field.
- **Drafts from a sentence, a voice note, or a photo.** Speech already works this way in Log work. Next, FieldLog will propose the record from a typed sentence or a photo and ask only for the field and area. Anything it parsed stays a draft until someone accepts it.
- **Reports for everyone who shares the work.** Season reports for farmers; client rosters, follow-ups, and signed recommendations for agronomists; protocols, bulk plot observations, and clean exports for researchers.
- **Connections the farmer switches on.** Questions to Soil Health Exchange and research from OpenAgData are in the app today, and we are connecting FieldLog with the other platforms we are building. [FarmDeck](https://www.farmdeck.co/) will let an input be followed from purchase to use. Guidance from Soil Health Exchange will come back as a next step on the field. [TerraValue](https://terravalue.tech/) will draw on the record to assess a practice's costs and environmental outcomes. Farmers will be able to contribute field evidence to [OpenAgData](https://open-ag-data.com/) research. The same record already reaches beyond row crops. FieldLog's Landscapes section keeps properties, management zones, tagged trees and shrubs, treatments, and follow-up visits that compare the same plant over time. Grazing does the same for herds and the pastures they move through.

## We are looking for testers

The redesigned app is new, and it improves fastest when people use it on real ground. Testing takes a free account and a phone. [Sign up at fieldlog.info](https://fieldlog.info/register), log this fall's work as it happens, and send what you find through **Help and feedback** in the app. We read every note, and testers' reports decide what gets fixed first.

# Weed Management Beyond a Single Tool: What Is Ready and What Still Needs Proof

**Author:** Soil Health Exchange
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0080
**Published:** 2026-05-22T00:42:14.470Z

##### The bottom line

The future of weed management is not a single replacement for glyphosate. It is a field plan that makes several tactics support one another. Begin with the weeds and resistance risks in each field. Prevent new introductions, build a competitive crop, use labeled herbicides where they remain effective, remove escapes before seed production, and add mechanical or harvest-time tactics where they fit. Precision spraying is commercially available and can reduce treated area, but savings depend heavily on weed density, field conditions, operating speed, and service costs. Camera-guided cultivation and harvest weed seed control are useful in the right crops and weed communities. Laser, electrical, autonomous, and RNA-based weed-control concepts still need field-scale proof, workable economics, and regulatory clearance. Budget any technology against the cost of the whole program, not the advertised reduction from one pass.

A new sprayer, robot, herbicide, or biological tool can be useful. None of them removes the need to know which weeds are present, why they escaped, and how many seeds they may return to the field. The most durable programs use several points of control across the season, then adjust those points from field records.

##### Start with the field, not the technology

For each field, write down the dominant weeds, suspected or confirmed resistance, emergence windows, last year's escapes, crop rotation, tillage limits, and available labor and equipment. A tool belongs in the plan only if it addresses one of those problems without creating a larger one.

## Why another single-tool program will fail

The International Herbicide-Resistant Weed Database reported 548 unique species-by-site-of-action resistance cases, involving 275 weed species and 21 of 31 known herbicide sites of action, as of August 8, 2026 ⁠[[1]](#source-1). Those figures describe confirmed resistance cases, not the number of farms or acres affected. Their value is the direction they show: repeated selection with the same effective site of action continues to narrow future choices.

Rotating brand names is not resistance management if the effective sites of action remain the same. A stronger program combines effective herbicide sites of action with tactics that do not depend on the same biology: clean seed and equipment, crop rotation, crop competition, cultivation or mowing where appropriate, and prevention of seed return ⁠[[2]](#source-2)⁠[[3]](#source-3).

## Build the program in layers

and prevention of seed return ⁠[[2]](#source-2)⁠[[3]](#source-3). ## Build the program in layers

#### Five layers of a field-level weed plan

| Layer | Question | Examples | Record after the season |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Prevention | How could a new weed or resistance trait enter? | Clean seed, equipment cleanout, field-border control, known manure or feed sources | New patches and likely entry route |
| Crop competition | How can the crop close space sooner? | Rotation, planting date, row spacing, stand uniformity, cover-crop residue | Canopy timing, gaps, crop injury |
| In-season control | Which tactics work at the weeds' current size? | Effective labeled herbicides, cultivation, mowing, hand or targeted removal | Weed size, weather, control, crop response |
| Seed-return control | Which escapes could replenish the seedbank? | Rogueing, patch treatment, harvest weed seed control where weeds retain seed | Escapes and seed-producing patches |
| Learning | What should change next year? | Maps, resistance testing, cost and yield records, treatment strips | Cost per acre and failure points |

Not every field needs every tactic. The goal is to avoid asking one tactic to carry the whole program [[2]](#source-2)[[3]](#source-3).

Long-term Iowa research found that diversified crop rotations could reduce herbicide use while maintaining yields and profitability under the conditions studied ⁠[[13]](#source-13). A global meta-analysis also found that crop rotation reduced weed density and increased crop yield on average, though results varied with rotation design and environment ⁠[[14]](#source-14). These findings support diversification; they do not promise that adding any crop to a rotation will solve a specific weed problem.

#### A practical readiness check

| Tool or strategy | Current status | Where it can help | What to verify |

| Diversified integrated weed management | Ready now | Reduces dependence on one tactic and adds control points across the rotation | Fit to the field's weeds, crops, labor, and soil-conservation goals |
| Targeted or spot spraying | Commercial; field-dependent | Avoids spraying weed-free portions of a field | Weed density, detection limits, speed, tendering, service, and rescue plan |

## Precision spraying can save product, but the field sets the savings

Targeted sprayers use sensors and software to identify where a spray is needed. USDA Agricultural Research Service work is testing these systems under field conditions ⁠[[8]](#source-8). In one ARS field study, targeted spraying reduced spray volume by about 79 to 80 percent when failed runs were excluded ⁠[[9]](#source-9). In five Iowa soybean fields totaling 415 acres, a GROW on-farm evaluation reported average product savings of 76 percent ⁠[[10]](#source-10). These are useful measurements, not a guaranteed savings rate.

Sparse weeds create more opportunity to turn nozzles off. Dense weeds can make a targeted pass resemble a broadcast pass. Performance can also change with weed size, canopy, dust, shadows, speed, nozzle control, and the system's ability to distinguish crops from weeds. Current industry interviews point to cost, dealer support, operating changes, and uncertain payback as adoption barriers even as the technology improves ⁠[[11]](#source-11).

##### Ask for the denominator

When a vendor reports a percentage reduction, ask whether it refers to spray volume, herbicide product, treated area, water, or total program cost. Then ask which fields, weed densities, operating speeds, and failed runs were included.

## Use harvest to protect the seedbank

Harvest weed seed control captures, concentrates, or destroys weed seed that is still held on plants when the crop is harvested. North American research describes strong potential and important limits: the target weed must retain enough seed at harvest, the crop and combine system must handle the tactic, and harvest moisture and timing must be workable ⁠[[16]](#source-16). Corn and weeds that shed seed early may be poor fits. Treat it as one seedbank tactic, not a substitute for controlling weeds during the crop year.

## Keep emerging claims in the correct category

Some technologies are scientifically interesting but not yet dependable field recommendations. Laser and electrical systems must prove crop safety, acres per day, reliability, energy use, and cost in the intended crop. Autonomous machines add questions about supervision, transport, service, liability, and what happens during a narrow weather window. Small-plot weed injury is not the same as whole-farm control.

##### A correction about RNA technology

Ledprona, sometimes cited in discussions of RNA-based agriculture, is registered by EPA as an insecticide for Colorado potato beetle in potatoes. It is not a herbicide and is not evidence that RNA weed control is commercially available [[15]](#source-15). RNA-based weed control should remain in the research category until a specific product has field evidence, registration, and a label for that use.

## Herbicides remain tools with labels, not assumptions

Glyphosate products remain registered in the United States when used according to their labels while EPA completes registration review ⁠[[4]](#source-4)⁠[[5]](#source-5). Dicamba use in dicamba-tolerant cotton and soybean has changed through court decisions and new registrations; EPA's current dicamba page should be checked before each season ⁠[[7]](#source-7). Spray-drift language and mitigation requirements also continue to evolve ⁠[[6]](#source-6). Build the plan from the current federal and state label, not last year's practice or a general article.

## A three-year field plan

1. Year 1: map weeds and escapes, confirm suspected resistance where testing is available, stop seed production in the worst patches, and record the cost and result of each pass.
2. Year 2: add one tactic that changes the selection pressure—such as a different crop and planting date, a competitive cover, cultivation, or harvest-time seed control—while keeping an effective rescue option.
3. Year 3: compare seed-producing escapes, herbicide use, labor, field passes, crop injury, yield, and total cost with the Year 1 baseline. Keep what reduced both risk and whole-program cost.

The useful question is not which technology will replace glyphosate. It is which combination leaves fewer survivors, returns fewer seeds, fits the farm's labor and soil goals, and remains affordable when the season does not go as planned. That is a weed-management system a farm can improve each year.

## Herbicides remain tools with labels, not assumptions

Glyphosate products remain registered in the United States when used according to their labels while EPA completes registration review ⁠[[4]](#source-4)⁠[[5]](#source-5). Dicamba use in dicamba-tolerant cotton and soybean has changed through court decisions and new registrations; EPA's current dicamba page should be checked before each season ⁠[[7]](#source-7). Spray-drift language and mitigation requirements also continue to evolve ⁠[[6]](#source-6). Build the plan from the current federal and state label, not last year's practice or a general article.

## A three-year field plan

1. Year 1: map weeds and escapes, confirm suspected resistance where testing is available, stop seed production in the worst patches, and record the cost and result of each pass.
2. Year 2: add one tactic that changes the selection pressure—such as a different crop and planting date, a competitive cover, cultivation, or harvest-time seed control—while keeping an effective rescue option.
3. Year 3: compare seed-producing escapes, herbicide use, labor, field passes, crop injury, yield, and total cost with the Year 1 baseline. Keep what reduced both risk and whole-program cost.

The useful question is not which technology will replace glyphosate. It is which combination leaves fewer survivors, returns fewer seeds, fits the farm's labor and soil goals, and remains affordable when the season does not go as planned. That is a weed-management system a farm can improve each year.

# Getting Soil Health Help When NRCS Has No Staff: A Practical Playbook

**Author:** Musfiq Salehin, Ph.D.
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0025
**Published:** 2026-07-04T16:05:00.000Z

If your local NRCS office feels impossible to reach right now, you are not imagining it. Between January 2025 and January 2026, USDA’s Natural Resources Conservation Service lost about **23% of its staff** — including 711 soil conservationists, the front-line role most farmers work with — and 141 counties that previously had NRCS staff were left with none (National Sustainable Agriculture Coalition, 2026).⁠[[1]](#source-1) Add tight limits on federal hiring, and the technical help many soil-health plans depend on has gotten much harder to get.⁠[[2]](#source-2) The good news is that NRCS is not the only place to start.

## Start with your state Cooperative Extension Service

If your local NRCS office is short-staffed or unavailable, Extension is often the best first stop for practical soil-health guidance. Contact your county Extension office, regional agronomy specialist, soil-fertility specialist, forage specialist, or state soil-health specialist and ask for help developing a field-level soil-health management plan. Extension advice is free, science-based, and not tied to selling you a product.

## Come prepared

Before the meeting, gather basic information for each field: soil-test results, crop-rotation history, tillage practices, residue management, irrigation or grazing history, fertilizer and manure records, yield history, problem areas, and photos showing erosion, compaction, ponding, salinity, bare ground, poor forage recovery, or low crop vigor. Extension can help you interpret these records and identify the main resource concerns.

title: Getting Soil Health Help When NRCS Has No Staff: A Practical Playbook
author: Musfiq Salehin, Ph.D.
text:
rigation or grazing history, fertilizer and manure records, yield history, problem areas, and photos showing erosion, compaction, ponding, salinity, bare ground, poor forage recovery, or low crop vigor. Extension can help you interpret these records and identify the main resource concerns.

## Build a plan around your system

Work with Extension to build a practical plan around your production system. Depending on your operation, this may include cover crops, reduced tillage, residue retention, nutrient management, manure or compost use, diverse rotations, prescribed grazing, forage improvement, irrigation water management, erosion control, or salinity management. The goal is a plan that fits your farm, equipment, climate, labor, and economics — not a generic soil-health checklist.

## Then loop in the cost-share partners

Once you have a draft plan, ask Extension to help connect you with the right conservation partners: the NRCS staff person covering your county, the local Soil and Water Conservation District, the NRCS state office, or a certified Technical Service Provider. If you are interested in EQIP, CSP, or other NRCS financial assistance, you will still need to work through NRCS for eligibility, ranking, contracting, and cost-share approval.⁠[[3]](#source-3)

Be realistic about the odds and the timeline. In fiscal 2025, only about **24% of EQIP applications and 37% of CSP applications won contracts**, down from 43% and 54% the year before (Institute for Agriculture and Trade Policy analysis of USDA data).⁠[[4]](#source-4) A plan that is already built and well-documented helps you compete when a funding round opens or when staff capacity frees up.

### Who does what

- **Cooperative Extension** (land-grant university): free, unbiased soil-health and fertility planning and soil-test interpretation. Find your office via nifa.usda.gov or extension.org.⁠[[5]](#source-5)
- **Soil & Water Conservation District (SWCD):** locally led conservation planning, often co-located in the USDA Service Center. About 3,000 districts nationwide.⁠[[6]](#source-6) Find yours at nacdnet.org.⁠[[6]](#source-6)
- **USDA-NRCS:** administers EQIP/CSP cost-share and conservation planning (free) — currently capacity-constrained. Locate an office at nrcs.usda.gov/contact/find-a-service-center.⁠[[7]](#source-7)
- **Technical Service Provider (TSP):** NRCS-certified individuals, businesses, nonprofits, tribes or public agencies who can write conservation plans when NRCS is short-staffed. Once you have an NRCS contract, NRCS can reimburse the TSP’s cost at the contracted rate.⁠[[3]](#source-3)⁠[[8]](#source-8) Find one via the NRCS TSP page.⁠[[8]](#source-8)

> Decision path: If your local NRCS office is short-staffed, start with Cooperative Extension to build a field-level soil-health plan. Then use your Soil and Water Conservation District or the NRCS state office to find the right NRCS contact. For EQIP, CSP, or other cost-share support, apply through NRCS or work with a certified Technical Service Provider.

# The Haney Test: What It Measures and How to Use the Results

**Author:** Soil Health Exchange
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0106
**Published:** 2026-09-18T03:39:24.026Z

##### How to use this test

The Haney test adds information about microbial activity and water-extractable carbon and nitrogen to a soil report. Its components can help track a field over time, but the Soil Health Score and nutrient credits need interpretation in the context of soil, climate, sampling conditions, and the laboratory’s methods. Research supports the 24-hour CO2 burst as a useful soil health indicator; evidence for the package’s fertilizer recommendations is more limited and varies by region. Keep locally calibrated testing for nutrient decisions, check which analyses the laboratory actually includes, and confirm current requirements before ordering for CEMA 216.

## Which decision will the test help with?

Are you tracking a management change, planning fertilizer, or ordering tests for a conservation program? Those uses require different evidence. The Haney test can add useful information about biological activity and nutrient cycling, particularly when the same field is sampled consistently over several years. A nutrient credit or a single score needs a separate check before it changes a fertilizer rate ⁠[[34]](#source-34) ⁠[[41]](#source-41).

text:
## How to read the report

The published 2018 method dries soil at 50 °C, sieves it to 2 mm, and uses separate water and H3A extracts plus a dried-and-rewetted sample for respiration ⁠[[1]](#source-1). Incubation and detection methods can differ: Ward’s archived instructions specify infrared CO2 analysis at 24 °C, while MVTL’s information sheet specifies 25 °C ⁠[[5]](#source-5) ⁠[[6]](#source-6). WEON is calculated as total water-extractable N minus nitrate-N and ammonium-N. It is an estimate of an extractable organic pool, not a direct measurement of the N a crop will receive.

#### The lines on a Haney report and what each one is

| Report line | How it is produced | What it can tell you | Interpretation boundary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1-day CO2-C, usually mg C/kg soil (ppm) | CO2-C released during a 24-hour incubation of dried, rewetted soil [1] [5] | Potential microbial activity under the test conditions | A respiration indicator, not a direct microbial count or field CO2 flux. Compare the same incubation and rewetting method. |
| WEOC, ppm | Organic carbon in the water extract [1] | A water-extractable carbon fraction relevant to microbial activity | It is not total soil organic carbon. Ward reports that many samples fall around 100-300 ppm; this is a laboratory observation, not a universal target [7]. |
| WEON, ppm | Total water-extractable N minus nitrate-N and ammonium-N [5] | An organic N fraction used in the nutrient-credit calculation | The pool size does not establish how much N will mineralize during the growing season. |
| Water-extract organic C:N | WEOC divided by WEON [7] | The balance of C and N in this extract | It differs from whole-soil or residue C:N. Archived Ward guidance assigns no N or P mineralization credit above 20:1; this is a calculation rule, not a universal field threshold [5]. |
| Microbially active carbon (%MAC) | 100 × 24-hour CO2-C / WEOC [7] | An index relating respiration to water-extractable carbon | The two values come from separate analyses. The ratio does not directly measure the fraction of the extracted carbon consumed by microbes. |

The original Haney method and current commercial packages are not necessarily identical. Retain the laboratory, method, units, sampling depth, and report version with each result.

Which score formula was used? Published documents are not uniform. The 2018 paper prints (CO2-C/10) × (WEOC/100) × (WEON/10) ⁠[[1]](#source-1). Ward’s archived information sheet prints CO2-C/10 + WEOC/50 + WEON/10 ⁠[[5]](#source-5); its report-definitions sheet describes respiration divided by organic C:N plus weighted WEOC and WEON ⁠[[8]](#source-8). These documents establish a version issue, not which formula every laboratory uses today. Ask the laboratory to identify its current calculation and whether older results can be recalculated before treating a score change as a management response.

The nutrient calculation also has assumptions. In the 2018 paper, potential N mineralization equals the CO2-C:WEOC fraction × WEON × 2.24 × n, where n represents growing-season rain or irrigation events greater than one inch; the paper suggests four as a starting value ⁠[[1]](#source-1). Its available-N equation uses 2.24 to convert ammonium-N from mg/kg to kg/ha and 1.6 for nitrate-N, with the latter incorporating an assumed 30% nitrate loss. The 1.6 factor is therefore not a simple increase in measured nitrate. Laboratory guidance may implement credits differently ⁠[[7]](#source-7). The biological rationale draws on several studies; the 2008 compost experiment on Houston Black clay is one example, not the entire evidence base ⁠[[1]](#source-1) ⁠[[9]](#source-9). These relationships still need field validation for the crop, region, and recommendation being used.

title: The Haney Test: What It Measures and How to Use the Results
author: Soil Health Exchange
text:
## What have field studies found?

Studies have evaluated several different questions: whether indicators respond to management, whether a score tracks yield, and whether a nutrient recommendation predicts fertilizer response. Success on one question does not settle the others. The studies below show useful biological signals alongside limits in consistency and regional calibration.

#### Selected evaluations of Haney indicators and related methods, 2016-2025

| Study | Where and how | What it found |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Morrow et al. 2016 [10] | Five long-term trials, inland Pacific Northwest, 2-30 years old | 1-day C mineralization and the Haney index were highly variable (coefficients of variation up to 53% and 37%) and consequently not very sensitive to tillage or cropping intensity; POX-C scored best on the authors' seven criteria |
| Roper et al. 2017 [11] | Three North Carolina trials with 17-32 years of contrasting management | The Haney test rated soil from every system except moldboard plowing as in good health; Cornell CASH rated the same mountain soils low or very low except the no-till organic system, which scored medium; neither test correlated with crop yield |
| Chahal & Van Eerd 2018 [12] | Six-year cover crop experiment, Ridgetown, Ontario, processing vegetables | Haney, Solvita, and SLAN results were inconsistent between years in detecting cover crop effects and in their relationships with yield, soil organic carbon, and a 2-day C-mineralization test. |
| Yost et al. 2018 [13] | 17 corn N-rate trials in eight Midwest states, one season (2016) | The N recommendation with expected yield explained at most 28% of variation in economically optimum N rate. The score and CO2 burst each explained about 55%; the two were strongly related (R-squared 0.98). |
| Chu et al. 2019 [14] | No-till corn-soybean cover crop trial established 2013, west Tennessee | H3A extracted the least P, K, Ca and Mg of three extractants; neither the score nor any component detected a cover crop effect; the Solvita CO2 value did not reliably estimate potentially mineralizable N |

These are study-specific findings, not a pooled estimate of test performance. Most study summaries are based on published abstracts; the NAPESHM minimum-suite paper was checked in full. Methods, score versions, soils, and management histories differ. Management sensitivity was inconsistent in several trials ⁠[[10]](#source-10) ⁠[[11]](#source-11) ⁠[[12]](#source-12) ⁠[[16]](#source-16). Nebraska provides a useful positive result: water-extract and H3A nitrogen measurements detected treatment differences missed by conventional nitrate testing, with similar analytical precision ⁠[[15]](#source-15). The North Carolina results also prompted a published disagreement about the Cornell CASH indicators ⁠[[21]](#source-21) ⁠[[22]](#source-22). That reanalysis focused on CASH, so its conclusions should not be transferred to the Haney score. For a farm, the relevant question is whether the selected indicator can detect the particular change being monitored. The North American Project to Evaluate Soil Health Measurements provides broader support for respiration as a monitoring indicator ⁠[[17]](#source-17) ⁠[[18]](#source-18). Its recommended minimum suite combines soil organic carbon, aggregate stability, and 24-hour carbon mineralization. WEOC also responded to management, but overlapped with other carbon measurements ⁠[[17]](#source-17) ⁠[[23]](#source-23). The project’s nitrogen analysis found strong relationships with carbon indicators and suggested organic carbon plus respiration as proxies for N-supply function ⁠[[24]](#source-24). This does not supply a field-specific fertilizer credit or validate the Haney score. A separate synthesis of 1,071 samples found that short-term mineralizable carbon and POX-C reflected different aspects of organic matter cycling, supporting their use as complementary indicators ⁠[[25]](#source-25). Can respiration help estimate nitrogen need?

Research in North Carolina and Virginia found promising relationships between a 3-day CO2 flush and corn response to N ⁠[[26]](#source-26) ⁠[[27]](#source-27). A later analysis across 111 fields explained 46% of variation in yield-scaled optimum N ⁠[[28]](#source-28). That method differs from the 24-hour Haney protocol in incubation duration, soil preparation, and rewetting. Its equations and thresholds should not be applied directly to a Haney report. In 29 Corn Belt N-rate trials, better biological soil health was associated with higher yield per unit of N, but the indicators offered limited advance information about a site’s fertilizer response ⁠[[29]](#source-29). Method consistency matters. A developer study found strong correlations among Solvita, titration, and infrared CO2 measurements, but correlation does not make their values interchangeable ⁠[[30]](#source-30). NRCS guidance has also evolved since its 2019 technical note ⁠[[33]](#source-33); the 2025 note discusses respiration methods lasting one to four days ⁠[[34]](#source-34). Keep the method fixed when monitoring, and check with the laboratory before combining results from different protocols. [Part 5](/blog/soil-co2-respiration-burst-interpretation) explains these differences.

## How should the field be sampled? Build the sampling plan before ordering. Purdue and NRCS recommend consistent locations, depth, seasonal timing, and laboratory methods for repeated comparisons ⁠[[35]](#source-35) ⁠[[34]](#source-34). Record crop, recent tillage and inputs, weather, and soil conditions. Consistency helps distinguish management effects from sampling variation; analytical precision still matters.

- **Confirm the depth and sampling design.** Ward’s archived Haney protocol specifies 10-15 cores at 0-6 or 0-8 inches for its fertility recommendations ⁠[[36]](#source-36). Regen Ag Lab asks for at least ten cores collected at a consistent depth ⁠[[37]](#source-37). These are laboratory examples; CEMA 216 has a separate sampling design ⁠[[38]](#source-38) ⁠[[48]](#source-48). Keep different depths separate and use the depth required for the intended interpretation.
- **Read a pounds-per-acre credit with its assumptions.** Ward’s archived conversion is sample depth in inches × 0.3 × the estimated organic-N-release value in ppm ⁠[[7]](#source-7). ## Can the nutrient lines support a fertilizer decision? First identify how the laboratory calculated the credit. Ward’s archived guidance bases organic-N release on the water-extract C:N ratio, respiration, and WEON pool, and caps the credit at the measured WEON pool ⁠[[7]](#source-7). Its older information sheet assigns no N or P mineralization credit above a 20:1 water-extract C:N ratio ⁠[[5]](#source-5). These are model rules. A line labeled “nitrogen savings” expresses an estimated difference from a nitrate-only calculation; it does not establish realized savings or maintained yield ⁠[[5]](#source-5). The 17-site, eight-state corn study found that the Haney N recommendation with expected yield explained at most 28% of variation in economically optimum N rate; the score and CO2 burst each explained about 55% ⁠[[13]](#source-13). That supports further investigation of the indicators, while leaving substantial uncertainty in a rate decision. Minnesota Extension also reports cases where Haney recommendations would have increased N rates relative to its guidelines, and advises against using soil health tests alone to determine fertilizer rates ⁠[[41]](#source-41) ⁠[[42]](#source-42). NRCS likewise cautions against using soil health package results for nutrient management planning ⁠[[34]](#source-34). If a package includes conventional fertility analyses, confirm that their methods, sampling, and interpretation meet the applicable local guidance. If a Haney-based N rate would change management, compare it with the locally recommended rate in small, replicated strips before extending it across the farm ⁠[[43]](#source-43). Record applied N, yield, and net return with an agronomist. Where locally validated, a pre-sidedress nitrate test can inform an in-season corn decision. A late-season stalk nitrate test answers a different question: it helps assess the season’s N management after most fertilizer decisions have already been made ⁠[[37]](#source-37).

Neither is interchangeable with a crop-response trial. For phosphorus and potassium, extraction method is central. Kansas and Tennessee comparisons found that H3A and Mehlich-3 values were related, but conversion errors were too large to transfer existing fertilizer calibrations reliably ⁠[[44]](#source-44) ⁠[[45]](#source-45). Iowa researchers tested H3A phosphorus against crop response and found weaker relationships than for Bray-1 and Mehlich-3 in those trials ⁠[[46]](#source-46). This is evidence for using method-specific, regional calibration; it does not show that H3A can never be calibrated. Wisconsin Extension makes the same practical distinction between measuring a nutrient and establishing a fertilizer recommendation ⁠[[47]](#source-47).

#### H3A versus the calibrated extractant: what three states found

| Study | Soils | H3A compared with Mehlich-3 (or routine tests) | Authors' conclusion |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rutter & Ruiz Diaz 2020 [45] | Kansas | r = 0.90 (P) and 0.91 (K); Mehlich-3 extracted about 25% more P and 250% more K; RMSE 15.4 ppm P, 83.4 ppm K | Errors too large to plug H3A values into existing Kansas calibrations |
| Adotey et al. 2025 [44] | Tennessee | R-squared 0.87 (P) and 0.39 (K); Mehlich-3 extracted about 60% more P and 25% more K | Inappropriate to estimate Mehlich-3 P and K from H3A-4 for fertilizer recommendations |
| Mallarino & Jones 2018 [46] | Iowa, 24 sites, 54 corn and 58 soybean site-years | R-squared 0.94-0.95 with Bray-1 and Mehlich-3, 0.97 with Olsen; yield-response model R-squared 0.33-0.40 (H3A) vs 0.60-0.73 (Bray-1, Mehlich-3) | H3A needs its own field calibration; preliminary critical ranges 12-16 ppm corn, 14-19 ppm soybean |

Correlation between extractants does not establish equivalent fertilizer recommendations. The Iowa study supplies preliminary phosphorus calibration evidence for its soils and crops; it does not establish a national H3A interpretation or a potassium calibration.

## Does the package meet CEMA 216 requirements?

Check the current standard and job aid with the Qualified Individual (QI) before ordering. The national documents listed by NRCS as 04-2026 require tests for five processes: aggregation, carbon cycling, microbial activity, carbon food source, and nitrogen food source, plus pH and texture ⁠[[38]](#source-38) ⁠[[61]](#source-61). The standard lists WEOC and WEON as alternate methods for the two food-source categories; the April 10, 2026 FAQ explicitly explains their connection to the Haney method ⁠[[48]](#source-48). A 24-hour respiration test can address microbial activity. The Soil Health Score and H3A nutrient credits do not substitute for the required analyses.

A Haney package may therefore supply several required measurements, but the name alone does not establish compliance. Confirm aggregate stability, the accepted organic-carbon method, texture, pH, and every other required method on the actual order. The QI must also arrange the pre-work conference and meet sampling and reporting requirements ⁠[[38]](#source-38) ⁠[[61]](#source-61). The FAQ describes an instance as three separate composite samples, each made from five subsamples, and estimates about $150 per sample before shipping ⁠[[48]](#source-48). Confirm the current laboratory qualifications and contracted requirements with the local NRCS office. SHE’s [CEMA 216 guide](/blog/cema-216-requirements-before-soil-sampling) covers the full workflow.

## What does the price include?

Compare package contents as well as price. Regen Ag Lab lists its Haney package at $60, while Ward lists a $61.90 Soil Health Assessment with different nutrient extraction methods ⁠[[52]](#source-52) ⁠[[51]](#source-51). The examples below were checked on September 17, 2026. Prices, turnaround, and package contents can change; request the current specification before ordering.

## Five interpretation checks

1. **Is the comparison fair?** Soil, climate, and management history influence indicator values. Use comparable sampling areas and methods rather than ranking unrelated farms by raw scores ⁠[[7]](#source-7). Cornell’s framework uses texture groups for selected indicators, but a scoring framework still needs regional context ⁠[[58]](#source-58) ⁠[[59]](#source-59).
2. **Is there a sustained change?** Compare several observations and their sampling records. A single increase or decrease can reflect season, weather, or recent inputs ⁠[[19]](#source-19) ⁠[[35]](#source-35).
3. **Does the score answer the farm question?** A management-sensitive indicator is not automatically a yield predictor. North Carolina trials found limited discrimination among some long-term systems and no correlation between the tested soil health assessments and yield ⁠[[11]](#source-11) ⁠[[59]](#source-59). Keep crop performance and field observations alongside the laboratory record.
4. **What has not been measured?** The core Haney indicators do not directly measure infiltration, bulk density, or water-holding capacity ⁠[[7]](#source-7). Use field observations and targeted measurements to investigate rooting, compaction, and water movement ⁠[[34]](#source-34). Distinguish inherent context, such as texture, from management-responsive conditions, such as pH.
5. **Whose benchmark is being used?** Ward’s archived “above 7” guidance is a laboratory interpretation, not a universal pass mark ⁠[[5]](#source-5) ⁠[[7]](#source-7). Purdue notes that the Haney calculation has no defined “high” threshold ⁠[[35]](#source-35). A nearby perennial reference area can provide context when soil and landscape position are comparable, but it is not automatically an attainable cropping-system target ⁠[[60]](#source-60) ⁠[[34]](#source-34).

## Five interpretation checks

1. **Is the comparison fair?** Soil, climate, and management history influence indicator values. Use comparable sampling areas and methods rather than ranking unrelated farms by raw scores ⁠[[7]](#source-7). Cornell’s framework uses texture groups for selected indicators, but a scoring framework still needs regional context ⁠[[58]](#source-58) ⁠[[59]](#source-59).
2. **Is there a sustained change?** Compare several observations and their sampling records. A single increase or decrease can reflect season, weather, or recent inputs ⁠[[19]](#source-19) ⁠[[35]](#source-35).
3. **Does the score answer the farm question?** A management-sensitive indicator is not automatically a yield predictor. North Carolina trials found limited discrimination among some long-term systems and no correlation between the tested soil health assessments and yield ⁠[[11]](#source-11) ⁠[[59]](#source-59). Keep crop performance and field observations alongside the laboratory record.
4. **What has not been measured?** The core Haney indicators do not directly measure infiltration, bulk density, or water-holding capacity ⁠[[7]](#source-7). Use field observations and targeted measurements to investigate rooting, compaction, and water movement ⁠[[34]](#source-34). Distinguish inherent context, such as texture, from management-responsive conditions, such as pH.
5. **Whose benchmark is being used?** Ward’s archived “above 7” guidance is a laboratory interpretation, not a universal pass mark ⁠[[5]](#source-5) ⁠[[7]](#source-7). Purdue notes that the Haney calculation has no defined “high” threshold ⁠[[35]](#source-35). A nearby perennial reference area can provide context when soil and landscape position are comparable, but it is not automatically an attainable cropping-system target ⁠[[60]](#source-60) ⁠[[34]](#source-34).

## Before the next sample

Write down the decision the test should support, then confirm the laboratory’s package, methods, and handling instructions. Save the component results and score formula with the sampling record. If the report suggests a different fertilizer rate, review its local evidence with an agronomist and plan a field comparison. On the next sampling round, return to comparable locations and conditions so the record becomes more useful over time.

##### Where this fits in the series

For respiration methods, see [Part 5](/blog/soil-co2-respiration-burst-interpretation). [ACE protein](/blog/what-an-ace-protein-test-actually-tells-you) and [PMN](/blog/interpreting-soil-health-indicators-pmn) assess different aspects of organic nitrogen; neither is interchangeable with WEON. [POX-C](/blog/poxc-active-carbon-soil-health-indicator) measures a different carbon fraction, while [PLFA](/blog/plfa-analysis-soil-biology-testing) estimates microbial biomass and broad community groups. Use [Fall Soil Sampling](/blog/fall-soil-sampling-what-to-test-when-to-sample-how-to-use-results) to plan repeatable comparisons.

title: How Do I Know Whether My Soil Is Actually Getting Healthier?
author: Soil Health Exchange
text:
# How Do I Know Whether My Soil Is Actually Getting Healthier?

**Author:** Soil Health Exchange
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0054
**Published:** 2026-10-11T17:07:14.662Z

You have kept the ground covered, changed the rotation, or reduced tillage. The soil seems easier to work. Then the laboratory report arrives: organic matter barely moved, one biological indicator rose, and the overall score fell. Is the field improving?

The strongest answer comes from a pattern: **the soil performs better, comparable measurements support that change, and the improvement persists across conditions that matter on your farm.** Start with the problem you wanted to solve, keep the comparison consistent, and read the laboratory results alongside what happens in the field.

Soil health describes a soil’s ability to keep supporting life and performing functions such as regulating water, cycling nutrients, and sustaining plant growth. Physical structure, chemistry, and biology work together. A field can improve in one function while another still needs attention ⁠[[1]](#source-1).

##### The short answer

Look for repeated evidence of better function in the same soil: more effective water entry, less erosion or crusting, roots exploring the profile, and suitable chemical conditions. Confirm the pattern with a small, consistent set of soil tests. Record weather and management so you can explain changes, then judge what those changes mean for production, costs, and risk.

# How Do I Know Whether My Soil Is Actually Getting Healthier?

**Author:** Soil Health Exchange
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0054
**Published:** 2026-10-11T17:07:14.662Z

You have kept the ground covered, changed the rotation, or reduced tillage. The soil seems easier to work. Then the laboratory report arrives: organic matter barely moved, one biological indicator rose, and the overall score fell. Is the field improving?

The strongest answer comes from a pattern: **the soil performs better, comparable measurements support that change, and the improvement persists across conditions that matter on your farm.** Start with the problem you wanted to solve, keep the comparison consistent, and read the laboratory results alongside what happens in the field.

Soil health describes a soil’s ability to keep supporting life and performing functions such as regulating water, cycling nutrients, and sustaining plant growth. Physical structure, chemistry, and biology work together. A field can improve in one function while another still needs attention ⁠[[1]](#source-1).

##### The short answer

Look for repeated evidence of better function in the same soil: more effective water entry, less erosion or crusting, roots exploring the profile, and suitable chemical conditions. Confirm the pattern with a small, consistent set of soil tests. Record weather and management so you can explain changes, then judge what those changes mean for production, costs, and risk.

title: How Do I Know Whether My Soil Is Actually Getting Healthier?
author: Soil Health Exchange
text:
Confirm the pattern with a small, consistent set of soil tests. Record weather and management so you can explain changes, then judge what those changes mean for production, costs, and risk.

## Start with the problem you want the soil to solve

Write one sentence before choosing a test: “I want this field to absorb intense rain with less runoff,” or “I want roots to explore below the compacted layer.” That sentence determines what you measure. If the concern is surface sealing, pair observations of crusting and water entry with aggregate stability. If it is acidity, use a pH test and the region’s lime-requirement procedure. If it is nutrient supply, use the appropriate fertility tests ⁠[[8]](#source-8).

Keep a record of the practice too: cover-crop establishment, grazing, residue removal, traffic, or tillage. Those records describe what you did. Measurements and field observations show how the soil responded. The connection between them becomes clearer when you repeat the assessment.

## Walk the field and give observations a record

Choose representative observation locations you can return to, plus separate locations for a specific trouble spot. Photograph them from the same position and include a ruler or another scale when documenting roots or soil layers. A wet depression, a headland, and the main field each deserve their own record ⁠[[3]](#source-3).

#### Field observations worth repeating

| What to examine | What to record | How to interpret it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water after rain | Ponding, runoff routes, sediment, rainfall amount, and time since rain. | Follow recurring trouble spots. Check drainage and landscape position when ponding persists. |
| Surface condition | Crusting, rills, exposed roots, residue cover, and establishment gaps. | Look for less sealing and soil movement under comparable events. |
| Roots and structure | Root depth and direction, visible pores, and the depth of dense or platy layers. | Look for roots using more of the profile. Dig where they turn sideways or stop. |
| Water entry test | Method, starting moisture, water amount, elapsed time, and repeated locations. | Compare repeated measurements made under similar starting conditions. |
| Soil organisms and residue | Visible organisms, residue type and age, season, and moisture. | Use these observations to help explain the field’s biology and decomposition. |

These are observation prompts. NRCS’s 2025 cropland assessment is a diagnostic tool for resource concerns; tracking change requires a repeatable monitoring protocol [[2]](#source-2)[[3]](#source-3)[[11]](#source-11).

A quick infiltration demonstration can reveal a difference worth investigating. For tracking, use a defined procedure and repeat it at several locations. Water entry depends on initial moisture, cracks, soil type, and the test setup. Preserve those details with the result ⁠[[11]](#source-11).

Likewise, record the conditions when assessing compaction. Penetration resistance rises as soil dries. Check a suspected layer by digging and looking at roots and structure. SHE’s [soil-compaction diagnosis guide](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/soil-compaction-diagnose-first-fix-second-a-field-protocol-with-thresholds) provides a fuller field sequence ⁠[[2]](#source-2).

Earthworms and their channels can be useful supporting observations where they occur. Their abundance depends on habitat, season, and moisture, and some environments naturally support few. Compare a consistent volume of soil under similar conditions ⁠[[11]](#source-11).

## Choose a small set of tests you can repeat

A broad North American study evaluated more than 30 measurements at 124 long-term agricultural research sites. Bagnall and colleagues recommended soil organic carbon, aggregate stability, and 24-hour carbon mineralization as a practical minimum suite for assessing management-related soil function. Use that suite as a starting point, then add measurements that address your field’s particular concern ⁠[[4]](#source-4).

#### Match the measurement to the question

| Measurement | What it helps you track | What to keep with the result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organic matter or organic carbon | The longer-term condition of the soil’s organic material or carbon pool. | Which quantity was measured, method, units, depth, and sampling area. |
| Aggregate stability | How well soil aggregates resist breakdown under the test’s wetting or disturbance. | Exact method and sample preparation; use the same procedure again. |
| Carbon mineralization or respiration | Microbial processing of carbon under defined incubation conditions. | Incubation length, preparation, temperature, moisture protocol, and reporting units. |
| Routine fertility tests | pH and nutrient status relevant to crop response and input decisions. | Extractant, units, crop, sampling depth, and regional interpretation. |
| A targeted physical test | A specific constraint such as compaction or restricted water entry. | Location, depth, texture, moisture, and the measurement procedure. |

## Make the samples comparable before comparing the numbers

Sampling design can change the apparent trend. University of Wisconsin guidance identifies sampling month, depth, field location, handling, and laboratory procedure as major sources of variation. Keep those factors as consistent as practical ⁠[[6]](#source-6).

- **Area:** map the sampling zone and repeat the same collection pattern. Keep distinct soils, drainage conditions, and management histories separate ⁠[[3]](#source-3).
- **Depth:** agree on the depth required for each test and purpose. Record it and keep it consistent; a shallower sample can emphasize surface organic material.
- **Timing:** use a repeatable seasonal or crop-stage window. Record recent rainfall and the timing of manure, fertilizer, tillage, and grazing.
- **Collection:** use representative cores and a consistent approach to rows, bands, and traffic lanes. Remove surface litter according to the protocol.
- **Handling:** follow the laboratory’s instructions for the selected assays and record any shipping delay or exposure to heat.
- **Analysis:** retain the laboratory, exact method, units, and score version. Confirm those details again when ordering the next test.

If you change laboratories, arrange an overlap: collect and homogenize a representative sample, then send subsamples to both labs using matching requested methods and handling. That comparison can identify a reporting shift. It does not measure how much the field varies; independent field samples are needed for that ⁠[[6]](#source-6)⁠[[10]](#source-10).

If you have no reliable baseline, establish one now. Preserve older reports with their sampling details, but begin a new comparable series when those details are missing. A well-documented starting point gives the next result meaning.

## Read a change in the context of its variability

Put the raw results beside one another, with their units and methods, before reading the score. Ask the laboratory which differences exceed its analytical repeatability, and ask your adviser how to assess variation among independently collected samples. Both matter when judging a small change ⁠[[6]](#source-6)⁠[[10]](#source-10).

##### A worked example with illustrative values

Suppose organic matter is \*\*3.2%\*\* at baseline and \*\*3.4%\*\* at the next comparable sampling. The difference is \*\*0.2 percentage points\*\*, or \*\*6.25% relative to the baseline\*\*: (3.4 − 3.2) ÷ 3.2 × 100. Those calculations describe the change in the reported concentration. To decide whether it represents a field trend, check sampling consistency, variability, and subsequent results.

Use plain descriptions in your record: “higher in this sample,” “a repeated increase across comparable samples,” or “no clear trend yet.” These descriptions match different amounts of evidence. A single composite sample represents a sampling area, but it provides little information about the spread of values within that area ⁠[[3]](#source-3)⁠[[10]](#source-10).

A score adds another layer of interpretation. Find out which indicators it contains, how they are weighted, and which reference population sets the rating. Read the components separately when an overall score moves unexpectedly. The useful question is which function changed and whether that change matters in your soil ⁠[[5]](#source-5)⁠[[12]](#source-12).

## Expect different indicators to move on different timelines

Water entry, root distribution, and biologically active fractions can respond on a different timeline from total organic matter. Organic matter usually changes slowly, and the detectable response depends on starting level, texture, climate, management, and measurement precision ⁠[[7]](#source-7).

University of Minnesota guidance gives illustrative expectations of roughly 3–5 years for organic-matter change in soils starting at 0–2%, and 7–10 years or more in soils starting at 4–7%. These are expectations from that guidance, not deadlines for an individual field. Wisconsin guidance also describes a multi-year monitoring horizon for many indicators ⁠[[7]](#source-7)⁠[[8]](#source-8).

A practical plan is to record field observations and operations each season, then agree with your adviser on a laboratory interval that fits the indicator, expected change, and budget. Use consistent annual testing where the question or program warrants it. For slower indicators, a planned multi-year revisit can be more informative than reacting to every small annual movement.

Protect a field that is already functioning well. Maintaining its condition through intensive production or difficult weather can be a meaningful result even when the laboratory numbers remain stable.

author: Soil Health Exchange
text:

## Use a reference that belongs to your soil

A sandy field in a dry climate and a fine-textured field in a wetter climate have different starting conditions and attainable ranges. Use your field’s own comparable history to assess direction. Use a matched reference to put its current condition in context ⁠[[3]](#source-3)⁠[[7]](#source-7).

For an external comparison, check texture, climate, drainage, landscape position, sampling basis, and the reference’s land-use history. A nearby grass strip may have received sediment, nutrients, or different traffic. Verify its suitability before treating it as a target ⁠[[12]](#source-12).

SHE’s [guide to fair soil-health targets](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/why-your-soil-health-targets-might-be-unfair-and-how-to-fix-them) explains ecological matching and reference selection. Use the benchmark to identify a relevant direction for improvement, while considering what is feasible in your production system.

## Separate a field trend from the effect of one practice

A repeatable trend tells you what happened in the field. To identify the effect of a cover crop, grazing change, or other practice, you also need a fair comparison. Weather, crop rotation, inputs, and drainage changes can affect the same outcomes ⁠[[10]](#source-10).

Where practical, establish a replicated comparison with your usual management, randomize treatment placement, and keep the other operations consistent. Collect baseline measurements and revisit both treatments in the same sampling window. An on-farm research adviser can help size the trial and choose the analysis. Iowa State recommends at least four replications as a starting point for its on-farm trial guidance ⁠[[10]](#source-10).

Several cores mixed into one bag improve representation of that sample. They do not create several independent treatment replications. Nor does retesting the same bag. Independent plots or strips are the units that help you distinguish a treatment response from field variability ⁠[[14]](#source-14).

## Use a reference that belongs to your soil

A sandy field in a dry climate and a fine-textured field in a wetter climate have different starting conditions and attainable ranges. Use your field’s own comparable history to assess direction. Use a matched reference to put its current condition in context ⁠[[3]](#source-3)⁠[[7]](#source-7).

For an external comparison, check texture, climate, drainage, landscape position, sampling basis, and the reference’s land-use history. A nearby grass strip may have received sediment, nutrients, or different traffic. Verify its suitability before treating it as a target ⁠[[12]](#source-12).

SHE’s [guide to fair soil-health targets](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/why-your-soil-health-targets-might-be-unfair-and-how-to-fix-them) explains ecological matching and reference selection. Use the benchmark to identify a relevant direction for improvement, while considering what is feasible in your production system.

## Separate a field trend from the effect of one practice

A repeatable trend tells you what happened in the field. To identify the effect of a cover crop, grazing change, or other practice, you also need a fair comparison. Weather, crop rotation, inputs, and drainage changes can affect the same outcomes ⁠[[10]](#source-10).

Where practical, establish a replicated comparison with your usual management, randomize treatment placement, and keep the other operations consistent. Collect baseline measurements and revisit both treatments in the same sampling window. An on-farm research adviser can help size the trial and choose the analysis. Iowa State recommends at least four replications as a starting point for its on-farm trial guidance ⁠[[10]](#source-10).

Several cores mixed into one bag improve representation of that sample. They do not create several independent treatment replications. Nor does retesting the same bag. Independent plots or strips are the units that help you distinguish a treatment response from field variability ⁠[[14]](#source-14).

#### When the evidence points in different directions

| What you see | What to check next |
| --- | --- |
| Better rooting and water entry, with little organic-matter change | Confirm conditions and locations. Keep tracking the physical improvement while following the slower carbon indicator. |
| Higher respiration after a recent manure application | Record the input timing and repeat at the planned window before interpreting it as a lasting trend. |
| Higher organic matter, with rising phosphorus or salts | Review amendment nutrient loading and crop-specific fertility or salinity guidance. |
| A lower score after a laboratory or depth change | Compare methods, units, sampling basis, and score version; establish an overlap or a new baseline. |
| Poor growth despite favorable biological results | Investigate rooting restrictions, moisture, disease, pH, and crop nutrient status. |
| No clear change after several comparable visits | Check practice establishment, measurement choice, and the size of change the sampling design could detect. |

## Follow the benefit through to the farm

Choose the outcome that matches the original problem: fewer establishment gaps, less sediment leaving the field, improved access after wet weather, more consistent forage recovery, or a change in yield variability. Record production and costs alongside the soil measurements ⁠[[13]](#source-13).

For each season, note the weather, cultivar or forage mix, planting and harvest timing, irrigation, and major input changes. Compare costs using the same basis: seed, labor, machinery passes, fuel, testing, and any additional treatment. If you receive a conservation payment, show the result with and without that payment so you can judge continuing the practice.

SHE’s [farm-value guide](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/farm-value-ledger-soil-health-economics) provides a way to connect measured soil functions to costs, production, and risk. Good economics strengthens the case for a practice; the soil measurements tell you whether its effect on the soil is also improving.

text:

## Build a record you can use next season

Choose one field and one priority concern. Make the monitoring plan simple enough to repeat:

1. **State the goal:** name the field problem and the change you want to see.
2. **Map the comparison:** record the sampling zones, observation points, and any treatment or reference areas.
3. **Choose the evidence:** select relevant field observations, a small test set, and a farm outcome.
4. **Fix the protocol:** save depth, seasonal window, method, units, sample handling, and laboratory details.
5. **Record the context:** keep photographs, weather, crop stage, recent inputs, and management operations with the report.
6. **Schedule the review:** decide when to repeat the assessment and which result would lead you to continue, investigate, or adjust.

Keep those records together in a notebook, spreadsheet, or [FieldLog](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/fieldlog-working-memory-for-every-field). A laboratory number is easier to use when you can see where it came from and what happened around it. SHE’s [soil-sampling guide](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/fall-soil-sampling-what-to-test-when-to-sample-how-to-use-results) can help you set up the collection plan.

At the next review, you should be able to explain the result in farm terms: where water entered better, whether roots passed the restrictive layer, which comparable measurements changed, and what the change meant for the operation. That is how “the soil seems better” becomes a conclusion you can build on.

**Have results that tell different stories?** Bring SHE your crop, location, sampling depth and date, laboratory methods, recent management, and the field problem you are trying to solve. Those details make the question useful to an expert—and the answer useful to your farm.

title: How Much Extra Water Does Healthy Soil Actually Hold? Debunking the 20,000 Gallons Claim
author: Dawood Atta, Ph.D.
text:
# How Much Extra Water Does Healthy Soil Actually Hold? Debunking the 20,000 Gallons Claim

**Author:** Dawood Atta, Ph.D.
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0027
**Published:** 2026-07-04T16:05:00.000Z

Healthy soil does hold more water — but not nearly as much as the popular claim that every 1% increase in soil organic matter stores “20,000 gallons of extra water per acre” would suggest. The science shows a real benefit, but it is usually modest, strongly dependent on soil texture, and often more valuable for infiltration, rooting, and drought resilience than for dramatically increasing the volume of water in storage.

## Where the 20,000-gallon number comes from

The figure has a real scientific root. Berman Hudson’s 1994 study in the Journal of Soil and Water Conservation showed that, within a given texture group, organic matter is strongly correlated with available water capacity.⁠[[1]](#source-1) But Hudson never published a gallons-per-acre number — that conversion was added later, using the assumption that organic matter holds roughly ten times its weight in water.⁠[[2]](#source-2) Run that math on the top six inches of an acre, which weighs about 1.8 million pounds at a typical bulk density.⁠[[2]](#source-2) One percent of it is about 18,000 pounds of organic matter; at ten times its weight, that would hold about 181,000 pounds of water, or roughly 21,700 gallons.⁠[[2]](#source-2) Rounded, that is the 20,000-gallon claim. The arithmetic counts every drop the organic matter itself could soak up, whether roots can reach it or not, and it ignores the water the mineral soil was already holding in the space the organic matter now occupies.⁠[[2]](#source-2)

USDA-NRCS uses a similar but larger figure, stating that each 1% increase in soil organic matter can hold “up to 25,000 gallons of available soil water per acre.”⁠[[3]](#source-3) Note the hedge: “up to.” These numbers are best treated as upper-end illustrations, not field results you can bank on.
