Yield needed to cover added net cost = added net cost/ac ÷ crop price. Keep establishment and transition costs visible even when the research plot began with a mature stand.

## Organic systems: plan the sequence and document the threshold

USDA organic rules require crop producers to begin with preventive practices, then use mechanical or physical methods, and use allowed substances only when those steps are insufficient. The organic system plan must document the management sequence and conditions for using a material. [[18]](#source-18)

For a living-mulch trial, confirm seed treatments, fertility products, flaming, cultivation aids, and any pest-control input with the certifier before use. Keep the product label, approval, agronomic reason, threshold, rate, field, and date with the strip map.

## Write the decision rules before harvest

- **Expand** only when stand and harvestable yield are acceptable, weeds remain manageable, the living mulch recovers, operations fit the farm, and net return is competitive in at least two contrasting seasons.
- **Redesign** when the trial identifies a correctable row problem: uneven seed placement, insufficient suppression, wrong timing, early N shortage, or an avoidable equipment conflict.
- **Stop scaling** when the living mulch repeatedly wins the row, moisture competition appears before canopy closure, the yield penalty exceeds captured benefits, or rescue work erases the reduced-tillage advantage.

## What the research still does not answer

- There is no single row-zone width validated across clover species, soils, slopes, planters, and climates.
- Organic living-mulch economics remain thin because many experiments lack a randomized farm-standard control or complete machinery and labor costs.
- Short trials cannot show whether early establishment costs are repaid by forage value, erosion control, nutrient retention, or later soil function.
- We need more replicated soybean work in established perennial mulches; planting-green evidence is not a substitute.
- Few studies define real-time rescue thresholds using crop water status, living-mulch regrowth, or early crop vigor.

- We need more replicated soybean work in established perennial mulches; planting-green evidence is not a substitute. - Few studies define real-time rescue thresholds using crop water status, living-mulch regrowth, or early crop vigor.

## Bottom line

Living mulch is not a plug-and-play cover-crop practice. It is a managed competition system. The evidence supports a clear design principle—protect the cash-crop row and retain living cover where the crop is not being limited—but it does not support a universal species, strip width, nitrogen credit, or expected yield response.

The farmer-ready path is a small, replicated test with a real benchmark, a moisture and rescue plan, separate harvest, and full operational accounting. That design lets the field answer the question the literature cannot: whether continuous living cover earns its place on this soil, with this clover, this equipment, and this season.

See how these principles were applied to a Pennsylvania organic corn question in the [companion Living Mulch Field Answer](https://soilhealthexchange.com/hub/organic-no-till-corn-living-mulch-pennsylvania).

# The same tanker of manure can save $20 an acre or cost $34

**Author:** Soil Health Exchange
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0110
**Published:** 2026-11-17T04:15:09.715Z

A tanker carries the same pounds out of the barn whichever way it turns. Where it stops determines how many of those pounds replace a fertilizer order. In the example below, the same load and application charge leave one field $19.60/ac ahead and the other $33.60/ac behind. That $53.20 difference starts with two lines on the fertilizer bill.

[Run the manure budget with a delivered quote](/learn/regenerative-economics#manure).

## Start with the fertilizer bill you can actually reduce

This liquid dairy manure example uses 4,000 gallons per acre and a $0 charge for the manure at the source. The pounds in the table are plant-available amounts that replace planned commercial purchases. Use a current manure analysis, soil test and nutrient plan to set the pounds you can credit and the gallons you can apply. If phosphorus limits the application, run the budget at that lower volume and price the nitrogen or potash you’ll still buy. [Penn State Extension on fertilizer replacement value](https://extension.psu.edu/manure-has-real-fertilizer-value-putting-a-dollar-value-on-local-nutrients)

| Fertilizer displaced | Usable lb per 1,000 gal | Assumed price | Value per 1,000 gal |

| N | 15 | $0.65/lb | $9.75 |

At Iowa State’s average $18.15 per 1,000 gallons for injection, the field that uses all three nutrients saves $4.90 per 1,000 gallons after application. Multiply by four for the **$19.60/ac** gain. The N-only field replaces $9.75 per 1,000 gallons of fertilizer and loses **$33.60/ac** at the same volume and application charge. Both cases hold yield flat and begin with zero separate freight. [Iowa State Custom Rate Survey, p. 4](https://www.extension.iastate.edu/agdm/crops/pdf/a3-10.pdf)

## The application quote can move the field past break-even

Iowa State’s 2026 survey received 16 expected rates for liquid injection. The average was $18.15 and the median $17 per 1,000 gallons. The reported range was $11 to $29, after dropping the lowest and highest responses. Apply those rates to the same full-nutrient budget and the spread between the two ends is **$72/ac**. author: Soil Health Exchange
text:
ssuming the same replacement value per gallon and zero minimum job fee. A smaller application can leave more fertilizer to buy for the same crop.

## Pay for a change in management when it changes an outcome

If improved placement costs $3 more per 1,000 gallons and the nitrogen you would otherwise buy costs $0.65/lb, the extra operation has to displace **about 4.6 more pounds of purchased N per 1,000 gallons** to pay through N alone. Minnesota Extension’s first-year planning factors for dairy manure give 55% of total N with sweep injection, 50% with knife or coulter injection, and 20% with broadcast and incorporation after 96 hours. With an illustrative lab result of 27 lb total N per 1,000 gallons, the sweep versus delayed incorporation difference is 9.45 lb of first-year N per 1,000 gallons. If all those pounds reduce the fertilizer order, they are worth about **$6.14 per 1,000 gallons**, or $24.57/ac at the example volume. Use the factors adopted for your area and plan. [University of Minnesota Extension, Table 1](https://extension.umn.edu/agriculture/animals-and-livestock/livestock-operations/calculating-manure-application-rates)

A two-year Minnesota corn trial shows how timing and calibration can change the yield line. In 2018, dragline-injected swine manure applied at the fourth leaf collar produced yields and returns to sidedressing costs comparable to anhydrous ammonia and UAN. In 2019, manure plots received about **45 lb/ac less plant-available N than targeted** and had a 6% lower stand than the no-sidedress control. Grain yield was 18% below UAN and 25% below anhydrous. Using the trial’s measured yields and cost assumptions, manure applied within 1.2 miles of the barn returned about **$400/ac over sidedressing and related costs**, versus **$488** for UAN and **$545** for anhydrous that year. Verify the N concentration and delivered application rate, and check the stand when putting manure into a growing crop.

author: Soil Health Exchange
text:
Independent and reader supported. Contributions are not tax-deductible. Our shared 2027 goal: $5,000 Through December 31, 2026 Confirmed contributions appear here.

## Give storage, separation and digestion their own budgets

A separator creates two streams and two routes. Compare the pump hours, electricity, dry matter and nutrient pounds delivered to each destination with your current handling. For compost, price the finished tons after shrink. A buyer pays for delivered material, so count testing, handling and freight before crediting a sale.

A digester brings a longer investment horizon. Include the energy contract, downtime, process power, financing, interconnection and digestate handling. If the original manure already replaces fertilizer, carry that existing value into the baseline. Compare whole-farm cash flows and price changes in fertilizer value separately from changes in hauling and storage. [EPA AgSTAR project planning and financing](https://www.epa.gov/agstar/project-planning-and-financing)

When two farms share the work, keep a crop budget and a livestock budget. Fertilizer avoided goes on the crop ledger. Storage or handling avoided goes on the livestock ledger. A payment between farms is revenue for one and expense for the other, so it cancels in a combined budget.

Start with two real destinations. Put the soil tests, manure analysis, allowable rates and all-in delivery charges side by side. The field closer to the barn can be the more expensive stop when it has less use for what the tanker carries. [Compare nutrient value in the SHE Manure Calculator](/tools/manure-calculator).

title: Nanobubble Oxygen Irrigation, Part 2: Installation, Costs, and Farm Payback
author: Bob Burger
text:
ment follows the investment decision from the pump station to the field comparison: what to install, what to measure, and how to calculate the return.

## Start with the water moving through your farm

A typical installation combines a nanobubble generator, an air or oxygen supply, controls, pipework, and any pump needed to move water through the equipment. The layout follows the farm's water source, storage, irrigation schedule, and peak flow. There are three common arrangements[[1]](#source-1):

- **Tank recirculation:** Water cycles through the generator and returns to storage before irrigation. Ask how much water can be treated, how long treatment takes, and what oxygen level remains when irrigation begins.
- **Inline treatment:** The unit treats the irrigation flow as water moves toward the crop. Size it for the actual operating flow and available pressure.
- **Sidestream treatment:** A portion of the flow passes through the generator and rejoins the main line. Measure oxygen after the streams mix and again at a distant outlet.

Swipe horizontally to inspect the full figure →

Click or tap to expand the figure

Figure 1. A full-flow planning layout with a service bypass and three sampling locations. The installer specifies the final pipework, protection assemblies and operating valve positions. ·  —  · Figure: Soil Health Exchange

Swipe horizontally to inspect the full figure →

Click or tap to expand the figure

Figure 2. Sidestream treatment needs a defined branch flow and mixing location. Tank recirculation needs a known storage volume, treatment period and irrigation schedule. ·  —  · Figure: Soil Health Exchange

Keep treatment capacity and storage capacity separate. A rating achieved by repeatedly treating a tank needs an operating-time calculation before it can be compared with continuous treatment of fresh water.

For pump-driven ChucaoTech injectors, the water pump supplies the energy used to generate bubbles. Include the pump, compressor or oxygen concentrator, and controls in the power budget. Ask the installer to document the pressure loss through the proposed unit and any change in pumping demand[[6]](#source-6)[[1]](#source-1).

## Ask for a complete installation quote

The useful quote describes a working system at your site. Have the supplier specify flow, water pressure, water temperature, gas supply, and expected dissolved oxygen at both the equipment outlet and the far end of the irrigation line.

Ask for an itemized scope covering:

- The generator, required pumps, compressor or oxygen concentrator, controls, and electrical work.
- Filtration, pipework, isolation and bypass valves, backflow protection, sampling points, and fertigation connections.
- Freight, installation, commissioning, training, warranty, and service arrangements.
- Expected operating hours, power demand, consumables, cleaning, and replacement parts.

Confirm that the proposed system maintains emitter pressure and irrigation uniformity. Choose sampling points that let you check performance during normal irrigation, with the water and fertilizer program you will actually use[[1]](#source-1).

My indicative installed-cost range is approximately **$5,000 for a small field or greenhouse system to $150,000 for a roughly 400-acre row-crop installation**. These are supplier estimates from my submitted manuscript; package scope and site requirements determine the actual quote[[1]](#source-1). At the upper example, $150,000 divided by 400 acres is **$375 per acre upfront**. Annual operating expenses belong on a separate line.

author: Bob Burger
text:
At the upper example, $150,000 divided by 400 acres is **$375 per acre upfront**. Annual operating expenses belong on a separate line.

## Install and hand over in six steps

Use Figure 1 to agree on the pipework and access points before equipment arrives. Figure 2 shows how the water route changes for a sidestream or storage-tank system. The selected model's installation manual supplies pipe sizes, connection details, gas settings, and the startup and shutdown sequence. 1. **Record the site conditions.** Measure the irrigation flow in gpm or m³/hour and operating pressure in psi or bar for each zone the unit will serve. Record water source, temperature, available electrical service, and the pump's performance information. For recirculation, add tank volume and the time available before irrigation. 2. **Approve the layout and operating limits.** Have the installer mark the injector, pump, filtration, source protection, gas supply, isolation valves, bypass, pressure taps, and sampling points on the drawing. Obtain the model's permitted water-flow range, pressure loss, gas purity, gas pressure and flow, and power requirements. Agree on acceptable pressure at the emitters and oxygen at S1 and S2[[6]](#source-6)[[1]](#source-1). 3. **Fit the water-side equipment.** The installer shuts down, isolates and depressurizes the work area, then fits and supports the pipework under the approved design. Label V1, V2 and VB to match the drawing and record their positions for treatment, bypass and service. Where fertigation is present, have the installer confirm the required backflow protection and injection arrangement[[9]](#source-9). 4. **Connect the gas supply and controls.** Have the supplier specify the compressor or oxygen package, gas-compatible components, regulation, metering, non-return protection and control interlocks. Document how gas delivery stops when water flow stops. Complete electrical connections and functional checks under the equipment manual[[1]](#source-1). 5. **Verify the hydraulics.** Follow the model's commissioning sequence, check for leaks, and measure flow and P1/P2 at the agreed pressure taps. Compare the treatment section's pressure loss with its specification.

Resolve any result outside the agreed limits before accepting the installation.

## Commission the system with measurements

Use the same dissolved-oxygen meter and sampling method at S0, S1 and S2. Calibrate the meter as its manufacturer directs and allow the readings to stabilize. Record dissolved oxygen in mg/L, temperature, sampling time and location. Account for salinity in the meter setup when relevant to the water source[[10]](#source-10).

Start with baseline readings under normal irrigation before oxygen treatment. After the supplier's startup procedure and a stable operating condition, measure untreated water at **S0**, treated or fully mixed water at **S1**, and delivery at a distant outlet at **S2**. For a tank system, include the oxygen reading at the actual irrigation time. Record water flow, P1/P2, gas settings and electricity use with the samples[[1]](#source-1).

Swipe horizontally to inspect the full figure →

Click or tap to expand the figure

Figure 3. Pair oxygen measurements with time, temperature and system settings. Compare commissioning records with the supplier’s agreed operating limits. ·  —  · Figure: Soil Health Exchange

Ask how the supplier verifies nanobubble production as well as dissolved oxygen. These measurements answer different questions: one characterizes the bubbles; the other measures oxygen dissolved in the water.

## Build the annual budget around changes you can measure

Begin with additional crop sales and documented savings, then subtract the added annual cash expenses and any lost sales. This follows the partial-budget approach used by Iowa State University Extension[[4]](#source-4).

For crop sales, use marketable production and the price received. Include the extra cost of harvesting, handling, packing, or hauling that production. For fruit and vegetables, record grade and size as well as total weight: a change in the saleable mix can matter as much as a change in tonnage.

For water savings, record the volume applied and the pumping or purchase expense avoided. If crop output rises while irrigation volume stays the same, record the benefit under crop sales. Fertilizer savings belong in the budget when a separate comparison shows that reduced purchases maintain acceptable yield and quality.

The lettuce paper supplied with this installment illustrates why the units matter. Researchers evaluated ten-day-old 'Little Gem' seedlings in a peat, coir, and vermiculite mix. Moderately diluted oxygen-nanobubble treatments improved early growth; the reported water saving of roughly 23% describes less water per unit of dry biomass. For a farm budget, measure seasonal irrigation volume and marketable harvest together[[3]](#source-3).

author: Bob Burger
text:
For a farm budget, measure seasonal irrigation volume and marketable harvest together[[3]](#source-3).

## Work out payback before buying

With a steady annual benefit, simple payback is the installed cost divided by the additional annual net cash benefit. If the benefit changes between seasons, accumulate the actual yearly cash flows until they recover the initial investment[[5]](#source-5).

Consider an **illustrative 100-acre installation costing $30,000**, or $300 per acre upfront. Assume additional annual crop sales of $18,000, measured input savings of $2,000, and added annual cash expenses of $8,000. The expenses include electricity, gas supply, maintenance, paid labor, and handling the extra harvest.

The annual net cash benefit is $18,000 + $2,000 − $8,000 = **$12,000**, or **$120 per acre**. Simple payback is $30,000 ÷ $12,000 = **2.5 years**.

#### Illustrative annual budget for 100 acres

| Annual budget item | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Additional crop sales | $18,000 |
| Measured input savings | $2,000 |
| Added annual cash expenses | −$8,000 |
| Additional annual net cash benefit | $12,000 |
| Simple payback on $30,000 installed cost | 2.5 years |

Illustrative assumptions for a 100-acre farm. Calculations by Soil Health Exchange.

These are teaching assumptions supplied by Soil Health Exchange. The example uses steady benefits from the first year and excludes financing, taxes, and resale value. Check equipment life and the timing of seasonal cash receipts when assessing the full investment[[5]](#source-5).

Now reduce the assumed additional crop sales by half. The annual benefit becomes $9,000 + $2,000 − $8,000 = **$3,000**, extending simple payback to **10 years**. With no added sales and the same savings and expenses, the annual result is **−$6,000**. Testing a weaker crop response shows how much the investment depends on yield.

You can also work backward from an acceptable recovery period. Recovering $30,000 in three years requires $10,000 of annual net cash benefit. With $8,000 in added annual expenses and $2,000 in savings, the crop must generate **$16,000 in additional annual sales**, or **$160 per acre** across 100 acres. That gives the field comparison a concrete target.

## Let the field comparison decide the next acres

Start with comparable treated and untreated blocks, replicated where practical. Keep crop variety, planting date, irrigation volume, and fertilizer management consistent for the initial comparison. Test input reductions separately so you can identify which change produced the result[[1]](#source-1).

Record marketable yield, grade, price, applied water, nutrient purchases, electricity, labor, and maintenance. In a crop with several cuttings or pickings, record each harvest and total the full season. Pair those records with oxygen readings, soil moisture, root observations, and weather.

Before expanding, put the measured additional cash benefit beside the installed cost per acre and the recovery period your farm can support. A successful trial leaves you with three things: an installation that works at your irrigation flow, a crop response you can measure, and a budget that supports the next investment.

title: Nanobubble Oxygen Irrigation: What It Means for Roots, Soil, and Crops
author: Bob Burger
text:
# Nanobubble Oxygen Irrigation: What It Means for Roots, Soil, and Crops

**Author:** Bob Burger
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0056
**Published:** 2026-10-14T20:10:11.348Z

When soil stays saturated or becomes compacted, roots can struggle even where water and fertilizer are plentiful. Oxygen in the root zone deserves the same attention as those more visible inputs. Plant roots need it to respire, grow, and take up nutrients.

Nanobubble oxygen irrigation offers a way to deliver oxygen through the water a farm is already applying. Its agricultural value rests on a practical question: can better oxygen delivery improve root function and crop performance in the grower's own system?

## Why root-zone oxygen matters

Plant roots use oxygen for respiration, which supplies energy for growth and active nutrient uptake. When water fills soil pores and drainage is slow, oxygen supply becomes restricted. Irrigation scheduling, drainage, and soil structure all help determine whether roots have the oxygen they need.

This is a long-standing agricultural concern. In 1935, A. R. C. Haas described avocado roots deteriorating in nutrient solutions and recovering when air was supplied. He connected that observation to irrigation and drainage in the field[[1]](#source-1). Nanobubbles bring a newer delivery method to an old root-zone problem.

Nanobubbles are tiny gas-filled bubbles in water, commonly around 100–200 nanometers in diameter. Oxygen-filled nanobubbles can enrich irrigation water with oxygen before it reaches the crop[[2]](#source-2). The useful measurement is how much oxygen reaches the root zone, at what time, and for how long.

title: Nanobubble Oxygen Irrigation: What It Means for Roots, Soil, and Crops
author: Bob Burger
text:
Oxygen-filled nanobubbles can enrich irrigation water with oxygen before it reaches the crop[[2]](#source-2). The useful measurement is how much oxygen reaches the root zone, at what time, and for how long.

## What nanobubbles do in soil

Oxygen delivery can influence roots, soil chemistry, and the microorganisms around them. A 2026 laboratory study irrigated small columns of commercial potting soil daily for four weeks. Oxygen nanobubbles raised the measured dissolved-oxygen level to an average of 28.7 mg/L, compared with 8.6 mg/L in the deionized-water control[[2]](#source-2).

The same experiment found changes in bacterial community composition and predicted metabolic pathways. Those predictions describe potential microbial functions; the experiment measured soil responses rather than crop yield. Its small potting-soil columns give a useful starting point for understanding the process[[2]](#source-2).

For a grower, the next step is to connect oxygen delivery with observable outcomes: healthier roots, plant-available nutrients, crop growth, and harvest. Each link deserves measurement in the production system being considered.

## Soil health and nutrient cycling

Healthy soil is a living system of minerals, organic matter, water, roots, fungi, bacteria, and other organisms. Oxygen supports aerobic organisms that decompose organic materials and participate in nutrient cycling.

That connection is especially relevant where compost, manure, cover crops, and crop residues contribute to fertility. Microbial processing helps release nutrients from organic materials. In a 2019 tomato study using soil incubation and soil-column experiments, oxygenation increased microbial biomass, activity, and diversity. Plant-available nitrogen and phosphorus were higher under nanobubble treatment than under conventional pump aeration and the untreated control[[3]](#source-3).

These findings make nutrient supply worth tracking alongside root growth. Base any fertilizer adjustment on soil and plant measurements, crop demand, and the nutrient plan.

Good physical management remains central. Build soil structure, manage traffic and compaction, maintain drainage, and schedule irrigation to match the crop. Oxygen-enriched water fits into that system alongside the practices that let water and air move through the soil.

## What crop studies have found

The most important question for a grower is whether the treatment improves the crop. Research gives several useful comparisons:

- **Tomatoes:** In the 2019 organic-farming experiment, final tomato yield was 23% higher with nanobubble oxygenation and 17% higher with conventional pump aeration than in the untreated control. Both oxygenation treatments improved soil biological measurements[[3]](#source-3).
- **Maize:** A two-year field experiment in saline clay-loam soil near Beijing tested micro/nanobubble oxygenation through subsurface drip irrigation. The highest-yielding treatment supplied water at 20 mg/L dissolved oxygen throughout the growing period and yielded 11.66% more than the untreated control. At 30 mg/L throughout the season, yield fell 10.97% below the control in one year. Concentration and timing mattered[[4]](#source-4).
- **Sugarcane:** A two-year field experiment in Guangxi, China, found improved yield and soil fertility under micro/nanobubble-water irrigation. Bacterial composition and predicted functions changed, while bacterial diversity decreased. The response involved changes in the community rather than a simple increase in diversity[[5]](#source-5).
- **Lettuce:** A study of drip irrigation with oxygen-nanobubble-treated wastewater reported improved soil aeration, lettuce yield, and plant physiology. It provides a crop-specific example where irrigation-water quality and oxygen delivery were studied together[[6]](#source-6). Responses also vary across systems. In field and controlled-environment experiments with sand-based creeping bentgrass putting greens, nanobubble-oxygenated water did not improve measured plant-health characteristics. Soil oxygen increased in one field year but was unchanged in the other two[[7]](#source-7). Read these results with their crop, soil, water source, and irrigation method attached. They help identify promising comparisons for a farm trial.

## Where it fits best

Nanobubble oxygen irrigation is worth evaluating where oxygen supply is a plausible production constraint. Drip-irrigated vegetables, intensively managed protected crops, and heavier soils with slow drainage offer useful questions to investigate. Frequent wetting, restricted rooting volume, and compacted layers can all affect root-zone aeration.

Start by walking the crop after irrigation. Look for persistent wet areas, uneven root development, and differences between healthy and struggling plants. Check irrigation uniformity and drainage. Where salinity or nutrient imbalance is involved, include those measurements so the oxygen question stays connected to the whole growing environment.

## Make the farm comparison useful

The strongest case for adoption comes from a well-designed comparison on your own soil, with your own water and crop. Use comparable treated and untreated areas, preferably with replicated plots. Keep crop variety, planting date, irrigation volume, and fertilizer management consistent, and record weather and any management differences.

Click to expand

Seedling containers from IngenuityWorx’s bench-testing work [[8]](#source-8). ·  —  · Photo: IngenuityWorx

Measure dissolved oxygen in the source water and at delivery to the crop. Pair those readings with soil moisture, root observations, marketable yield, and crop quality. Choose the measurements before starting so the season produces a clear answer.

The investment decision also needs a budget. Obtain a quote covering equipment, installation, electricity, oxygen supply where required, maintenance, and monitoring. Compare those costs with the value of the measured harvest change and any demonstrated input savings. Equipment costs and payback require a farm-specific assessment.

Oxygen is easy to overlook because it is invisible, yet roots depend on it every day. Nanobubbles give growers another way to investigate that part of crop production. Pair the technology with sound irrigation management, good drainage, organic-matter building, and careful field measurement. Let the roots, harvest, and farm budget show where it earns a place.

# What the fields were telling me in Nebraska

**Author:** Saurav Das, Ph.D.
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0050
**Published:** 2026-09-13T19:04:30.572Z

The fields looked a little different through the truck window this time.

I was back in Scottsbluff visiting friends and family. Along the roads we took, I noticed less corn than I remembered, more sorghum-sudan and alfalfa, and people busy haying and stacking bales. The farmers I spoke with had put up good hay this year. I wanted to understand what had worked, and what they were thinking about for next season.

When I started talking with farmers, precipitation kept coming up. There hadn’t been enough. What people could grow, how much they could harvest, and what they would feed later all depended on how far the available water would stretch.

I also saw the main irrigation canal dry during my visit. I wondered how its delivery schedule had lined up with planting and cutting. That is a detail I still want to follow up on. In the fields around it, those hay stacks told another part of the story: people had found ways to bring a harvest home.

author: Saurav Das, Ph.D.
text:
That is a detail I still want to follow up on. In the fields around it, those hay stacks told another part of the story: people had found ways to bring a harvest home.

## The rain was only part of the water story

Back at my desk, I looked up the rainfall. NOAA’s county estimates put March–August precipitation in Scotts Bluff County at **8.36 inches**, against a **1991–2020 average of 11.18 inches**. That leaves **2.82 inches missing**, with about **75% of the usual total** received. [Explore the NOAA source data](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/county/time-series/NE-157/pcp/6/8/1990-2026?base_prd=true&begbaseyear=1991&endbaseyear=2020).

Swipe horizontally to inspect the full figure →

Click or tap to expand the figure

*NOAA NCEI Climate at a Glance, retrieved September 13, 2026. March–August precipitation estimates for Scotts Bluff County.*

Those numbers gave the conversations some context. Water in the soil, supplies in the river system and the timing of irrigation deliveries also shape a growing season. For a farmer planning the next cutting, when that water arrives matters a great deal.

UNL had described the wider problem before planting: western Panhandle growers were entering 2026 with both dry soil and a severely constrained surface-water supply. Farmers were making crop and irrigation decisions with that combination in mind. [Read the Panhandle Research, Extension and Education Center’s account](https://preec.unl.edu/news/growing-crops-limited-water-2026/).

The State Climate Office’s September 10 outlook offered better rain prospects, especially in eastern Nebraska. Around Scottsbluff, making the available water count was still very much on people’s minds. [Read the rainfall outlook](https://nsco.unl.edu/news/wetter-pattern-ahead/).

author: Saurav Das, Ph.D.
text:
Around Scottsbluff, making the available water count was still very much on people’s minds. [Read the rainfall outlook](https://nsco.unl.edu/news/wetter-pattern-ahead/).

## A good harvest, and the ground underneath

The hay stacks made me curious about the decisions behind them. Which fields had irrigation? When had the crop gone in, and when was it cut? How much useful feed did it provide? Those details would help explain what worked and which parts another farmer might try. Click to expand

*Haying and stacked bales were part of the view along the roads we took.*

Start with the job the crop needs to do. Sorghum-sudan can provide substantial summer forage. Pearl millet offers another hay or grazing option; foxtail millet fits a shorter, usually single-cut hay window. Established alfalfa has perennial roots and its own rhythm of cutting and recovery. [UNL’s summer-forage guide](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/pasture-and-forage-minute-getting-ahead-summer-grazing-challenges/) and [alfalfa guidance](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/pasture-and-forage-minute-managing-drought-stunted-alfalfa-and-first-cutting-irrigation/) help connect those choices to the farm’s needs. Purpose matters here. A forage crop is grown to feed animals; a cover crop is planted primarily to serve the soil and cropping system, and may also provide forage. Residue is the material left on the surface. The same species can play more than one role, but harvesting it changes how much cover and plant material remain. Living plants use water. Their canopy shades the ground, and stubble and residue can reduce evaporation and erosion after harvest. Water use and soil protection belong in the same conversation, with the next crop’s water supply kept in view.

title: What the fields were telling me in Nebraska
author: Saurav Das, Ph.D.
text:
Living plants use water. Their canopy shades the ground, and stubble and residue can reduce evaporation and erosion after harvest. Water use and soil protection belong in the same conversation, with the next crop’s water supply kept in view.

[NRCS explains soil cover](https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/state-offices/north-dakota/soil-health-principle-1-of-4-soil-armor) and [how harvest management affects what remains](https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-12/nrcs144p2_061991_Overview.pdf). For me, that brings the question into focus: **what can this field provide now, and what will it carry into next season?**

A recent Nebraska experiment gives some perspective on how much the season can change the opportunity. At **Rogers Memorial Farm in Lancaster County**, summer cover crops were planted after wheat and sampled in October over three years:

Swipe horizontally to inspect the full figure →

Click or tap to expand the figure

*Source: [UNL’s 2022–2024 summer cover crop study](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/summer-cover-crop-potential-eastern-nebraska/). Reported treatment-group means; dry aboveground biomass, before feeding or harvest losses. Species within the groups changed in some years. These are eastern Nebraska observations, where climate and soils differ from the Panhandle.*

The range catches my attention. Both groups produced much more in 2023 than in 2022, while 2024 brought useful biomass with considerably less rain than 2023. Stored water, rainfall timing and the plants themselves help shape the outcome. I would plan around a conservative harvest and keep a use in mind for extra feed or cover when conditions allow. There is another useful lesson closer to the Panhandle. In a **1999–2002 Sidney experiment**, subsequent wheat averaged **29.9 bushels/acre after fallow** and **23.2 after oat–pea forage**. Yet oat–pea forage and proso millet were economically competitive with fallow under that study’s conditions. The harvested crop had value of its own.

Reported treatment-group means; dry aboveground biomass, before feeding or harvest losses. Species within the groups changed in some years. These are eastern Nebraska observations, where climate and soils differ from the Panhandle.*

The range catches my attention. Both groups produced much more in 2023 than in 2022, while 2024 brought useful biomass with considerably less rain than 2023. Stored water, rainfall timing and the plants themselves help shape the outcome. I would plan around a conservative harvest and keep a use in mind for extra feed or cover when conditions allow. There is another useful lesson closer to the Panhandle. In a **1999–2002 Sidney experiment**, subsequent wheat averaged **29.9 bushels/acre after fallow** and **23.2 after oat–pea forage**. Yet oat–pea forage and proso millet were economically competitive with fallow under that study’s conditions. The harvested crop had value of its own.

## From having enough water to knowing what is in it

As we talked, another concern kept returning: nitrate. It came up in discussions about household water and about livestock feed.

For families in nearby Bayard, the concern was close to home. News Channel Nebraska reported a “Do Not Consume” notice on September 8. The city’s notice recorded a nitrate result of **61.6 mg/L** and said further sampling was underway. Residents can follow the city’s updates for instructions on their water supply. Nebraska’s wider investigation included nearly 3,500 returned private-well test kits. People want to understand the water their families and animals rely on. Testing a household well or livestock supply brings that question down to the place where a decision has to be made. [Nebraska’s study announcement and resources](https://dwee.nebraska.gov/news-events/press-releases/dwee-releases-report-statewide-nitrate-drinking-water-study) offer a starting point.

Nitrate can move through soil into groundwater. It can also accumulate in drought-stressed forage. Sampling the water and feed lets a farmer look at both sources of exposure with a veterinarian or nutritionist. For drinking water, boiling does not remove nitrate and can increase its concentration. ## The worry in the hay stack

For ranchers and livestock producers, a good harvest brought a practical question: how could they feed that hay with confidence after such a dry season?

Click to expand

*A closer look at the hay stacks along the route.*

Nitrate toxicity is well studied. In cattle, nitrite formed during digestion can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen. Severe poisoning can be fatal. [UNL’s livestock guide](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1779/na/pdf/view) explains why the feed concentration, intake and water supply all matter when planning a ration.

The concern has a history. A [March 2019 University of Missouri report](https://www.agriculture.com/livestock/cattle/in-last-30-days-200-dead-cows-in-the-state-of-missouri) described more than **200 cattle deaths from nitrate poisoning diagnosed by its veterinary laboratory in the preceding month**. Rapid or difficult breathing, tremors, staggering or collapse after feeding need an immediate call to a veterinarian.

One farmer told me her hens had stopped laying and wondered whether nitrate was involved. Her observation stayed with me. What would water and feed tests show alongside the timing of the change and the flock’s daily records? I would like to hear from farmers who have followed a similar question and researchers who could help investigate it. [Extension’s laying-flock guide](https://poultry.extension.org/articles/poultry-management/raising-chickens-for-egg-production/) offers a starting point for those records.

Farmers noticing a change can help identify where to look more closely and which research questions matter on the ground.

## What I would want to know before feeding—or buying

I would start with a sample that represents the hay being fed. UNL recommends a hay probe and **15–20 bales per representative lot** for feed analysis. Suspect bales or field areas may need separate toxin sampling. Ask the lab for nitrate testing alongside moisture, protein and energy. [UNL’s sampling guide](https://beef.unl.edu/sampling-and-testing-hay/) explains the process. Sorghum-family forage also needs attention to a separate prussic-acid risk and the laboratory’s sample-handling requirements. Pearl millet does not produce prussic acid, but it can accumulate nitrate. [UNL’s May 2026 guidance](https://beef.unl.edu/drought-increases-risk-prussic-acid-and-nitrate-poisoning/) is useful here. Nitrate can persist in stored hay, while ensiling can reduce it; silage still needs testing. [Tennessee Extension discusses storage](https://utbeef.tennessee.edu/cattle-nutrition-nitrates-do-they-dissipate/). Then the report needs to become a feeding plan. Nitrate and nitrate-nitrogen are different reporting units; dry-matter and as-fed results also differ. A veterinarian or nutritionist can interpret the feed and water results together for the animals involved. [UNL describes management options](https://beef.unl.edu/beefwatch/2021/what-do-high-nitrate-forage/), including dilution with low-nitrate feed and gradual adaptation. The feed available, equipment, labor and cost determine what is workable on a particular farm. Sometimes disposal enters that discussion. [Oklahoma State Extension](https://extension.okstate.edu/fact-sheets/nitrate-toxicity-in-livestock) discusses burning or burying forage with extremely high nitrate concentrations. A test result and local advice on handling the material should guide that decision.

[Oklahoma State Extension](https://extension.okstate.edu/fact-sheets/nitrate-toxicity-in-livestock) discusses burning or burying forage with extremely high nitrate concentrations. A test result and local advice on handling the material should guide that decision.

After paying to grow, cut and bale a crop, that is a difficult possibility to face. It is also a reason to bring testing into the plan early. The report matters to buyers, too. In his [August 3, 2026 guidance](https://preec.unl.edu/news/buying-feed-during-drought-keys-consider/), Nebraska Extension’s Aaron Berger recommends requesting a feed analysis before purchase, inspecting hay when uncertain and testing annual forages for nitrate. A grower with good hay to sell can use those results to explain its feeding value. Prices give that conversation another dimension. USDA’s **September 10, 2026** Nebraska report listed western-region good alfalfa in 3×4 large squares at **$285/ton, FOB farm/ranch**, and good/premium at **$330**. Grade, freight and feeding losses matter when valuing another lot. [Check the dated USDA report](https://www.ams.usda.gov/mnreports/ams_2935.pdf). For silage buyers, [UNL’s September 9 example](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/pasture-and-forage-minute-pricing-corn-silage-managing-nitrates-and-last-alfalfa-cutting/) values standing silage at **$38.25/ton at about 65% moisture**, using an illustrative **$5/bushel corn price**, before harvest and storage costs. Comparing feeds means putting them on the same dry-matter and feeding-value basis. That brings me back to next season: how could management make more of the harvest useful, protect the field and leave a margin for the farmer?

## Putting the practices together for next season

This is where the pieces start to fit. Crop choice, harvest timing, ground cover and nutrient management all affect what the farmer takes home and what the field has left. A useful combination gives each practice a job and checks how it affects the others.

Swipe horizontally to inspect the full figure →

Click or tap to expand the figure

*A way to think across two seasons, drawing on the linked Extension and NRCS guidance. The arrows show connected decisions; this is a planning framework rather than a measured water or nutrient balance.*

For a farm growing sorghum-sudan for hay, that might mean planting into retained residue, matching nitrogen to a realistic crop demand, choosing a suitable harvest stage and stubble height, and testing each hay lot. An alfalfa grower might put more attention into stand condition, irrigation timing and recovery between cuttings. A dryland field going into wheat needs a plan for the water carried forward.

Before ordering seed, check the previous crop’s herbicide records against the current labels for planting, haying and grazing restrictions. That can determine which options will fit. [UNL explains what to check](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/2019/check-herbicide-restrictions-planting-and-using-cover-crops/).

#### Combining management choices for next season

| Starting point | Practices to consider together | When to change the plan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Limited irrigation | Match crop and acreage to likely deliveries; time water to crop need; retain residue. | If deliveries shrink or arrive late, revisit acreage and priority fields before committing more inputs. |
| Summer annual hay | Match species, cutting stage and stubble height to feed needs; plan nitrogen; test each lot. | If regrowth or drying conditions deteriorate, reassess the next cutting and its costs. |
| Established alfalfa | Assess the stand; coordinate irrigation with cutting and recovery. | If water or stand vigor cannot support another profitable cutting, reassess harvest timing with local advice. |
| A forage window before the next crop | Choose species for the available window; set planting and termination decisions around soil water. | If establishment moisture or the usable window is inadequate, retain existing residue and conserve water. |
| Cattle available to graze | Combine suitable forage, feed testing, fencing and water access; set an exit point that retains cover. | Move cattle when soil conditions or remaining cover reach the limits agreed before grazing. |

| Combine suitable forage, feed testing, fencing and water access; set an exit point that retains cover. | Move cattle when soil conditions or remaining cover reach the limits agreed before grazing. |

*Planning choices to adapt with local Extension or an adviser, drawing on the forage, water and soil-cover sources in this article. Each row is a possible combination for a particular situation.*

A mixture can give species complementary jobs: forage, persistent residue or a legume contribution. Each addition still has to earn its seed cost and fit the planting and harvest window. For a farm already equipped to make hay, a change in cutting management or residue retention may be a manageable place to begin. Grazing would need its own budget for fencing, water and animal care, including any arrangement with a neighbor or custom grazier. There is research behind a flexible planting decision. A **2013–2018 Garden City, Kansas study** tested forage during fallow only when soil moisture and the seasonal outlook met its criteria; the flexible treatments were planted only in **2016**. The useful idea is to agree beforehand on conditions for planting and for conserving existing residue and water. A Panhandle farm would set those limits for its own soil, crop and rotation. [Read the flex-fallow study](https://acsess.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/csc2.20543). Grazing offers another way to make the pieces work together. A **2023 research review** found no subsequent crop-yield effect from grazing compared with ungrazed cover crops in **eight of 13 studies**. Compaction indicators increased in **six of 11 studies**, generally below the cited root-restricting level. That makes soil conditions and grazing management central to the opportunity. The authors identify wet ground and high stocking rates as concerns and call for more long-term work in water-limited regions. [Read the review](https://www.ars.usda.gov/research/publications/publication/?seqNo115=435874). Nutrients travel through this story too. Every bale carries some away from the field, including phosphorus and potassium. If hay is sold, that export belongs in the soil-testing and fertility budget.

If it is fed on the farm, where manure and urine return matters. Feeding in one place concentrates nutrients there; another field may still need them. [Aaron Berger’s discussion of nutrients in hay](https://beef.unl.edu/beefwatch/2022/value-hay-fertilizer/) connects feeding location with future forage production. Water can bring nutrients in. Hypothetical irrigation water containing **10 mg/L nitrate-nitrogen**, applied as **12 inches of effective irrigation**, supplies about **27 pounds of nitrogen per acre**, using [UNL’s conversion](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/ec117/2023/pdf/view/ec117-2023.pdf). The fertilizer credit depends on the crop and timing. Soil tests, manure history and an irrigation-water analysis help account for what is already available before buying more. title: What the fields were telling me in Nebraska
author: Saurav Das, Ph.D.
text:
The earlier stage should stay within locally appropriate harvest guidance. Compare all four combinations:

#### A proposed comparison of harvest timing and stubble height

| Comparison | First-cut timing | Stubble height |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current practice | Farmer’s usual acceptable stage | Farmer’s usual acceptable height |
| Timing change | Earlier suitable stage | Usual height |
| Height change | Usual stage | Higher retained stubble |
| Both changes | Earlier suitable stage | Higher retained stubble |

*Proposed comparison, not trial results. Set both stages and heights for the crop and growing conditions before starting.*

The layout separates the effects of timing and height, including how they work together. Keep variety, seeding rate, fertilizer and planned irrigation consistent. The [Nebraska On-Farm Research Network](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/on-farm-research/) can help repeat and randomize comparisons across the field; [UNL’s design guide](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/2016/10-steps-farm-research-success/) explains the approach.

Weigh and moisture-test every cutting, sample the hay lots for feed quality and nitrate, and record harvest and handling costs. Follow regrowth, photograph or measure ground cover on common dates, and measure soil moisture at consistent depths through the next planting. Where the rotation allows, follow the next crop’s yield too. A feed test and an agreed feeding plan remain part of using any trial hay.

Then compare the value of usable feed or purchased feed avoided, counted once, after extra costs and any change in the following crop’s return. Put that result beside the cover remaining. An earlier cut may reduce first-cut tonnage while changing quality, drying and regrowth. The trial lets a farmer weigh those outcomes using their own prices.

Even a result that favors the current practice is useful. It identifies something already working and gives the next experiment a better starting point.

## The questions worth following for longer

One season can teach us about a harvest. I would also like to see research that stays with the farm long enough to follow the soil, the rotation and the animals.

For water, that means measuring both crop use and what is left at the next planting. Which combinations retain more cover without drawing down the next crop’s water supply too far? How do the answers change between dryland fields and fields with dependable or delayed irrigation?

For feed, I would like to follow how variety, nitrogen supply, cutting height and growing conditions influence nitrate concentrations within a field and between cuttings. Alongside that, farmers’ water tests, feed records and animal observations could help researchers focus on exposure patterns and practical management questions. The hen observation is one invitation to that kind of work.

For farm economics, the costs of equipment, labor, nutrient replacement and a market belong beside production. Which combinations work with the resources a farm already has? The [Nebraska cover crop research resources](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/new-educational-resources-address-common-cover-crop-questions-nebraska/) bring water, biomass and partial budgets into the same discussion.

Longer trials could follow soil carbon, infiltration and nutrient movement alongside production. A network of farms using shared measurements through wet and dry years would help show which improvements last and what needs adapting locally. Farmers’ observations can shape the questions and help explain the results.

## What I brought home

I went to Nebraska to see people I care about. I came home thinking about the hay farmers had put up and the decisions behind it.

Those stacks give us something to build on. The next question is which parts of the season made them possible, and how farmers can carry that success forward while caring for the ground beneath them.

This fall, a useful start could be keeping hay-lot records and test results together. Before buying seed, review water, nutrients and the next crop’s needs. Then choose one manageable change, with a fallback if conditions turn dry. That could be a different cutting decision, a better place to return nutrients or a few strips set aside to learn from. The hope is in building on what already works, one season and one shared experience at a time.

And a hello from Lucky and Steel before I go.

If you tried cover crops or changed a management practice, I would like to hear how that went too. Those details can help another farmer and shape the next research question. We’ll ask before sharing your story.

# Nematodes as Soil Health Indicators: What Can a Test Tell You?

**Author:** Soil Health Exchange
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0055
**Published:** 2026-10-11T18:00:44.699Z

A nematode report can put two very different results on the same page: evidence of a more developed soil food web and a warning about organisms feeding on your crop. Both can be true. The useful question is which nematodes were found, how they were measured, and what the result changes about your next decision.

Nematodes are roundworms. Many soil-dwelling forms are microscopic and live in the water films around soil particles. Their feeding habits place them at several points in the food web, from organisms grazing on bacteria to predators eating other animals. That range makes the community informative about soil biology ⁠[[1]](#source-1)⁠[[2]](#source-2).

##### Begin with the decision

For a crop-pest concern, order a diagnostic assay that identifies and quantifies the relevant plant-parasitic nematodes. For a question about the soil food web, request a community assessment with feeding groups and clearly defined indices. Compare repeated samples collected with the same protocol, and connect the findings to roots, soil conditions, and crop performance.

## What management experiments show

Bongiorno and colleagues examined nematodes in 10 European long-term experiments using molecular profiling. In the seven experiments contributing to the tillage analysis, reduced tillage had higher MI, SI, and CI than conventional tillage, while EI was higher under conventional tillage. Estimated plant-feeder abundance was also 70% higher under reduced tillage ⁠[[4]](#source-4).

Swipe horizontally to inspect the full figure →

Click or tap to expand the figure

Topsoil results from the seven experiments in the tillage analysis, sampled in spring 2016. Points are model-estimated means; bars are their published 95% confidence intervals. The full model, including both soil layers, supported higher SI and lower EI under reduced tillage [[4]](#source-4). ·  —  · Figure: Original SHE plots using Bongiorno et al. (2019), Table 3

The practical lesson is to retain both readings: the food-web pattern and the identity and density of crop pests. A higher structure index can be useful evidence in monitoring a management change while the next crop still needs a separate pest-risk assessment.

A global meta-analysis by Puissant and colleagues brought together 103 publications and 4,855 effect sizes. Responses differed among feeding groups and practices: organic fertilization promoted microbial feeders, while rotation reduced plant feeders in the pooled evidence. Cover crops also changed nematode communities. The time since an intervention and the length of practice adoption influenced responses ⁠[[5]](#source-5).

Use those findings to choose a hypothesis worth testing locally. If you expect a cover crop to support a different community, decide which groups to follow and when to sample. If you expect pest suppression, measure the particular pest and check whether that cover-crop species and cultivar supports its reproduction ⁠[[5]](#source-5)⁠[[12]](#source-12).

## Where correlation ends and causation begins

Three relationships matter: management can change the nematode community; nematodes can influence soil processes; and a nematode measurement can track a process that several organisms drive. Each relationship asks for different evidence.

For example, Ferris and Matute studied vegetation-free microplots receiving different organic materials. Their average enrichment index was positively associated with cumulative mineral nitrogen, with a reported R² of 0.49. Both the nematodes and nitrogen release responded to the resources supplied and the activity of decomposers. That association made the index useful for following the process ⁠[[7]](#source-7).

Swipe horizontally to inspect the full figure →

Click or tap to expand the figure

A shared resource response helps explain an association between nematodes and nitrogen release. Controlled additions test the contribution of nematodes themselves [[6]](#source-6)[[7]](#source-7). ·  —  · Figure: Soil Health Exchange

Direct effects are supported by controlled experiments too. Ingham and colleagues added bacterial-feeding nematodes to simplified soil microcosms containing bacteria and blue grama grass. Plants initially acquired more nitrogen and grew faster than with bacteria alone. Adding fungal feeders did not produce the same growth response in that experiment ⁠[[6]](#source-6).

That establishes a mechanism under the tested conditions. Turning it into a fertilizer-rate decision requires evidence about nitrogen supply and crop response in the relevant field system. Use locally calibrated nutrient recommendations and suitable nitrogen tests for that decision; the community profile helps explain the biology alongside them ⁠[[15]](#source-15).

For a management question on your farm, compare replicated plots or strips, randomize the treatment within suitable blocks, and collect a baseline and comparable follow-up samples. Record crop, soil, weather, inputs, and outcomes. Several cores combined into one bag make one composite sample; independent treatment plots provide the replication needed to estimate a practice effect ⁠[[14]](#source-14).

## Collect a sample the laboratory can interpret

Arrange the protocol with the laboratory first. Community monitoring and pest diagnosis can require different sampling locations, timing, depths, and root material. For repeated monitoring, preserve the collection and laboratory methods; month, depth, field position, and handling can all change biological results ⁠[[16]](#source-16). 1. **Define the area.** Map a zone with reasonably consistent soil and management. Keep distinct soil types, drainage areas, and problem patches separate. 2. **Choose the window.** For monitoring, repeat a comparable crop-stage or seasonal window and record recent rainfall, tillage, amendments, and crop history. 3. **Collect the specified cores.** Spread them through the zone and use the laboratory’s depth and volume. Virginia Tech’s community protocol specifies 20–30 sub-cores at 6–8 inches in the root zone and late-summer sampling ⁠[[9]](#source-9). 4. **Mix and label the sample.** Use clean equipment, mix cores from the same zone, and record the zone, depth, collection date, crop, and purpose. 5. **Protect the organisms.** Keep the live-community sample field-moist and separate from soil being dried for other tests. Protect it from heat and follow the laboratory’s cooling instructions. Confirm any preservative required for a molecular assay. 6. **Ship promptly.** Virginia Tech requests cool, unfrozen samples and mailing within 24–48 hours. Confirm receipt arrangements before shipping ⁠[[9]](#source-9). For diagnosing poor growth, NCDA&CS recommends separate samples from the affected area and nearby normally growing plants, including roots where possible. Sample around the margin of the problem where affected plants are alive. Protect samples from overheating and freezing, and combine nematode testing with checks for other causes of poor growth ⁠[[10]](#source-10). Those are examples of laboratory protocols.

## Find out how the laboratory extracted and counted them

Microscopy-based assessments extract nematodes from soil, count them, and identify a subset closely enough to assign feeding and life-history groups. A Baermann-type method relies on living nematodes moving out of the sample into water. Other methods use physical separation such as sieving or centrifugation ⁠[[8]](#source-8).

Extraction is part of the measurement. Cesarz and colleagues experimentally varied soil thickness, filters, and sieving in Baermann extraction. Those choices changed recovery and community composition. Retain the extraction protocol when comparing reports across dates or laboratories ⁠[[8]](#source-8).

Molecular methods answer related questions through DNA. Ask whether the result is an assay for a target organism, calibrated qPCR abundance, or a sequencing profile of the community. Sequencing read proportions reflect recovered DNA and the analytical workflow; interpretation as organism counts requires suitable calibration ⁠[[4]](#source-4).

Before paying, request a sample report. It should let you find the soil mass or volume analyzed, moisture basis, count or DNA units, extraction method, identification detail, number of individuals identified where applicable, and the index definitions. If your next decision depends on a pest, confirm that the assay detects the relevant species and life stages.

## Find out how the laboratory extracted and counted them

Microscopy-based assessments extract nematodes from soil, count them, and identify a subset closely enough to assign feeding and life-history groups. A Baermann-type method relies on living nematodes moving out of the sample into water. Other methods use physical separation such as sieving or centrifugation ⁠[[8]](#source-8).

Extraction is part of the measurement. Cesarz and colleagues experimentally varied soil thickness, filters, and sieving in Baermann extraction. Those choices changed recovery and community composition. Retain the extraction protocol when comparing reports across dates or laboratories ⁠[[8]](#source-8).

Molecular methods answer related questions through DNA. Ask whether the result is an assay for a target organism, calibrated qPCR abundance, or a sequencing profile of the community. Sequencing read proportions reflect recovered DNA and the analytical workflow; interpretation as organism counts requires suitable calibration ⁠[[4]](#source-4).

Before paying, request a sample report. It should let you find the soil mass or volume analyzed, moisture basis, count or DNA units, extraction method, identification detail, number of individuals identified where applicable, and the index definitions. If your next decision depends on a pest, confirm that the assay detects the relevant species and life stages.

author: Soil Health Exchange
text:
Use comparable measurements for monitoring and crop-specific interpretation for pest management.

Cover-crop choice is a particularly useful decision point. NC State’s host-status guidance distinguishes southern root-knot, guava root-knot, and soybean cyst nematodes. A cover crop that interrupts one pest can support another; cultivar differences matter too. Identify the nematode first, then match the crop choice to that organism and the wider rotation ⁠[[12]](#source-12).

With a biological monitoring result, define the follow-up before buying an amendment or changing a practice. A result suggesting a resource pulse calls for a repeat measurement at a planned interval. A persistent pattern suggesting a simplified food web calls for a closer look at the habitat and a comparison that can test the suspected management cause.

## When is the test worth adding

A diagnostic nematode assay earns its place when the result can change a crop, variety, rotation, or pest-management decision. A community assessment earns its place when you need a baseline or comparison for a biological question and have the budget and sampling plan to repeat it.

Write the decision before ordering: “If this pest is present at a locally meaningful density, I will reconsider the next variety,” or “I want to know whether this change in disturbance is accompanied by a repeatable shift in the food web.” Ask who will interpret the result and what follow-up would distinguish the likely explanations.

Keep the profile beside routine fertility results, root observations, aggregate stability or water-entry measurements where relevant, and crop performance. SHE’s [guide to tracking soil-health progress](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/how-do-i-know-my-soil-is-getting-healthier) provides the broader monitoring framework.

The report becomes valuable when you can name the change, explain how it was measured, and decide what to do next. Nematodes offer a detailed view of the living soil. A good sampling plan connects that view to the field you manage.

**Have a nematode report to interpret?** Share your crop and location, sampling date and depth, laboratory method, group counts and units, indices, recent management, and the decision you are considering. Those details help SHE’s experts move from a number to a useful answer.

# NLFA vs. PLFA: What Do These Soil Biology Tests Measure?

**Author:** Soil Health Exchange
**Identifier:** SHE-ART-2026-0043
**Published:** 2026-08-04T17:03:15.218Z

##### The short answer

\*\*PLFA is mainly a membrane-lipid test; NLFA is mainly a storage-lipid test.\*\* PLFA is useful for estimating total living microbial biomass and detecting broad shifts in community composition. For AMF in mixed soil, NLFA 16:1ω5 is usually the more defensible lipid proxy. Neither result is a direct count of organisms or a measurement of microbial activity, diversity, plant benefit, or soil health [[1]](#source-1)[[2]](#source-2)[[8]](#source-8)[[9]](#source-9).

The acronyms look almost identical, which is why reports are often misread. **PLFA** means phospholipid fatty acid. **NLFA** means neutral lipid fatty acid. The important difference is not the instrument at the end of the analysis; it is the lipid fraction separated from the sample before the fatty acids are measured.

title: NLFA vs. PLFA: What Do These Soil Biology Tests Measure?
author: Soil Health Exchange
text:
The important difference is not the instrument at the end of the analysis; it is the lipid fraction separated from the sample before the fatty acids are measured.

#### NLFA and PLFA at a glance

| Feature | PLFA | NLFA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Full name | Phospholipid fatty acid | Neutral lipid fatty acid |
| Main biological pool | Cell-membrane phospholipids | Neutral storage lipids, especially triacylglycerols in fungi |
| Common soil use | Total microbial biomass proxy and broad community fingerprint | Storage-lipid or reserve-carbon proxy; targeted use for AMF |
| AMF-associated marker | PLFA 16:1ω5, with a disputed bacterial background in mixed soil | NLFA 16:1ω5, generally more sensitive and specific for AMF-associated biomass |
| Does it identify species? | No | No |
| Does it measure activity or crop benefit? | No | No |

Both are operational laboratory measurements: the result depends on the extraction, fractionation, marker rules, unit, and sample condition [[1]](#source-1)[[2]](#source-2)[[3]](#source-3)[[5]](#source-5).

## Start with the lipid, not the acronym

A fatty acid is a chemical building block that can occur in several kinds of lipids. Phospholipids form much of the membrane around microbial cells. Neutral lipids are uncharged compounds used prominently for energy and carbon storage. AMF store large quantities of lipids in spores, vesicles, and mycelium. The same fatty acid can therefore occur in both a membrane phospholipid and a neutral storage lipid; the fraction tells you which pool the laboratory recovered ⁠[[2]](#source-2)⁠[[5]](#source-5)⁠[[6]](#source-6).

author: Soil Health Exchange
text:
The same fatty acid can therefore occur in both a membrane phospholipid and a neutral storage lipid; the fraction tells you which pool the laboratory recovered ⁠[[2]](#source-2)⁠[[5]](#source-5)⁠[[6]](#source-6).

##### 16:1ω5 and C16:1cis11 name the same fatty acid

Both notations describe a 16-carbon fatty acid with one cis double bond. Counting from the methyl, or omega, end puts the double bond at omega-5; counting from the carboxyl end puts it at carbon 11. A report may also write 16:1ω5c or 16:1ω5cis. The notation does not tell you whether it came from the PLFA or NLFA fraction—that must be stated separately.

Click to expand

The fraction changes the biological meaning. Teal outlines represent membrane phospholipids contributed by many living organisms; amber droplets represent neutral storage lipids concentrated here in AMF hyphae and spores. In a common workflow, total lipids from one soil extract are separated into neutral-, glycolipid-, and phospholipid fractions; the figure follows only the neutral- and phospholipid paths. Fatty acids are converted to methyl esters (FAMEs) and analyzed by gas chromatography. The color key is conceptual, not a stain, and neither fraction by itself identifies AMF, species, or biological activity [[1]](#source-1)[[2]](#source-2)[[3]](#source-3)[[5]](#source-5)[[6]](#source-6). ·  —  · Photo: Soil Health Exchange scientific illustration (AI-assisted; scientifically reviewed)

## How the laboratory produces the number

1. **Collect and preserve the soil.** The sample is kept under the laboratory's specified temperature and holding time so the living community does not change before extraction.
2. **Extract the lipids.** An organic-solvent mixture removes a broad set of lipids from a known mass of soil.
3. **Separate lipid classes.** Solid-phase chromatography separates neutral lipids from glycolipids and polar phospholipids. This fractionation is what distinguishes NLFA from PLFA.
4. **Convert fatty acids to methyl esters.** A chemical reaction produces fatty-acid methyl esters that are suitable for gas chromatography.
5. **Separate and quantify the peaks.** Gas chromatography identifies compounds by retention behavior and measures them relative to standards.
6. **Apply biomarker rules.** The laboratory sums selected peaks into categories such as total PLFA, Gram-positive bacterial markers, Gram-negative bacterial markers, saprotrophic fungal markers, or AMF-associated 16:1ω5 ⁠[[1]](#source-1)⁠[[2]](#source-2)⁠[[3]](#source-3).

The method produces a **chemical fingerprint**, not a microscope image, culture, or DNA identification. Several organisms can share a fatty acid, and one organism contains many fatty acids. Group assignments are therefore proxies defined by a biomarker list, not a taxonomic census ⁠[[1]](#source-1)⁠[[2]](#source-2).

## What PLFA can tell you

Total PLFA concentration is widely used as a proxy for microbial biomass because phospholipids are central membrane components and generally do not accumulate as long-lived soil residues. A controlled paddy-soil incubation found half-lives of 14–27 hours for added phospholipids at 25°C, with an average near 20 hours; turnover was nearly twice as slow at 15°C ⁠[[4]](#source-4). This supports the membrane-biomass interpretation, but the exact values are not universal decay constants for every soil.

Longest measured half-life27 hours

Minimum, average, and maximum half-lives reported for added bacterial and fungal phospholipids in one paddy-soil incubation at 25°C. The study supports using intact phospholipids as a living-biomass proxy; it does not establish one half-life for all soils [4].

Individual or summed PLFA markers can also reveal whether two samples have different lipid profiles. That makes PLFA useful for monitoring a management change, land-use contrast, contamination gradient, or treatment experiment. It is rapid and sensitive to community shifts, but it cannot resolve individual species and should not be converted into a conventional species-diversity index ⁠[[1]](#source-1)⁠[[2]](#source-2).

#### How to read common PLFA outputs

| Report line | Defensible meaning | What it does not mean |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total PLFA | Sum of quantified phospholipid fatty acids under that protocol; a broad living-microbial-biomass proxy | Total cells, activity, diversity, or universal soil health |
| Bacterial PLFA | Sum of fatty acids the laboratory assigns to bacterial groups | Every bacterium or a species count |
| Fungal PLFA | One or more fungal-associated membrane markers, often including 18:2ω6,9 | All fungi; plant tissue can contribute some markers |
| AMF PLFA 16:1ω5 | A membrane-associated fatty acid that may include AMF and non-AMF background | A stand-alone AMF census in mixed soil |
| Fungal:bacterial ratio | Ratio of the laboratory's selected fungal marker sum to its selected bacterial marker sum | A literal biomass ratio or a universal optimum |
| Stress ratios | Changes in selected fatty-acid ratios that may be consistent with physiological or community shifts | A diagnosis of the cause of stress |

Marker names and sums vary among laboratories. Ask for the exact fatty acids included in every category [[1]](#source-1)[[2]](#source-2).

##### PLFA is a living-biomass proxy, not a viability assay

Rapid phospholipid turnover supports association with cells alive near sampling, but PLFA does not test whether an organism can grow, infect a root, reproduce, or perform a desired function. Use a culture, host bioassay, or another purpose-built viability test when viability is the question [[4]](#source-4).

## What NLFA can tell you

NLFA analysis measures fatty acids in neutral lipids. In fungi, that fraction commonly represents stored energy and carbon reserves rather than cell membranes. For AMF, the fatty acid 16:1ω5 can be abundant in neutral lipids of spores, vesicles, and mycelium. Controlled work linked spore number most strongly with NLFA 16:1ω5, while hyphal length related more closely to the phospholipid fraction in that experimental system ⁠[[5]](#source-5)⁠[[6]](#source-6).

A later comparison grew maize in three soils and compared root colonization and spore density with three lipid methods. NLFA 16:1ω5 had the highest correlation with spore counts. PLFA 16:1ω5 was not significantly correlated with spore density and did not reproducibly correlate with root colonization ⁠[[7]](#source-7). That study supports NLFA as an AMF-associated storage-biomass proxy, not as a substitute for every AMF measurement.

##### A higher NLFA number is not automatically better

Higher NLFA 16:1ω5 means more of that AMF-associated storage lipid per stated sample unit. It does not by itself show more arbuscules, greater infectivity, faster nutrient transfer, higher crop yield, or a beneficial fungal community. Storage allocation changes with AMF taxon, life stage, sporulation, host carbon supply, soil phosphorus, and season [[5]](#source-5)[[6]](#source-6)[[10]](#source-10).

## The hard question: can PLFA 16:1ω5 measure AMF?

In a sterile or otherwise well-controlled AMF experiment, PLFA 16:1ω5 can track membrane-rich AMF mycelium. The difficulty is assigning the same peak in mixed field soil. Olsson and Lekberg's 2022 review found that more than half of published studies had used PLFA 16:1ω5 to quantify AMF biomass without controls that could estimate the non-AMF contribution. They argued that bacterial background cannot be separated reliably and recommended NLFA 16:1ω5 for more accurate and sensitive AMF biomass assessment ⁠[[8]](#source-8).

There is a published scientific disagreement. Joergensen argued that there is no experimental evidence for marked amounts of PLFA 16:1ω5 in Gram-negative bacteria and supported its use as an AMF indicator ⁠[[2]](#source-2). A multi-author response concluded that specificity remains uncertain and recommended NLFA unless a control estimates contributions from other microbes ⁠[[9]](#source-9). The careful interpretation is therefore not that PLFA 16:1ω5 is useless, nor that it is universally AMF-specific: **its strength depends on the sample, comparison, and controls.**

The careful interpretation is therefore not that PLFA 16:1ω5 is useless, nor that it is universally AMF-specific: **its strength depends on the sample, comparison, and controls.**

#### When the 16:1ω5 marker is more or less convincing

| Situation | Interpretation strength | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Controlled AMF culture with a matched non-mycorrhizal control | Stronger for PLFA and NLFA | Background 16:1ω5 can be estimated |
| Field soil with NLFA 16:1ω5 and standardized comparison | Useful AMF-associated biomass proxy | Neutral fraction is generally more responsive and has less bacterial interference |
| Field soil with PLFA 16:1ω5 but no control | Weak as a stand-alone AMF estimate | AMF and non-AMF contributions cannot be separated confidently |
| Generic fungal PLFA or fungal:bacterial ratio | Not an AMF measurement | Pools broad groups and depends on the laboratory's marker definitions |

Specificity is a study-design property as much as a chemical property [[2]](#source-2)[[8]](#source-8)[[9]](#source-9).

## What about the NLFA:PLFA ratio?

The ratio of NLFA 16:1ω5 to PLFA 16:1ω5 has been used in controlled AMF studies as an index of carbon allocation to storage relative to membranes, sometimes described as fungal nutritional status. In the 1997 phosphorus experiment, the ratio changed with phosphorus supply ⁠[[6]](#source-6). But both numerator and denominator inherit the marker and extraction limitations, and the PLFA denominator may include non-AMF background. There is no universal ratio that defines a healthy field, an active fungus, or an optimal crop–AMF partnership.

#### What selected studies actually found

| Evidence | Data or result | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Controlled AMF phosphorus experiment [6] | Spore number related most closely to NLFA 16:1ω5; hyphal length to PLFA 16:1ω5 | The lipid fraction changes the biological pool represented |
| Maize grown in three soils [7] | NLFA had the highest correlation with spore counts; PLFA did not significantly correlate with spores and was inconsistent for root colonization | One AMF endpoint cannot be inferred reliably from another |
| 2022 critical review [8] | More than half of reviewed studies used PLFA 16:1ω5 for AMF biomass without proper controls | Published use does not guarantee valid specificity |
| Three-year cover-crop field study [10] | Propagule counts and NLFA C16:1cis11 were the most consistently responsive AMF measures; PLFA response was marginal | Treatment sensitivity and crop-performance relevance are separate questions |
| Seventeen prairie soils under alternative handling [11] | Air-drying, room-temperature storage, and oven-drying all caused significant PLFA losses and shifted biomarker ratios | Sample handling can change both totals and apparent community structure |

These results are method-specific observations, not calibration values for every soil.
