## Part 3: CREU — making comparisons fairer by matching potential

> CREU classifies land into units with similar soil-forming and climatic context, so that reference benchmarks actually mean something.

For practical benchmarking, a CREU can be delineated with three layers: the Major Land Resource Area (MLRA), soil texture, and a climatic moisture zone.

That moisture zone should not treat annual precipitation as a universal quantity. The same inch of rain can mean something very different where atmospheric water demand is higher, so precipitation is better interpreted relative to potential evapotranspiration (PET)—often expressed as an aridity index, or precipitation divided by PET.

Ecological Site Descriptions and State-and-Transition Models then help identify the appropriate reference plant community within that matched land context. Put simply, the CREU defines the fair comparison area; ecological information helps identify the reference condition.

The 2022 CREU paper demonstrated the method in Nebraska MLRA 67A and identified 45 CREUs. It turned a general warning—‘context matters’—into a repeatable land-classification approach. The next step is to extend and calibrate that approach with regional partners and reference data.

> Now we had two of the pieces: a measurable definition of “improvement” (a shrinking gap), and a fairness unit that controls for ecological potential.

But the hardest operational question was still open: where do the reference sites actually come from?

## Part 4: Reference sites — the fence-line problem (and why it matters)

Everyone reaches for fence lines, and I understand why — they look undisturbed, they’re easy, and they’re right there. But fence lines are often poor references. They can be shaped by runoff, dust and nutrient drift, compaction, invasion, and a long, invisible disturbance history; in windy regions, aeolian processes rework them outright.

More fundamentally, a fence line doesn’t necessarily represent the *productive ecological potential* of that land.

#### So we asked a different question: how do you identify a reference condition that is ecological, defensible, and repeatable?

## Part 5: What do we measure, realistically?

Soil health has too many indicators to measure everything, everywhere. Ask a farmer or program to repeat a 25- to 40-indicator panel, and cost and complexity quickly become the limiting factors. The practical question is which measurements carry distinct information and can be repeated consistently. Other national work has reached a similar conclusion: after evaluating more than 30 indicators across 124 North American sites, the Soil Health Institute recommended three core measurements ([Bagnall et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.soisec.2023.100084)).

Our [peer-reviewed Two-Tier framework](https://doi.org/10.1002/agg2.70449), published in *Agrosystems, Geosciences & Environment* in 2026, separates measurement from interpretation.

**Tier 1** is the repeatable core: organic matter, pH, nitrate-N, and bulk density. **Tier 2** interprets those same measurements against CREU-based reference distributions. A fungal-to-bacterial ratio can be added as an optional Tier 1+ biological measure when the question and budget justify it.

The study assessed 30 indicators using 53 composite soil samples collected across 16 native reference sites in two Nebraska MLRAs. Statistical screening identified the four Tier 1 indicators as representatives of carbon, chemical environment, nutrient availability, and physical condition. When principal component analysis was repeated on that four-indicator set, the first three principal components explained 88.6% of the variation within the reduced four-indicator dataset.

##### How to use the core set

Treat organic matter, pH, nitrate-N, and bulk density as a practical first layer measured with consistent methods. Add a biological indicator when it serves a clear purpose. Then use Tier 2 to interpret the values within their soil, climate, sampling, and management context.

Tier 2 draws its interpretation ranges from ecological reference distributions, using the 25th percentile, median, and 75th percentile within each available MLRA × texture context. These ranges work as reference envelopes: they show what is typical for a comparable native soil and help locate the size and direction of a cropland's gap.

## How to use this idea on a farm

Most farmers will not find a CREU label on a laboratory report today. That is okay. The useful first step is to ask what comparison sits behind the score. A target should reflect the soil, climate, landscape position, and production system closely enough to guide a real decision.

When you read a soil-health result, ask four questions:

- **What was this target built from?** — a national average, similar farms, or an ecological reference?
- **Does that comparison fit this field?** — consider texture, climate, drainage, landscape position, and crop system.
- **Was the sample collected comparably?** — depth, timing, laboratory method, and recent management all matter.
- **Is the field moving in the right direction?** — track the gap alongside yield stability, nutrient use, water movement, erosion, cost, and risk.

A native reference is a compass, not a prescription to return every field to native vegetation. For working cropland, a useful pathway is hierarchical: compare first with similar farms using feasible practices, then ask whether additional management can move the field closer to its ecological potential.

That changes the conversation from ‘Did I pass?’ to ‘What is realistic here, what direction am I moving, and what is the next useful step?’

That changes the conversation from ‘Did I pass?’ to ‘What is realistic here, what direction am I moving, and what is the next useful step?’

## What this changes for advisers and programs

A fair assessment can be both consistent and local. The framework separates those jobs so a program does not have to choose between them:

- Use a common Tier 1 measurement set and consistent sampling protocols.
- Match interpretation to the field's soil and climate context through Tier 2.
- Select reference sites from the intended ecological state, not simply the nearest undisturbed-looking fence line.
- Track soil indicators beside outcomes that matter to the farm, including productivity, water, nutrient efficiency, profitability, and risk.

This matters for incentives and carbon markets because the benchmark influences who appears to improve. Ecologically matched targets help programs reward change created through management instead of geography or inherited soil stocks. In plain terms, the baseline should distinguish new improvement from what would have existed anyway ([Kannegieter & Medlock, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44264-026-00155-8)).

## How the four papers build the framework

One practical question led to the next:

### 1. Soil Health Gap (2020): What counts as improvement?

The first paper defined improvement as closing the distance between managed soil and a relevant reference condition. It gave us a number that can be followed through time instead of a generic pass-or-fail score.

### 2. CREU (2022): Which soils are fair to compare?

The second paper created a land-classification approach for grouping soils with similar potential. It made the benchmark more local by accounting for soil-forming and climatic context.

### 3. Reference-site selection (2024): What should set the benchmark?

The third paper made reference selection repeatable through ecological sites, state-and-transition models, soil, and precipitation. The nearest fence line was no longer enough; the reference needed an ecological reason for being chosen.

title: A Fairer Way to Set Soil Health Targets
author: Saurav Das
text:
### 4. Two-Tier framework (2026): How can assessment stay practical and fair?

The fourth paper joined a four-indicator measurement core with CREU-based interpretation. It keeps the laboratory list manageable while allowing the meaning of each result to change with ecological context.

Seen together, the four papers move from defining the problem to a practical assessment architecture. The next work is to expand the reference network and test the framework across more working farms, regions, seasons, management systems, and outcomes.

## Where this goes next

Publication is an important step; usefulness on working farms is the larger goal. Soil Health Exchange can help move the framework from a research architecture into a practical, transparent tool.

- **Digitize CREU** — a map layer that identifies the CREU for any parcel from geospatial inputs: MLRA, soil texture or series, and an aridity zone based on precipitation relative to potential evapotranspiration.
- **Build reference distributions for each CREU** — the reference-based thresholds that drive Tier 2 interpretation.
- **Test Tier 1 on working farms** — pair reference sites, cropland, management records, and repeated measurements to see how the core indicators respond through time.
- **Make it farmer-usable** — a grower enters location, soil type/texture, and a few lab values (OM, pH, NO₃-N, BD), and gets back:
- “This is your CREU.”
- “These are your reference-informed thresholds.”
- “This is your soil health gap.”
- “And here’s what it implies — the management pathways that typically close that gap in your context.”
- **Connect scores to consequences** — test whether smaller gaps predict yield stability, nutrient-use efficiency, greenhouse-gas outcomes, water quality, and farm profitability.

The broader field is moving in the same direction. Production-environment benchmarks in New York stratify results by texture and cropping system, while the national SEMWISE model adjusts indicator expectations for clay and climate. These approaches are complementary: production data can define what is currently attainable; ecological references can show the longer-term potential and the distance still remaining.

That is the goal: simple measurement, local interpretation, and a target that helps rather than judges. Soil health does not need one universal scorecard. It needs a consistent way to ask a fairer question.

[Explore the CREU Map](/creu-map) to see how ecological context changes the benchmark, or [start a soil health assessment](/assess) and bring your own field into the conversation.

# 2026 Crop Year Agriculture Risk Coverage (ARC) and Price Loss Coverage (PLC)

**Funder:** USDA

**Type:** Payment program

**What you can get:** ARC provides support when covered farm revenue falls below its guarantee; PLC when covered commodity prices fall below the effective reference price.

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, Agricultural producers with a share interest in covered commodities grown on a farm with base acres

**Coverage:** Available nationwide

**Deadline & timing:** Due December 11, 2026. 2026 ARC/PLC election and enrollment runs September 16 through December 11, 2026. If no 2026 election is submitted by December 11, the prior (2025) election carries over and the farm is ineligible for 2026 payments. Producers must enroll through a signed contract each year (a new multi-year contract for 2026-2031 is optional). 2027 election and enrollment runs November 2, 2026 through March 15, 2027. Contact your local FSA office.

## Eligibility

Landowners without a share interest in the crops cannot enroll. An annual signed enrollment contract is required; consult FSA about the new multi-year option.

**Official program URL:** https://www.fsa.usda.gov/resources/income-support/arc-plc

**Funder:** Agoro Carbon Alliance (Yara)

**Type:** Payment program

**What you can get:** Per-tonne payments for new soil carbon above a sampled baseline; choice of issuance payments or upfront prepayments • One of the few programs covering grazing land as well as row crops; agronomic support included

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, farms and ranches with a minimum of 400 enrolled acres (farmland, range/pastureland, or a combination; acres need not be contiguous) adopting at least one new practice cover crops, reduced till, improved grazing, or N management under a 10 year contract

**Coverage:** Available nationwide

**Deadline & timing:** Current official program page offers a producer inquiry and tailored eligibility evaluation, without a fixed application deadline or dated bonus offer. US farms and ranches generally need at least 400 acres, three or more years in crop or livestock production, legal rights to implement practices, and a qualifying new practice maintained for a 10-year term. Producers who already adopted some conservation practices may still qualify after an individual evaluation.

**Funder:** AgriCapture

**Type:** Payment program

**What you can get:** Direct per-acre incentive payments for verified methane reductions; rates are quoted per operation and are not published • AgriCapture contracts directly with the farmer and handles registration, verification, and credit sale, so the grower takes an incentive payment rather than managing credits. Satellite and remote-sensing monitoring. Also runs row-crop premium and grassland soil-carbon programs.

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, rice growers in the Lower Mississippi Delta and Gulf rice states who adopt Alternate Wetting and Drying or Furrow Irrigated Rice plus efficient fertilizer management

**Coverage:** AR, LA, MS, MO, TX

**Deadline & timing:** Rolling enrollment via the farmer contact form on AgriCapture's For Farmers page; no deadline is posted. Provide crop type, acreage, location, and management practices so the farm management team can evaluate eligibility. Rice farmers in the U.S. project (acreage spans Missouri to Texas) use methane-reducing practices such as alternate wetting & drying (AWD) or furrow irrigation.

**Tags (stated on page):** water quality, nutrient management, climate smart, soil health

**Official program URL:** https://agricapture.com/farmers/

text:
# Agricultural Revolving Loan Fund (ARLF)

**Funder:** Alaska Department of Natural Resources, Division of Agriculture

**Type:** Loan

**What you can get:** Loan-class maximums from $200,000 to $3,000,000; $3,000,000 total outstanding per borrower • Fixed rates 3.0–4.0%. Classes: short-term operating ($200,000, 4.00%), chattel equipment/livestock ($3,000,000, 3.00%), farm development ($3,000,000), irrigation ($3,000,000), product processing ($500,000), land clearing ($250,000). Loans may not exceed 75% of collateral value less existing liens.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, Alaska residents engaged in commercial agriculture — individuals, partnerships, joint ventures, or corporations with demonstrated farming experience

**Coverage:** AK

**Deadline & timing:** The October 17, 2026 application-entry cutoff for the November 17 board meeting has passed. December board meeting is only if needed; no later application-entry cutoff is published. Loan applications continue through ARLF staff for a future scheduled board review; contact the loan officer for timing.

## Eligibility

Individuals and business entities must provide proof of current Alaska residency at loan closing and evidence of agricultural or related business experience and skills. Funds are limited to agricultural production or processing in Alaska, with adequate collateral and loans limited to 75% of collateral value less existing liens.

**Tags (stated on page):** beginning farmer, livestock infrastructure, energy efficiency, land programs

**Official program URL:** https://dnr.alaska.gov/ag/ag_arlf.htm

text:
# Groundwater Conservation Tax Credit Program

**Funder:** Arkansas Department of Agriculture, Natural Resources Division

**Type:** Other

**What you can get:** 25–50% of project cost as a state income tax credit • Impoundments of 20+ acre-feet: 50%. Surface water conversion: 25% outside critical groundwater areas, 50% inside, $35,000 lifetime cap. Land leveling: 25%. Annual agricultural credit capped at the lesser of tax due or $18,000, with a 15-year carryforward. A 3% application fee ($100–$1,500) applies.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, Arkansas agricultural landowners and water users who build surface water impoundments, convert from groundwater to surface water, or land level to reduce irrigation water use

**Coverage:** AR

**Deadline & timing:** Rolling. Applications go to the local Conservation District and are reviewed by the Natural Resources Commission. Critical: the project must be approved BEFORE construction begins and maintained for 10 years after completion.

## Eligibility

Eligible applicants: producer, Arkansas agricultural landowners and water users who build surface water impoundments, convert from groundwater to surface water, or land-level to reduce irrigation water use.

**Tags (stated on page):** water quality, energy efficiency, climate smart

# Beginning with Compeer Grant

# California FarmLink Farm Loans (Operating, Term, Conservation, Disaster & Land)

**Funder:** California FarmLink (nonprofit CDFI)

**Type:** Loan

**What you can get:** $5,000 - $2.2 million depending on loan type • Nonprofit CDFI lender. Operating and term loans from $5,000 at 7.00% fixed (1% discount for graduates of FarmLink courses; limited to 3 loans, first $100K and first 5 years, not on land loans); Conservation loans up to $100,000 at 3.5% as bridge financing for EQIP, Healthy Soils, SWEEP, Carl Moyer or organic transition, and require an agreement to work with a Resource Conservation District; Disaster Relief loans up to $50,000 at 0-3.5% with no fees (limited funds available); Land and housing loans up to $2.2M at competitive index-tied rates. Closing fees 0.5-2%, no prepayment penalty. More than $80 million lent since 2012.

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, Farmers, ranchers, and fishers in a current management role in a California based operation, with at least two years of farming/fishing experience earning income as an owner or employee, secure land tenure (written lease or ownership), and active sales channels; no minimum credit score.

**Coverage:** CA

**Deadline & timing:** Open and lending on a rolling basis as of August 2026. No deadline - three-step process (inquiry, application, decision) taking roughly 2-4 months from initial contact to closing.

Eligible applicants: producer, Farmers, ranchers, and fishers in a current management role in a California-based operation, with at least two years of farming/fishing experience earning income as an owner or employee, secure land tenure (written lease or ownership), and active sales channels; no minimum credit score..

text:
# Carbon by Indigo

**Funder:** Indigo Ag

**Type:** Payment program

**What you can get:** Farmers receive 75% of the net price buyers pay for verified carbon credits, paid over five years • Outcome-based: pays for carbon sequestered, not a lump sum for practice change. Credits issued by the Climate Action Reserve (independent registry); 2M+ credits issued to date. Payments are paid on a five-year schedule, contingent on maintaining practices and soil carbon, and subject to a buffer pool holdback of up to 20% of credits.

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, row crop farmers growing any of 18 eligible crops adopting new carbon sequestering practices

**Coverage:** AL, AZ, AR, CA, CO, CT, DE, FL, GA, ID, IL, IN, IA, KS, KY, LA, ME, MD, MA, MI, MN, MS, MO, MT, NE, NV, NH, NJ, NM, NY, NC, ND, OH, OK, OR, PA, RI, SC, SD, TN, TX, UT, VT, VA, WA, WV, WI, WY

**Deadline & timing:** Rolling enrollment; program ongoing.

## Eligibility

Enrollment is open to growers in the lower 48 United States. Fields must meet Climate Action Reserve Soil Enrichment Protocol requirements and adopt eligible new practices. The standard program pays growers 75% of carbon-credit revenue, subject to vesting; confirm field eligibility and current contractual terms with Indigo.

**Tags (stated on page):** soil health, cover crop, climate smart

**Official program URL:** https://www.indigoag.com/carbon-credits

# Catalyzing Agroforestry Grant Program

**Funder:** Virginia Tech Agroforestry with regional partners (funded by Edwards Mother Earth Foundation and Southern SARE)

**Type:** Grant

**What you can get:** Field practices up to $1,500/acre (first 4 acres), $1,000/acre (acres 5-8), $750/acre beyond; forest farming up to $1,000 for 1/4 acre plus up to $500/acre site prep • Reimbursement of documented project expenses after project completion, capped per acre by practice • Projects must be completed within 18 months of award. **Readiness:** Prep docs first

# Foodshed Capital Farm & Food Business Loans

**Funder:** Foodshed Capital (nonprofit CDFI loan fund)

**Type:** Loan

**What you can get:** $5,000 - $150,000 • Nonprofit CDFI loan fund. Rates 0%-6.75% (2024 average was 1.88%), with a half-point reduction for auto-pay; terms 3-7 years with an optional 3-month grace period. No credit score is pulled and credit scores are not part of underwriting. Businesses without historical financials are capped at $15,000 unless bridging a grant award. Loans cover equipment, working capital, sustainability improvements, and staffing - NOT farmland purchase. Free business advising is included for applicants navigating the loan process.

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, Farmers and food business owners age 18+ who own or manage a registered business centered on food production and use regenerative agricultural practices, with at least two full seasons of production experience (one year for non farm food businesses); operations focused on hydroponics, aquaponics, alcohol, cannabis/hemp, commodity crops, or monoculture are not eligible.

**Coverage:** Available nationwide

**Deadline & timing:** Intake is available through the online lending portal with no published cutoff. Foodshed considers new U.S. locations through intake; its FAQ reports past lending in 19 states, DC and Puerto Rico.

## Eligibility

Standard loan size cannot exceed the prior year of revenue. Applicants need an eligible food-focused regenerative business and relevant experience; evidence of business structure may include Schedule F. Tax compliance and financial need are considered. No farmland purchase. Geography is considered through intake; national coverage is not guaranteed.

**Tags (stated on page):** soil health, beginning farmer, organic transition, livestock infrastructure

**Official program URL:** https://www.foodcap.org/lending

# Guaranteed Farm Loans

**Funder:** USDA Farm Service Agency

**Type:** Loan guarantee

**What you can get:** The current official page lists $2,558,000 for standard operating, ownership and conservation guarantees; limit adjusts annually each fiscal year. • A commercial lender advances the loan, with an FSA guarantee of up to 95%; rates and repayment terms are negotiated within FSA limits.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, Eligible family farm owner operators or tenant operators who need an FSA guarantee to obtain a loan; Conservation Loan applicants have exceptions to the family farm and credit elsewhere tests

Applicants must meet FSA citizenship/residency, credit, legal capacity and federal-debt requirements. text:
# Livestock Forage Disaster Program (LFP)

**Funder:** USDA Farm Service Agency

**Type:** Payment program

**What you can get:** Monthly payments based on drought severity (U.S. Drought Monitor) and eligible livestock units; for eligible fire losses, livestock numbers and grazing days lost. • Drought payment months: D2 for at least four consecutive weeks = 1 (was eight weeks before the Working Families Tax Cuts Act update); D2 for at least 7 of 8 consecutive weeks = 2; D3 at any time = 3; D3 for at least four weeks or D4 at any time = 4; D4 for four weeks, not necessarily consecutive = 5.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, Livestock producers with qualifying drought related grazing losses or fire related grazing losses on federally managed land

**Coverage:** Available nationwide

**Deadline & timing:** Due March 1, 2027. For grazing losses occurring in 2026, apply by March 1, 2027. The official deadline is March 1 after the calendar year of loss. Eligibility depends on qualifying drought or fire, and required local FSA documentation.

## Eligibility

Livestock producers who own or lease grazing land or pastureland in a county with qualifying drought, or who cannot graze permitted livestock on federally managed rangeland because of fire. A one-month drought payment now triggers after four consecutive weeks of D2 (severe) drought on the U.S. Drought Monitor during the normal grazing period, down from eight weeks. Verifiable documentation of grazing losses is required.

**Tags (stated on page):** risk management, grazing, rangeland

**Official program URL:** https://www.fsa.usda.gov/resources/disaster-recovery/livestock-forage-disaster-program-lfp

# The Farmer Fund (Natural Disaster & Medical Crisis Relief)

**Funder:** Georgia Organics

**Type:** Grant

**What you can get:** Emergency relief grants, capped by an annual per-farm relief cap • Natural disaster aid covers qualifying weather damage to crops, livestock, equipment or infrastructure, excluding pests, predators, drought, lack of infrastructure and unrelated sales losses. For this track, owners must have been in business for 6 months before applying. Medical crisis aid covers sudden unexpected work/income loss due to injury, physical or mental illness, or family death, excluding chronic conditions and medical bills; owners must have operated, and workers been employed, for 6 months before the medical emergency. Both tracks require applying within 60 days of the qualifying event. Annual relief cap applies; no dollar amount is posted.

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, Established Georgia based producers (not resellers) who are current active Georgia Organics Farmer Members, farm using soil based sustainable practices, and sell through farmers markets, CSAs, wholesale, or restaurants; a separate track covers farm employees hit by a medical crisis or a death in the family.

**Coverage:** GA

**Deadline & timing:** Natural-disaster and medical-crisis aid applications remain active as checked October 10, 2026. Apply within 60 days of the qualifying weather event or medical crisis; this is an individual event-triggered deadline. Hurricane Helene and November 2025 SNAP/EBT loss tracks are closed; SNAP/EBT closed January 12, 2026.

Eligible applicants: producer, Established Georgia-based producers (not resellers) who are current active Georgia Organics Farmer Members, farm using soil-based sustainable practices, and sell through farmers markets, CSAs, wholesale, or restaurants; a separate track covers farm employees hit by a medical crisis or a death in the family..

# Regenerative Farmer Assurance Fund (RFAF)

**Funder:** FarmBridge Fund (Healing Soils Foundation)

**Type:** Grant

**What you can get:** Up to $50,000 per farmer • Recoupable bridge capital, repaid only when the delayed public funding or contracted payment is received; no interest rate is published

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, Certified organic or regenerative farmers in 12 Midwest states, Farmers with a verifiable trigger: documented public reimbursement or grant approval (e.g., EQIP, CSP, REAP, CRP, FLSP), signed buyer contract or purchase order, time sensitive infrastructure need tied to practice adoption, or an emerging market opportunity such as a retailer/processor letter of intent

**Coverage:** IL, IN, IA, KS, MI, MN, MO, NE, ND, OH, SD, WI

**Deadline & timing:** Rolling applications; funds are distributed as available. Current Round 3 program page verified November 7, 2026; no fixed application deadline stated.

Recoupable bridge grant: the farmer reimburses the fund if and when the delayed public funding or contracted payment arrives; if a validated reimbursement never arrives despite signed contracts the grant converts to non-recoupable aid. Farmers may reapply for larger infrastructure needs. Short application with supporting documentation; rapid review of readiness, timing, regenerative impact and documentation; approved farmers receive funds upfront.

text:
# Habitat Improvement Program (HIP)

**Funder:** Idaho Department of Fish and Game

**Type:** Cost-share

**What you can get:** generally up to 75% of out-of-pocket expenses • general limit of $10,000 per project • Limits and percentages vary for food plot and wetland projects; per the HIP Guidelines, 100% cost-share if project lands are enrolled in Access Yes for 5 years.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, local government, state government, Private landowners in Idaho (upland game bird / waterfowl habitat on farm and ranch land)

**Coverage:** ID

**Deadline & timing:** Contact the nearest Idaho Fish and Game habitat biologist to request HIP assistance. No fixed application window is stated. Approved projects require a cooperative agreement and project plan.

## Eligibility

Technical and financial help for private landowners and public land managers creating or enhancing upland game bird and waterfowl habitat. Eligible work includes grass/legume nesting cover, fencing livestock out of woody areas, farmstead and field windbreaks, winter food plots, managing livestock use of existing cover, and creating or restoring wetlands. Agreements usually require maintaining the project for at least 10 years (food plots 1-2 years). Fee hunting is not allowed on HIP-contract lands. The HIP Guidelines page lists practice rates, e.g. $20/acre for leaving grain stubble (max $2,000 per operation). Some rates there (e.g. a 2009 AUM lease rate) look dated, so confirm with the regional biologist.

**Tags (stated on page):** grazing, water quality

**Official program URL:** https://idfg.idaho.gov/conservation/habitat/hip

**Last verified:** Nov 14, 2026

# County Agricultural Incentives Program (CAIP)

**Funder:** Kentucky Office of Agricultural Policy / Kentucky Agricultural Development Board (Kentucky Agricultural Development Fund), administered by county program administrators

**Type:** Cost-share

**What you can get:** Reimbursement-based cost-share on approved investments after project completion and proof of payment; county sets per-producer cap • County maximum per producer, not to exceed $5,000 statewide per producer per program year. Investment areas include farm infrastructure/fencing/water enhancement, forage and grain improvement, beef and dairy cattle, goats and sheep, horticulture, poultry, swine, bees, timber, energy, marketing and value-added production. Applications are competitively scored (producer questions, 140 points).

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, Kentucky resident producers (owners or tenant farmers with landowner approval), 18+, with a Kentucky Agriculture Water Quality Act plan or self certification; one applicant per household per program year

**Coverage:** KY

**Deadline & timing:** Producer application windows are set by each county program administrator for at least 15 business days. Confirm current local enrollment and the county award limit. The state October 30, 2026 county-program submission deadline is for administrators, not producer applications. No statewide producer reopening date is announced.

## Eligibility

Eligible applicants: producer, Kentucky resident producers (owners or tenant farmers with landowner approval), 18+, with a Kentucky Agriculture Water Quality Act plan or self-certification; one applicant per household per program year.

**Tags (stated on page):** livestock infrastructure, grazing, water quality, energy efficiency, marketing

**Official program URL:** https://www.kyagr.com/agpolicy/2026-Program-Guidelines-and-Applications.html

**Funder:** Sand County Foundation

**Type:** Grant

**What you can get:** $10,000 award • Recognition award for exceptional soil, water, and habitat stewardship on working lands

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, private working land owners (farmers, ranchers, forestland owners) in 28 participating states; self nomination allowed

# Maryland Conservation Buffer Initiative

**Funder:** Maryland Department of Agriculture, through local Soil Conservation Districts

**Type:** Payment program

**What you can get:** Practice-specific payments range from $500/acre for existing grass buffers to $4,500/acre for specified riparian forest buffers with pasture fencing. Forest buffers may receive an additional $1,000/acre tree bonus and up to $330/acre/year maintenance support for five years. • Payments split 75% upfront and 25% after planting verification. Confirm the applicable practice rate, width and contract requirements with the district; these are per-acre figures, not an award cap.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, Maryland farmers and landowners responsible for eligible streamside, ditchside or pasture adjacent land; tenants need a lease covering the buffer term or landowner agreement

**Coverage:** MD

**Deadline & timing:** Due April 30, 2027. Current 2026-2027 enrollment accepts applications November 1, 2026 through April 30, 2027. Apply through the local soil conservation district; obtain approval and required plans before installation.

## Eligibility

Must be in good standing with state/USDA cost-share programs and submit a current Nutrient Management Plan Certification. Land already enrolled in MACS, CRP, CREP, EQIP or mandated by an easement is ineligible. Grass-buffer agreements run five years; forest-buffer agreements run ten years. Buffer width, placement and maintenance requirements apply; field ditches cannot receive woody buffers. Plant within one year of the signed agreement.

**Tags (stated on page):** water quality, land programs, grazing

**Official program URL:** https://mda.maryland.gov/conservation/grants-soil-water-conservation/conservation-buffer-initiative

# Maryland Manure Transport and Injection Grants

**Funder:** Maryland Department of Agriculture Conservation Grants Program

**Type:** Cost-share

**What you can get:** Dairy/livestock transport: up to 87.5% of eligible costs • Poultry transport: up to $28/ton; liquid-manure injection: up to $45/acre • Dairy/livestock FastTrack receiving farms: $15,000/season,$30,000/year cap per current linked factsheet; rates vary with distance and manure type. Poultry is ineligible for injection.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, Eligible farmers receiving manure and registered manure brokers; pathway specific conditions apply.

**Coverage:** MD

**Deadline & timing:** Fall 2026 funding available. Work must finish December 15, 2026. Livestock/dairy transport and injection payment claims due January 15, 2027; poultry claims within 40 days of final transport. Standard grants need preapproval; qualified FastTrack permits haul-now/apply-later. These are work/claim dates, not a fixed application cutoff.

## Eligibility

Poultry transport: Maryland source farm raising broilers for participating Delmarva companies; distance >7 miles; receiving fields P-FIV ≤150. Dairy/livestock FastTrack: receiving farm, distance >1 mile, P-FIV ≤100, crops/hay <25% legumes; organic nutrient-plan recommendations required. Standard dairy/livestock transport permits P-FIV 101–150 with phosphorus-based recommendations; preapproval required. Injection fields require P-FIV <500; poultry excluded. Out-of-state receiving-field eligibility remains unconfirmed. Source

# Wolf-Livestock Conflict Prevention Grant

**Funder:** Minnesota Department of Agriculture (MDA)

**Type:** Reimbursement

**What you can get:** $500–$10,000 per project per FY2027 RFP; $25,000 total round funding. • 80% reimbursed by grant; 20% grantee cost-share • Reimbursement of documented expenses • $25,000 total available in this round

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, Minnesota livestock producers within the wolf range or with documented wolf depredation

**Coverage:** MN

**Deadline & timing:** Due November 17, 2026. Conflicting official dates: live program page states November 17, 2026 at 4 p.m. Central; linked FY27 RFP and September 29 news release state December 18 at 4 p.m. Central. Use the earlier November 17 date for planning and confirm with MDA before relying on either. Live-page questions cutoff November 10 conflicts with RFP December 11. Work/expense reporting due October 31, 2027.

## Eligibility

# Montana Beginning Farm/Ranch Loan Program

**Funder:** Montana Department of Agriculture (Montana Agriculture Loan Authority)

**Type:** Loan

**What you can get:** $558,000 for agricultural land and improvements; no more than $125,000 for depreciable agricultural property, of which no more than $62,500 for used property • No minimum loan amount. Lender makes the credit evaluation and sets terms with the borrower.

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, Beginning farmers/ranchers (first time producers) who are Montana residents

**Coverage:** MT

**Deadline & timing:** Official page (checked 2026-09-30): "There is no formal or defined application period. The loan program is ongoing, therefore an application may be submitted at any time." Application requires the application form, current financial statement, background letter and a non-refundable $50 application fee.

## Eligibility

Tax-exempt bond program: the beginning farmer's lender (or a seller on contract) obtains a federally tax-exempt bond through the department, lowering the interest rate. Applicant must be at least 18, a first-time producer, net worth not to exceed $450,000, a Montana resident when the bond is issued, with documented training/experience; may not have previously owned any substantial amount of farm/ranch land. Funds may be used to purchase agricultural land, improvements and depreciable agricultural property.

text:
# NC AgVentures Farm Grant

**Funder:** NC AgVentures (NC State Extension, funded by the NC Tobacco Trust Fund Commission)

**Type:** Grant

**What you can get:** Up to $10,000 • Direct grants to individual farms for new or expanded agricultural ventures - new farm directions, technology adoption, and projects that strengthen farm resilience and efficiency. Applicants must contact their county Extension Agent by December 1 to discuss the proposal before submitting.

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, North Carolina family farms in 46 eligible counties whose farm has been revenue generating for at least one year (local non profit community organizations are also eligible); priority goes to current or former tobacco growers, quota holders, tobacco workers and close family descendants, farms that have not received previous grants, and applicants earning at least 50% of gross personal income from the farm operation.

**Coverage:** NC

**Deadline & timing:** Due December 15, 2026. Applications open October 15, 2026 and close December 15, 2026 at 6 p.m., or as soon as 200 applications have been submitted, whichever comes first, so apply early in the window. Maximum award is $10,000. Your farm must have generated revenue for at least one year and be in one of the program's eligible North Carolina counties (listed on the application page). Contact your Extension agent by December 1 to consult on your project proposal and review your application.

## Eligibility

NC-resident independent family farm in one of 46 listed counties, revenue-generating at least one year. One application per farm; married couples, domestic and business partners submit one. 2025–2026 recipients must wait one year; farms with three prior AgVentures grants are ineligible. Current NC State Extension agents and spouses/partners, and NC State University employees, cannot receive personal grants. Grant funds cannot purchase land or animals. Match requirement: Guidelines require a cash contribution of 15% of total project cost (no in-kind). The application page describes a budget at least 15% above the requested grant; confirm the required match basis with Extension..

# Bank of North Dakota Ag PACE

**Funder:** Bank of North Dakota

**Type:** Loan

**What you can get:** Total loan amount may not exceed project cost. • Interest buydown on local lender/BND loans. General cap: $50,000 per project or biennium, up to $100,000 lifetime on separate projects or biennia. Subsurface field tiling and irrigation instead share a $50,000 lifetime buydown cap. General rate reduction up to 4 percentage points; tiling/irrigation up to 2 points; minimum borrower rate 1%.

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer

**Coverage:** ND

**Deadline & timing:** Rolling through participating local lenders; contact your lender before applying.

North Dakota resident whose principal occupation is farming or ranching. The project must be in North Dakota and a qualifying nontraditional or value-added business integrated into the farm operation; traditional production agriculture is excluded. Buydowns above $50,000 require applicant net worth below $1,500,000.

text:
# Soil and Water Conservation Grants (Farmland Preservation Program)

**Funder:** New Jersey State Agriculture Development Committee

**Type:** Cost-share

**What you can get:** Up to 50% • Eligible projects: terrace systems, diversions, water impoundment reservoirs, irrigation systems, sediment retention and erosion or water control systems, drainage systems, animal waste control facilities, and land shaping and grading. Landowners apply to their local Soil Conservation District, which helps develop the farm conservation plan; applications are forwarded to the NJ State Soil Conservation Committee, which recommends projects to the SADC for funding approval.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, New Jersey landowners or farm operators with written landowner permission whose farms are permanently preserved or in an 8 year or 16 year term farmland preservation program

**Coverage:** NJ

**Deadline & timing:** No fixed producer deadline is posted. Apply through the local Soil Conservation District for approved soil and water conservation projects on farms in permanent or 8-year/16-year term preservation programs. SADC reimburses up to 50% after approval. The separate preserved-farm wildlife fencing program accepts applications at any time.

## Eligibility

Eligible farms are permanently preserved or enrolled in term farmland preservation programs of 8 or 16 years. The landowner or current farm operator with written permission applies through the local Soil Conservation District; a farm conservation plan and technical approval are required.

**Tags (stated on page):** water quality, manure management, soil health, land programs

**Official program URL:** https://www.nj.gov/agriculture/financial-services/grants/

# Central Tri-County Small Acreage Agriculture Program

**Funder:** Central Tri-County Soil & Water Conservation District

**Type:** Cost-share

**What you can get:** 85% of actual eligible project costs • $10,000 maximum reimbursement for all projects • Payments follow completed work and district inspection; eligible examples include water management, livestock water, fencing, windbreaks and planting.

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, Owners of small agriculture properties from one lot to 1,000 acres within Central Tri County SWCD, outside city limits

**Coverage:** NM

**Deadline & timing:** Applications opened October 7, 2026, first come/first served while funding remains. Original application must be hand-delivered or mailed; no electronic or fax submissions. **Funder:** New Mexico Economic Development Department

**Type:** Grant

**What you can get:** FY27 awards of $50,000, $100,000 or $150,000; alternative opportunity up to $20,000 plus 10 hours of technical assistance. • FY27 flyer supports these award levels. Current eligibility PDF: production projects cannot use predevelopment category; R&D is limited to climate-smart pre-production. No match percentage asserted.

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, Small New Mexico farmers/ranchers with gross cash farm income under $250,000 and NM Grown Approved Supplier certification or working toward it

**Coverage:** NM

**Deadline & timing:** Due November 18, 2026. FY27 applications opened October 14, 2026 at 9 a.m. MT and close November 18, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. MT. Awards expected mid-February 2027; funds must be used by December 2027.

## Eligibility

FY27 eligibility PDF dated September 23, 2026 excludes FY26 awardees. Projects primarily for self-use are ineligible; production plus distribution/sales qualifies when funds primarily support supply-chain work. Legal site-use authority is required for improvements. The newer PDF allows limited project-related staffing up to 20% and some non-durable goods, contrary to older generic exclusions on the landing page; use current FY27 guidance and clarify final terms with EDD.

text:
# Salado SWCD Conservation Cost-Share

**Funder:** Salado Soil & Water Conservation District (Datil, NM)

**Type:** Cost-share

**What you can get:** 50% • $5,000 per project • The district pays 50% of approved project costs, up to $5,000.

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, Private landowners within the Salado SWCD (portions of Socorro, Catron and Cibola counties, NM)

**Coverage:** NM

**Deadline & timing:** No fixed deadline. Official page (checked 2026-09-30): "Applications are reviewed by the board at its regular monthly meetings; one project per applicant per year." Applications received before the meeting packet goes out are taken up at the next regular meeting. Submit at the Datil NRCS Field Office, by mail (PO Box 136, Datil, NM 87821) or by email.

## Eligibility

The district pays part of the cost of conservation practices on private land within its boundary, about a third of Socorro County, a quarter of Catron County and a small part of Cibola County in west-central NM. Eligible practices: livestock water pipelines and drinkers, solar-powered pumps, fencing, brush control, noxious weed control and erosion control. One project per applicant per year. A separate grant-funded wildfire-mitigation cost-share (defensible space) pays a 50% match, up to $2,500 per home per year. Match requirement: Landowner pays the remaining 50% of approved project costs..

**Tags (stated on page):** rangeland, grazing, livestock infrastructure

**Official program URL:** https://saladosoilandwater.org/

# Farmer Emergency Fund

**Funder:** NOFA Vermont (Northeast Organic Farming Association of Vermont)

**Type:** Grant

**What you can get:** $2,500 - $5,000 • Non-repayable grants: up to $2,500 for NOFA-VT member farms; up to $5,000 for VOF certified organic farms (one-year membership waiting period waived). **Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, Vermont commercial farmers who have been NOFA VT members in good standing for at least one year, or any farm certified organic by Vermont Organic Farmers (VOF), who have suffered a disaster related loss.

For Vermont commercial farmers who have been NOFA-VT members in good standing for at least one year, or farms certified organic by VOF (waiting period waived), facing disaster-related financial need. Does not cover losses paid by insurance or other sources, or projected income from lost crops.

# Agricultural Water Resources Assistance Program (AgWRAP)

**Funder:** North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, Division of Soil and Water Conservation (NC Soil and Water Conservation Commission via local SWCDs)

# Advancing U.S. Pork Sustainability and Market Value Grant

text:
# Regenerative Pilot Program (RPP)

**Funder:** USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS)

**Type:** Cost-share

**What you can get:** EQIP and CSP financial assistance for whole-farm regenerative practices via a single application • FY2027 national allocation $1 billion: $650 million EQIP + $350 million CSP. FY2026 pilot obligated more than 5,100 contracts for more than $851 million.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, Forestland owners (forestry operations have monitoring options)

**Coverage:** Available nationwide

**Deadline & timing:** Announced September 29, 2026: USDA increased RPP financial assistance from $700 million to $1 billion for fiscal year 2027 ($650 million through EQIP, $350 million through CSP). 'Producers can now apply for assistance.' Apply through the local NRCS Service Center by your state's ranking dates for FY2027 funding consideration; ranking dates vary by state (see NRCS ranking dates). FY2027 changes: CSP resource concern threshold lowered from 100% to 75%; State Technical Advisory Committees may add conservation practices reflecting local resource concerns.

## Eligibility

Whole-farm regenerative planning addressing soil, water and natural vitality under a single application covering both EQIP and CSP; producers can bundle multiple regenerative practices into one application. Designed for both beginning and advanced producers. Monitoring and evaluation options for cropland, grazing lands and forestry operations. Standard NRCS/USDA program eligibility applies. Soil health testing is required at minimum in the first and last years of participation.

**Tags (stated on page):** soil health, water quality, grazing

**Official program URL:** https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/programs-initiatives/regenerative-pilot-program

# Sustainable Nitrogen Outcomes (SNO)

**Funder:** Nutrien Ag Solutions

**Type:** Payment program

**What you can get:** $35 per ton of CO2e emissions reduced, with a $2/acre minimum payment • Outcome-based. Page FAQ requires 5-30% nitrogen reduction; published program conditions specify a minimum 5% applied-N reduction with a nitrogen inhibitor included. Agrible records, one historical crop year and one-year agreement required. Potential annual re-enrollment for up to ten years. Confirm field eligibility with a Nutrien crop consultant.

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, growers of corn, cotton, wheat, sorghum, or barley who reduce applied nitrogen by at least 5% and record practice data in a Nutrien Agrible account

**Coverage:** Available nationwide

**Deadline & timing:** Current sponsor page accepts grower eligibility inquiries with no fixed deadline as of October 10, 2026; a Nutrien crop consultant confirms enrollment eligibility.

## Eligibility

Eligible U.S. corn, cotton, wheat, sorghum and barley growers must confirm field eligibility with a Nutrien consultant. Published program conditions include at least 5% applied-nitrogen reduction with a nitrogen inhibitor and Agrible records. Select counties/products have additional incentives.

**Tags (stated on page):** nutrient management, soil health, climate smart

**Official program URL:** https://info.nutrienagsolutions.com/sno

# Nevada Conservation Credit System (Private Land Credit Projects)

**Funder:** Nevada Sagebrush Ecosystem Program (Nevada Department of Conservation and Natural Resources)

**Type:** Payment program

**What you can get:** Sale of habitat credits to debit project proponents • Credit amount determined through the SETT quantification process; see Sagebrush Ecosystem Program Manual.

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

# NYS Grown & Certified Research and Development Grant (2026)

**Funder:** New York Farm Viability Institute / New York State Department of Agriculture and Markets

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Deadline & timing:** Due October 25, 2027. Noncompetitive rolling applications June 26, 2026–October 25, 2027, or until funds are exhausted. Projects run 18 months from contract execution.

First-time processed-food creators need a feasibility consultation before approval. Grantees must finance project costs upfront. # H2Ohio Agriculture Incentive Program

**Funder:** Ohio Department of Agriculture

**Type:** Cost-share

**What you can get:** Published nutrient-management payments are $10/acre/year for approved and implemented Basic VNMP/CNMP or $15/acre/year for Precision VNMP/CNMP, plus separately specified incentives for overwintering cover and other BMPs. Confirm the current county enrollment cycle and contract rates with the SWCD. • ODA and local SWCDs implement H2Ohio practices on more than 2.2 million acres of Ohio farmland.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, crop producers in eligible counties (Western Lake Erie Basin focus, expanding statewide) with current soil tests and an approved nutrient management plan

**Coverage:** OH

**Deadline & timing:** Enrollment availability is county- and cycle-specific; a currently open statewide new-producer window was not verified. Existing participants are implementing contracted practices, while some 2026 opportunities were extensions for already-enrolled producers. Contact your county SWCD before applying to confirm whether new enrollment or a waitlist is available. An approved nutrient management plan and current soil tests are required.

## Eligibility

Ohio cropland producers work through their local SWCD and must have an approved VNMP or CNMP, with soil tests no older than four years. Nutrient-management acres paid by another county, state or federal program, including CSP practice 590, are ineligible for duplicate payment. Livestock operations may require a CNMP; confirm with the SWCD.

# Beginning & Expanding Farmer Loan Program (Aggie Bond)

**Funder:** Business Oregon

**Type:** Loan

**What you can get:** $520,000 maximum Aggie Bond financing • Tax-exempt bond lets the lender offer a lower interest rate. Uses: purchase of farm land or depreciable farm property. New depreciable property (farm buildings, new equipment) limited to $250,000; used depreciable farm property limited to $62,500.

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, Beginning or expanding Oregon farmers working with an eligible agricultural lender

**Coverage:** OR

**Deadline & timing:** No application window or deadline is stated on the official page; farmers first find an eligible lender willing to provide financing, then submit the program application form to Business Oregon.

## Eligibility

Per Business Oregon: applicants must be an Oregon resident; have a net worth of no more than $750,000; be a principal user of the farm and materially and substantially participate on the farm; and have never owned/operated a farm larger than 30% of the county's median farm size. The lender assumes all credit risk; the State does not guarantee repayment.

**Tags (stated on page):** beginning farmer, land programs

**Official program URL:** https://www.oregon.gov/biz/programs/aggiebond/pages/default.aspx

**Last verified:** Nov 14, 2026

# Energy Trust of Oregon Farms and Ranches Incentives

**Funder:** Energy Trust of Oregon

**Type:** Reimbursement

**What you can get:** Prescriptive per-unit incentives or custom per-energy-saved • Examples from the page: drip irrigation conversion $500 per acre; sprinkler package upgrades $45 per drop with VFD / $25 without; rotating sprinklers replacing impacts $11 each; gaskets $2 each (limit 4 per irrigated acre). Custom capital projects up to 90% of project cost at $0.45/kWh or $5/therm saved; O&M projects max $125,000.

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, Oregon farms and ranches served by Portland General Electric, Pacific Power, NW Natural, Cascade Natural Gas or Avista (paying the public purpose charge)

**Coverage:** OR

**Deadline & timing:** Rolling; no application window. Submit forms and documentation within 180 days of purchasing the equipment; check arrives in 60-90 days. Incentives are subject to funding availability and may change. Some offers require reviewing the equipment form requirements before purchasing.

## Eligibility

Project site must be in Oregon and served by PGE, Pacific Power, NW Natural, Cascade Natural Gas or Avista and contribute to the public purpose charge. Covers irrigation sprinklers/nozzles/gaskets, drip conversion, pivot/linear sprinkler package upgrades (MESA/LESA/LEPA/PMDI), battery chargers, building insulation, lighting, custom capital and O&M energy projects; solar and irrigation modernization offered separately.

**Tags (stated on page):** energy efficiency, renewable energy

**Official program URL:** https://www.energytrust.org/incentives/agriculture-farms-and-ranches/

text:
# Jackson SWCD Soil Health Rebate Program

**Funder:** Jackson Soil and Water Conservation District

**Type:** Reimbursement

**What you can get:** 50% of eligible project costs • Reimbursement • $5,000 maximum rebate

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, Jackson County, Oregon agricultural producers; other Jackson County landowners addressing a soil health concern through an eligible agricultural practice

**Coverage:** OR

**Deadline & timing:** Official page: 'Beginning October 1, 2026, Jackson County agricultural producers and other eligible landowners can receive a 50% rebate—up to $5,000'. No closing date or deadline is stated (checked 2026-09-30). First step is to talk with JSWCD's Agriculture Resource Conservationist (Josh Bilbao, 541-423-6172) about the soil concern and whether the rebate fits.

## Eligibility

Must address an identified soil health concern and introduce at least one eligible practice not already in use; existing/continuing practices (e.g., continuing cover crops already used) are not eligible. Pre- and post-project soil health testing required, following NRCS Conservation Evaluation and Monitoring Activity (CEMA) 216 guidelines. Projects built around four soil health principles. No particular type of agriculture is prioritized (livestock, hay/pasture, specialty crops, orchards, vineyards, etc.). Match requirement: Participants pay remaining 50% of project costs and any costs above the $5,000 maximum..

**Tags (stated on page):** soil health, cover crop

**Official program URL:** https://www.jswcd.org/soil-health-rebate-program

**Last verified:** Oct 24, 2026

text:
# Wasco County SWCD District Cost Share Program

**Funder:** Wasco County Soil and Water Conservation District

**Type:** Cost-share

**What you can get:** 50% cost share • Reimbursement after completion; cost limits per current EQIP cost list; no reimbursement of expenses before the award date • Not to exceed $7,500 per project unless board exception granted • Over $150,000 available at the start of each fiscal year (program-wide): $100,000 general conservation + $50,000 Haul Road program.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, Wasco County, Oregon landowners and agricultural producers

**Coverage:** OR

**Deadline & timing:** Year-round monthly batching. Program policy (application PDF, rev. 10/23/2023): 'Applications must be submitted 7 working days prior to the first Wednesday of the month'; the board considers applications at its first meeting of each month. Program page says over $150,000 is available at the start of each fiscal year (policy: $100,000 general conservation + $50,000 Haul Road). Separate contact and application for the haul road program.

## Eligibility

Wasco County residents/landowners (and educational/resource organizations in Wasco County). Eligible projects include irrigation upgrades (must improve water- or energy-use efficiency by at least 15%), livestock watering facilities, juniper removal, rain harvesting systems, and rock for erosion-prone agricultural harvest (haul) roads. Must follow NRCS technical standards, maintain the practice at least 10 years (or EQIP lifespan), and complete within 2 years of approval. Match requirement: Applicant pays 50% of project cost (labor match at no more than BOLI prevailing rates).

**Tags (stated on page):** water quality, livestock infrastructure, rangeland

**Official program URL:** https://www.wascoswcd.org/district-cost-share-program

**Last verified:** Oct 17, 2026

# PepsiCo & Partners Regenerative Ag Incentive

**Funder:** Precision Conservation Management (Illinois Corn Growers Association) with PepsiCo

**Type:** Payment program

**What you can get:** Up to $35/acre for qualifying conservation practices, with no cap on enrolled acres • Stackable with state and federal cost-share, but not with another carbon or ecosystem-services market — PepsiCo claims the resulting credits. One-year renewable contract; payments issue the summer after a PCM Specialist verifies practices.

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, row crop farmers in Illinois, Kentucky, or Nebraska who enroll their acres in Precision Conservation Management and adopt or maintain cover crops, reduced tillage, or nitrogen reduction

**Coverage:** IL, KY, NE

**Deadline & timing:** Enroll through a regional PCM Specialist, who confirms eligibility. No published application cutoff; current offer verified October 10, 2026.

## Eligibility

Available regionally in Illinois, Kentucky and Nebraska; a PCM Specialist must confirm location and farm eligibility. All of the grower’s acres must be enrolled in Precision Conservation Management, with W-9 provided. Each field may receive two new cover-crop years (one ahead of corn and one ahead of soybeans). Additional requirements apply to MRTN or 10% nitrogen-reduction payments. PepsiCo claims credits; enrolled acres cannot participate in another carbon, ecosystem-services or sustainability marketplace.

**Tags (stated on page):** soil health, cover crop, nutrient management, climate smart

**Official program URL:** https://www.precisionconservation.org/farmers/pepsico-partners-regenerative-ag-incentive/

# Cost-Share for Extended Rotations

**Funder:** Practical Farmers of Iowa

**Type:** Cost-share

**What you can get:** $20 per acre • Per acre • Participants receive $20 per acre by completing one or both program scenarios (small grains cost-share and/or nitrogen reduction on corn).

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, farmers in Iowa, farmers in eligible counties of MN, MO, NE, SD

**Coverage:** IA, MN, MO, NE, SD

**Deadline & timing:** Due April 30, 2027. Official page: 2027 enrollment window Aug. 24, 2026-April 30, 2027 (Application Deadline: 04/30/2027), or until the program's allotted acres are filled; PFI says to enroll ASAP as it may close early. Wrap-up survey and documentation due Sept. 30, 2027. Payments processed by Dec. 31, 2027 after paperwork is received and confirmed.

## Eligibility

Nitrogen scenario: reduce usual corn-soybean N rate by 40 lb/acre or apply no more than 100 lb N/acre on 2027 corn following small grain plus cover crop or leguminous hay (agronomist call required by May 28, 2027). Small grain cover crop must contain at least one legume; soybeans do not count, and double-/relay-cropped soybeans are ineligible. Conventional and organic-transition acres are eligible; certified-organic acres are ineligible. No PFI membership required; no acre cap. Acres may stack with public programs (EQIP, CSP) but not with PFI fall cover crop cost-share (2026 or 2027), the 2027 N Rate Risk Protection Program, or privately funded cost-share/carbon programs. Requirements include signing the agreement within 30 days, attending a learning event in 2027, and submitting documentation and wrap-up survey by Sept. 30, 2027. Only select counties outside Iowa are eligible (county list linked on page).

text:
# N Rate Risk Protection Program

**Funder:** Practical Farmers of Iowa

**Type:** Payment program

**What you can get:** $5/acre for every enrolled corn acre with a reduced-nitrogen plan, plus a $30/acre warranty payment if yield falls below 95% of the farmer's ten-year APH average • Must reduce N about 20 lb/acre (agronomist discretion for already-low rates). Certified organic acres ineligible. Acres cannot overlap privately funded programs such as Indigo, SWOF or TruCarbon; stackable with EQIP/CSP/RCPP and state cost-share. Warranty voided by an insurance yield-loss payment for hail, wind or other events. Contract is non-binding; includes free one-year PFI membership.

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, Conventional corn farmers in eligible counties of IA, IL, MN, MO, NE, SD or WI who reduce N by about 20 lb/acre and carry MPCI Revenue or Yield Protection (min. 65% coverage)

**Coverage:** IA, IL, MN, MO, NE, SD, WI

**Deadline & timing:** Due April 30, 2027. Enrollment Aug. 3, 2026 to April 30, 2027 (2027 corn crop); sign agreement and FSA release by May 31, 2027; claims and wrap-up survey by Dec. 10, 2027; all payments processed by April 30, 2028.

## Eligibility

Eligible counties in IA, IL, MN, MO, NE, SD and WI; conventionally managed corn acres and minimum 65% Multi-Peril Crop Insurance Revenue or Yield Protection coverage required. Reduce nitrogen about 20 lb/acre subject to agronomist discretion for lower rates. No overlapping privately funded program acres; PFI Extended Rotations and the U.S. Pork Sustainability Grant are listed as not stackable. A yield-loss insurance claim for other causes voids the $30 warranty; revenue loss due only to price changes does not.

**Tags (stated on page):** nutrient management, water quality, risk management, climate smart

**Official program URL:** https://practicalfarmers.org/programs/n-rate-risk-protection-program/

# Precision Conservation Analysis (with Precision Conservation Incentive Payment)

**Funder:** Practical Farmers of Iowa

**Type:** Payment program

**What you can get:** Low alternative adoption (5-9% of the original field): $8.00/ac; Medium (10-15%): $18.00/ac; High (>16%): $26.00/ac • One-time per-acre incentive paid on the acres that remain in production after a management change, tiered by share of the original field changed • Incentive payment capped at $10,000 per producer • Consultation and profitability analysis provided at no cost through Pheasants Forever precision ag and conservation specialists. Payment is in addition to any federal, state or local conservation practice payments.

**Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, Iowa and Minnesota farmers, landowners

**Coverage:** IA, MN

**Deadline & timing:** Official page: Accepted on a rolling basis. Submit a contact form to start; consultation with a local precision ag and conservation specialist is provided at no cost.

This program is eligible in Iowa and Minnesota. At least 50% of the changed area must be unprofitable to be eligible for the payment, and participants must meet NRCS EQIP eligibility criteria. Consultations and farm data are confidential; no public access requirement.

# Soil and Water Outcomes Fund

**Funder:** AgOutcomes, a subsidiary of the Iowa Soybean Association

**Type:** Payment program

**What you can get:** Customized payment based on modeled environmental outcomes; no standard per-acre rate. **Readiness:** Ready to apply

**Who can apply:** producer, row crop farmers beginning or expanding cover crops, no till/reduced till, or nutrient management in an active project geography

**Coverage:** Available nationwide

**Deadline & timing:** Enrollment is open for returning farmers; new farmers can join the waitlist for remaining acres. Fields must be in an eligible county — check SWOF's enrollment map. SWOF reports impact across 21 states.

Fields must lie in an eligible SWOF county; ALL denotes multistate scope, not universal availability. At least one additional conservation practice is required. # Interest Rate Reduction Program (IRR / Farmer IRR, including Young Farmer IRR)

**Funder:** Texas Department of Agriculture - Texas Agricultural Finance Authority (TAFA)

**Type:** Loan

**What you can get:** Linked-deposit interest rate buy-down: the State Comptroller places a below-market time deposit at the lender, which charges below-market interest on the linked loan • Program page: total linked-deposit loans to any one borrower cannot exceed $500,000 (IRR, Ch. 44) or $1,000,000 (Farmer IRR, Ch. 58). Maximum borrower rate per program page: deposit rate plus 4% (IRR) or deposit rate plus 1% (Farmer IRR). Proceeds may fund agriculture-related operating expenses, land or fixed-asset purchase and improvements, equipment, or any enterprise based on agriculture; existing debt only when the lender requires it to finance expansion. TDA's IRR Overview describes a Young Farmer version (YFIRR) for businesses owned at least in part by someone under 46 at loan closing. Pricing enhancement only, not a loan guarantee; no program fees currently. Can be paired with TAFA's Agricultural Loan Guarantee program.

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, Texas farmers, ranchers and agricultural businesses, applying jointly with an eligible lender (state funds depository or Texas headquartered Farm Credit institution)

**Coverage:** TX

**Deadline & timing:** Deadline: Applications are accepted year-round and subject to available funding. Joint lender-borrower application submitted to TDA.

## Eligibility

Eligible applicants: producer, Texas farmers, ranchers and agricultural businesses, applying jointly with an eligible lender (state-funds depository or Texas-headquartered Farm Credit institution).

text:
# Pennsylvania Cover Crop & Nutrient Management Support Program

**Funder:** The Nature Conservancy (with Precision Sustainable Agriculture, USDA NRCS, Willard Agri-Service and GROWMARK FS)

**Type:** Cost-share

**What you can get:** Up to $80 per acre • Cover crop cost-share of up to $80/acre, plus a yield warranty of up to $50/acre reimbursed if participating reduces income. • Also included at no cost to the farmer: PlantMap3D cover crop mapping after spring termination, nutrient management planning services, and technical assistance on seed mixes, seeding rates and timing. Financial assistance is available for sidedress application activities whether the farmer or an agribusiness partner does the work. Funded through a Regional Conservation Partnership Program (RCPP) award from USDA NRCS. Willard Agri-Service or GROWMARK FS scan the terminated cover crop with PlantMap3D cameras on a spray rig; partners turn that imagery into variable-rate sidedress nitrogen maps that credit the nitrogen the cover crop supplied.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, Pennsylvania farmers whose ground sits inside the project area of the Chesapeake Bay watershed (TNC publishes the boundary as a downloadable map; western PA counties draining to the Ohio are outside it). Farm must be eligible for USDA NRCS Farm Bill programs such as EQIP or CSP, must have an established mixed species cover crop that includes a legume and will be terminated in spring 2027, and must have — or be willing to develop — a current Nutrient Management Plan for the enrolled acres. The program is built around multi species cover crops and the corn crop that follows them.

**Coverage:** PA

**Deadline & timing:** No application deadline is posted. Enrollment starts with an interest form and TNC follows up to confirm eligibility. The requirement that the cover crop be terminated in spring 2027 effectively ties the current round to a cover crop seeded in fall 2026, so the practical window is this fall rather than an open-ended one. Confirm timing with TNC before counting on it.

## Eligibility

Only farms inside The Nature Conservancy's Chesapeake Bay project area in Pennsylvania qualify; the boundary map is on the program page and western counties draining to the Ohio are outside it. The farm must be eligible for NRCS Farm Bill programs, have a multi-species cover crop including a legume that will be terminated in spring 2027, and have or develop a nutrient management plan for the enrolled acres.

**Tags (stated on page):** soil health, cover crop, nutrient management, water quality

**Official program URL:** https://www.nature.org/en-us/about-us/where-we-work/united-states/pennsylvania/stories-in-pennsylvania/cover-crop-nutrient-management-support/

text:
# Vermont Farm Fund Emergency Loan

**Funder:** Vermont Farm Fund / Center for an Agricultural Economy

**Type:** Loan

**What you can get:** Up to $15,000, 0% interest • Zero-interest revolving loan repayable over 36-48 months with a flexible payment schedule and an option to defer payments up to 12 months. Cap was raised from $10,000 to $15,000 after the 2023 floods. Cash shortfalls from equipment failure, business miscalculation, or unrelated cash-flow problems are not eligible. The Fund also runs Business Builder Loans and New Producer Loans for non-disaster needs.

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

# Working Lands Enterprise Initiative Business Enhancement Grant (FY2027)

**Funder:** Vermont Working Lands Enterprise Initiative (Vermont Agency of Agriculture, Food and Markets)

**Type:** Grant

**What you can get:** $10,000 - $50,000 • $508,000 available in FY2027; applicants must show they can pay for project costs the grant won't cover

**Readiness:** Prep docs first

**Who can apply:** producer, small business, co op, nonprofit, Value added food and fiber businesses sourcing at least 50% Vermont grown raw ingredients OR applying to significantly increase Vermont grown ingredient use

**Coverage:** VT

**Deadline & timing:** Due December 10, 2026. FY2027 applications are open October 9–December 10, 2026 at 2:00 p.m. via WebGrants. Webinar recording and drop-in Q&A dates are available on the program page. Funding decisions late February/early March 2027; project period April 2027–April 2028. $508,000 available; applicants may apply to one WLEI grant in FY2027.

## Eligibility

FY2027 RFA eligibility: farms of any size producing eligible food or fiber and qualified working-lands businesses may apply. Applicants must have generated revenue in 2025 and provide 2025 financial statements; operation for the full year is not required. Vermont-based applicants qualify; out-of-state headquarters need sponsor confirmation that the project is 100% focused on Vermont working lands. Incorporated entities and sole proprietors using an assumed name must be registered. Indoor-only production, cannabis, Christmas trees, equine, flowers, topical-CBD hemp and horticulture are excluded. RFSI recipients and specified recent Working Lands/related grantees are ineligible; previous awards must be closed. Eligible projects include equipment, infrastructure, marketing, R&D and workforce training. Land purchases/rent/leases, livestock purchases, farmworker housing, general business planning, recurring business costs and soil/water equipment eligible under existing VAAFM programs are excluded. Match requirement: No match required. Applicants must demonstrate capacity to pay project costs exceeding the grant request..

text:
# Natural Resource Investments (NRI) Conservation District Cost-Share

**Funder:** Washington State Conservation Commission (SCC), delivered by local conservation districts

**Type:** Cost-share

**What you can get:** Cost-share on best management practices installed by landowners; conservation district pays the remaining portion of project cost • Conservation districts use NRI funding from SCC to offer local, incentive-based programs for landowners to voluntarily install BMPs addressing water quality, habitat, salmon recovery, climate resilience and forest health. Conservation districts meeting CAPP requirements are eligible for ongoing NRI funding. NRI Guidelines: maximum cost-share per landowner per fiscal year is $100,000; practices must meet NRCS standards (or a PE-approved or SCC-approved design); a Contract for Cost Share is required for each landowner. Cost-share rates are set by the local district.

**Readiness:** Local office first

**Who can apply:** producer, Washington landowners and farmers applying through their local conservation district (districts must meet SCC CAPP requirements)

**Coverage:** WA

**Deadline & timing:** Ongoing program; landowners apply through their local conservation district on the district's own schedule. No statewide deadline posted.

## Eligibility

Apply through the local conservation district; local funding and rates vary. NRI capital funds support structural conservation practices with a design life greater than one year. Standalone cover-crop or reduced-tillage management practices are not eligible. The $100,000 annual cost-share limit applies across SCC programs and all properties/businesses of the participant unless an approved exception applies.

**Tags (stated on page):** water quality, soil health, livestock infrastructure, manure management

**Official program URL:** https://www.scc.wa.gov/programs/natural-resource-investments

title: Envita
author: FarmDeck
text:
# Envita

**Category:** biologicals
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026

A liquid inoculant of the nitrogen-fixing bacterium Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus, labeled in-furrow at 0.8–1 oz/ac in at least 2.5 gal/ac of water or…

Biologicals · Conventional + organic · In-furrow or foliar · Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus · Reported OMRI-listed

## What the research measured

The ten-state land-grant review reported no yield benefit from in-furrow Envita in 11 of 12 corn trials; the exception was Missouri 2020, about 6 bu/ac, equivalent to a 12 lb N/ac fertilizer rate. Foliar Envita did not change yield in North Dakota corn, spring wheat or canola. In a 2020 Nebraska on-farm trial, Envita as a seed treatment yielded 6–7 bu/ac less than the same N rate without it at 100, 150 and 200 lb N/ac. North Dakota’s four 2022 sites found no yield gain at 0 or 80 lb N/ac. Independent replicated trials 2020–2022: a ten-state review (12 in-furrow and several foliar Envita trials across ND, IL, MN, MO, IN and MI), NDSU’s four-site 2022 N-rate study, one Nebraska on-farm seed-treatment trial, and a UW–Madison extension review of the same programs. No US peer-reviewed field study and no independent soybean or potato data were found.4 independent sources.

**What it is.** A liquid inoculant of the nitrogen-fixing bacterium Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus, labeled in-furrow at 0.8–1 oz/ac in at least 2.5 gal/ac of water or foliar at 0.5–2.5 oz/ac in early vegetative stages, for corn, soybeans, cereals, alfalfa and potatoes. The company’s stated claims, as quoted by university reviewers, are a 6+ bu/ac average corn increase, or replacing 27% of a corn plant’s nitrogen need, or a 5–13% yield increase with a full N program.
