title: Envita
author: FarmDeck
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- Application differed across trials: in-furrow at planting, foliar at V2–V3 or later, and a seed treatment in Nebraska; the Michigan State trial used 3.2 oz/ac in-furrow, above the 0.8–1 oz/ac label rate the Wisconsin review lists.
- The one positive site-year was tied to a rate and a season: Missouri’s gain appeared at 100 lb N/ac in 2020 and did not repeat in 2021 or 2022 at the same site.
- Nebraska 2020 priced Envita at $5/ac; at 100, 150 and 200 lb N/ac the treated strips returned about $26–31/ac less than the same N rate alone ($754.80 vs $786.23, $763.98 vs $792.53, $752.63 vs $778.51).
- In Minnesota’s 2022 on-farm strips, the mean across three N rates was 191 bu/ac without and 182 bu/ac with Envita; the authors reported no yield benefit.
- Handling: mix only what will be used within a day, use non-chlorinated water, add Envita last, do not freeze, and keep it out of direct sunlight and unopened until use.
- The UW–Madison review lists Envita as OMRI approved; this profile did not check the OMRI product list directly. Read the sources · 4

1. [Performance of Selected Commercially Available Asymbiotic N-fixing Products in the North Central Region ↗](https://www.ndsu.edu/agriculture/extension/publications/performance-selected-commercially-available-asymbiotic-n-fixing-products)

   Extension · Franzen et al., NCERA-103 · North Dakota State University Extension, SF2080 · 2023

   Twelve in-furrow Envita corn trials across the region through 2022: no yield benefit in eleven; the exception was Missouri 2020, about 6 bu/ac, equivalent to a 12 lb N/ac fertilizer rate.

author: FarmDeck
text:
Foliar Envita at Minot gave no yield improvement in corn (123 vs 125 bu/ac), spring wheat (60.6–61.8 vs 60.2 bu/ac) or canola (2,005–2,176 vs 2,058 lb/ac). 2. [Nitrogen Fixing Bacteria for Corn: Testing Two Commercial Products ↗](https://www.ndsu.edu/agriculture/sites/default/files/2023-02/22%20Nitrogen%20Fixing%20Bacteria%20for%20Corn.pdf)

title: Utrisha N
author: FarmDeck
text:
## What the research measured

The cited North Central review and three Iowa organic trials reported no significant corn yield increase at the nitrogen rates tested. Kentucky reported responses at particular nitrogen-rate and soil combinations. The linked Australian wheat study and manufacturer trials cover different crops or conditions. Independent replicated trials across five North Central states plus three Iowa on-farm strip trials, but the US independent record is small and ends in 2023, with no US peer-reviewed field study.4 independent sources · 1 manufacturer-authored, labelled.

**What it is.** A foliar-applied biological containing the nitrogen-fixing bacterium Methylobacterium symbioticum, sprayed at 5 oz/ac at V4–V8 on top of a normal N program. OMRI-listed, and marketed as an average +5 bu/ac in corn and +2.5 bu/ac in soybean. Study conditions and limitations

- Application is demanding: 10–25 gal/ac of water with under 2 ppm chlorine and pH 5–8, on a healthy canopy, rain-fast after one hour; Corteva’s soybean data show about four times the response from morning sprays.
- It often needs its own pass: Iowa cooperators found it incompatible with their post-emergence tank mixes, which is what pushed the cost to about $17/ac, and none planned to use it again.
- Where responses appeared (Kentucky 2022) they were tied to one N rate on one soil and did not repeat at other rates, limiting the applicability of the response to other conditions.
- Corteva’s own corn trials report the largest gains in low-yield environments (+7.2 bu/ac under 179 bu/ac; +3.3 bu/ac over 220 bu/ac); those are company trials.
- The organism’s measured N contribution in Portuguese field maize varied between 58.8 kg N/ha in one year and 14.5 kg N/ha the next.
- OMRI-listed, so it is one of the few N biologicals allowed on organic corn, but the three organic Iowa trials showed no yield gain.

title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal inoculants
author: FarmDeck
text:
# Arbuscular mycorrhizal inoculants

**Category:** biologicals
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026
**Cited DOIs:** 10.1016/j.apsoil.2024.105559, 10.1016/j.soilbio.2015.02.020

Propagules of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (the MycoApply line uses four Glomus species: G.

Biologicals · Conventional + organic · In-furrow liquid or granular · Glomus species · Some formulations OMRI-listed

## What the research measured

Independent corn and soybean field results show no yield gain. Iowa 2019 strips differed by 4 bu/ac in corn and 2 bu/ac in soybean, inside LSDs of 11 and 14; Nebraska 2019 measured 226 vs 235 bu/ac, a 9 bu/ac loss (P=0.003); Alabama’s five soybean site-years (2022–23) showed no statistical difference among any treatments, with the Glomus seed treatment ranging 36.4–70.9 bu/ac against checks of 41.7–72.9. A 2024 Kansas assessment of 23 retail inoculants found half produced no root infection and eight colonized no pot at all. A meta-analysis of 38 wheat field trials, mostly with research inoculants, reported higher grain yield on average. Three US on-farm or research-station trials in corn and soybean (Iowa, Nebraska, Alabama; 2019–2023), one greenhouse assessment of 23 US retail products, and one global meta-analysis of wheat field trials. No multi-site US corn or soybean trial of a named product was found.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** Propagules of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (the MycoApply line uses four Glomus species: G. intraradices, G. mosseae, G. aggregatum and G. etunicatum) applied in-furrow at planting, either as a liquid concentrate tank-mixed with starter fertilizer (EndoPrime SC: one gallon treats 64 acres, 2 oz/ac in the Nebraska trial) or as a 2 lb/ac granular. The fungi are meant to colonize roots and extend nutrient and water uptake; they are already present in most farm soils.

title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal inoculants
author: FarmDeck
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- Product quality varies: in the Kansas assessment, 8 of 23 inoculants showed no fungal colonization in any pot, 50% produced no infection in sorghum, carrot or lettuce, the best commercial product reached about 10% infection potential, enumerated spores were under 2% of labeled propagules, and 5 products carried the root pathogen Olpidium.
- Cost without a measured return in the two Midwest trials: the Iowa cooperator paid $12.50/ac and recorded no yield effect; Nebraska costed EndoPrime SC at $8.66/ac and measured a $41.63/ac lower marginal net return.
- The Nebraska trial also recorded a lower early-season stand with the product (21,619 vs 22,571 plants/ac on June 5), with no difference in the September count or in stalk rot.
- Alabama’s trials were seed-applied to soybean in no-till rye residue at two to three stations over two seasons; they are not corn and not in-furrow.
- The wheat meta-analysis found response depended on soil organic matter, pH, total N, available P, texture, climate and the fungal species inoculated, and did not evaluate retail products or US corn.
- OMRI status differs by formulation: Mycorrhizal Applications lists its Injector Endo powder as OMRI Listed, while the EndoPrime SC product page does not mention OMRI. Read the sources · 5

1.

title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal inoculants
author: FarmDeck
text:
[Evaluating Microbial Seed Treatments for Alabama Crops (ANR-3259) ↗](https://www.aces.edu/blog/topics/farm-management/evaluating-microbial-seed-treatments-for-alabama-crops/)

   Extension · Pacheco-Verdon, Franca de Freitas & Francisco · Alabama Cooperative Extension System, Auburn University · 2026

   Soybean seed treatments at two to three research stations in 2022–23, including a four-species Glomus mix: the mix yielded 40.7 vs 40.8 (EVS 2022), 25.2 vs 23.5 (TV 2022), 70.9 vs 72.9 (EVS 2023), 65.0 vs 63.8 (TV 2023) and 36.4 vs 41.7 bu/ac (PARU 2023) against the untreated check, and yield P>F was not significant at every site-year. 4. [An assessment of twenty-three mycorrhizal inoculants reveals limited viability of AM fungi, pathogen contamination, and negative microbial effect on crop growth for commercial products ↗](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10595566)

   Peer-reviewed · Koziol, Lubin & Bever · Applied Soil Ecology 202, Kansas Biological Survey, University of Kansas · 2024 · [doi:10.1016/j.apsoil.2024.105559](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apsoil.2024.105559)

   Greenhouse assessment of 23 retail inoculants under organic conventions: eight produced no fungal colonization in any pot, 50% gave no infection in sorghum, carrot or lettuce, the best commercial product reached about 10% infection potential, spores were under 2% of labeled propagules, and five products carried Olpidium. With fertilizer effects removed, 13 commercial products were neutral for crop growth, two inhibited it and one promoted it, while every laboratory-grown culture promoted growth. 5.

title: PROVEN 40
author: FarmDeck
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- Any response shows up at low to moderate N: in Illinois the gain appeared at 45–135 kg N/ha and vanished at 0 and 225 kg N/ha, and the fertilizer-N equivalent fell from 38.5 kg/ha at V8 to 11.5 kg/ha for grain yield.
- Kentucky saw a significant gain in 2023 and, in 2024, only at 215 lb N/ac under heavy rye residue; the Kentucky authors say they cannot predict where or when a product will work.
- Cutting N without an untreated reduced-N check can hide a loss: a 2022 Nebraska comparison at 106 lb N/ac plus PROVEN 40 yielded 195 bu/ac against 235 bu/ac for a 142 lb N/ac check.
- Handling is strict: use within 24 hours of opening, non-chlorinated water, add it last, and avoid 7-21-7, ATS or UAN as a carrier.
- Gene-edited bacteria are not OMRI-listed, so it is not an option for organic corn.
- The manufacturer’s own 2024 Northern Plains strip trials (20 locations) reported −0.4 bu/ac with 38.5 lb/ac less N; that is company data, not independent. Read the sources · 5

1. [Performance of Selected Commercially Available Asymbiotic N-fixing Products in the North Central Region ↗](https://www.ndsu.edu/agriculture/extension/publications/performance-selected-commercially-available-asymbiotic-n-fixing-products)

   Extension · Franzen et al., NCERA-103 · North Dakota State University Extension, SF2080 · 2023

   Land-grant trials in ten states through 2022: 59 of 61 corn site-years showed no yield increase from any product over the N rate alone. The review reported a significant yield benefit for PROVEN 40 in 0 of 15 site-years and Utrisha N in 0 of 11. 2.

title: PROVEN 40
author: FarmDeck
text:
[Soil inoculation with nitrogen-fixing bacteria to supplement maize fertilizer need ↗](https://doi.org/10.1002/agj2.21729)

   Peer-reviewed · Woodward, Sible, Seebauer & Below · Agronomy Journal 117(1), University of Illinois · 2025 · [doi:10.1002/agj2.21729](https://doi.org/10.1002/agj2.21729)

   Four Illinois site-years (2019–21): the PROVEN 40 inoculant raised grain yield by an average 0.11 Mg/ha (about 1.8 bu/ac), with the gain at 45–135 kg N/ha and none at 0 or 225. The authors calculate a 2–6 bu/ac gain is needed to profit at $25–75/ha and conclude the effect did not warrant replacing fertilizer N. 3. [Biological N Fixation Products for Corn: An Update ↗](https://graincrops.mgcafe.uky.edu/articles/biological-n-fixation-products-corn-update)

   Extension · Grove & Lee · University of Kentucky Grain Crops · 2025

   Kentucky 2023: PROVEN 40 plots averaged 200 bu/ac at both 140 and 180 lb N against 199 and 191 without, a significant difference the authors report as 9 bu/ac; in 2024 it helped only at 215 lb N under heavy rye residue. Regionally, 2 positive site-years out of 61. 4. [Biological Nitrogen Fixation in Corn: Wisconsin Trial Results ↗](https://cropsandsoils.extension.wisc.edu/articles/biological-nitrogen-fixation-in-corn-wisconsin-trial-results)

   University trial · Geissinger & Marzu · UW–Madison Nutrient & Pest Management Program · 2024

   Five 2023 Wisconsin N-rate trials (0–280 lb N/ac) found neither corn grain yield nor the yield response to N was affected by PROVEN 40 at any site. The authors see no significant current evidence that a gene-edited N-fixer can meet corn N needs in Wisconsin. 5.

text:
# SOURCE

**Category:** biologicals
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026

A foliar-applied chemistry, not a living organism, that the company calls a microbiome activator: it is described as mimicking a plant signal so resident…

Biologicals · Conventional · Foliar, tank-mixable · Not a living microbe · Marketed as 25 lb N and P

## What the research measured

Independent 2023 results cluster near zero and split by field. Iowa Soybean Association’s six soybean sites averaged −0.5 bu/ac with one significant site at −3.6; Ohio State’s Ashland County corn strips averaged 211 vs 202 bu/ac, not significant at an LSD of 9; Delaware’s irrigated corn showed no product, SOURCE included, significantly different from the check at any N rate; four South Dakota corn fields on one farm ran −10.1, +3.1, +5.3 and +8.2 bu/ac, with the −10.1 and +8.2 results both significant. ISA’s 2021–22 corn sites averaged +1 bu/ac, 10 of 25 showing a gain. Independent on-farm and university strip trials in Iowa, Ohio, Delaware and South Dakota, 2021–2023, mostly single-season and single-field, plus the company’s own compilation of third-party trials. No peer-reviewed field study and no multi-state replicated small-plot program were found.4 independent sources · 1 manufacturer-authored, labelled.

**What it is.** A foliar-applied chemistry, not a living organism, that the company calls a microbiome activator: it is described as mimicking a plant signal so resident soil microbes supply nitrogen, phosphorus and micronutrients, and is marketed as supplying 25 lb of N and P from a single pass that can ride along with a herbicide or fungicide. SOURCE DC is sold for corn, soybeans, canola, potato and sugar beet and SOURCE XC for wheat, cotton, alfalfa and grass hay; the independent trials here used 0.7 fl oz/ac of DC on corn (at V4 in Delaware) and SC/DC combinations on soybean at R1–R3.

Iowa Soybean Association’s six soybean sites averaged −0.5 bu/ac with one significant site at −3.6; Ohio State’s Ashland County corn strips averaged 211 vs 202 bu/ac, not significant at an LSD of 9; Delaware’s irrigated corn showed no product, SOURCE included, significantly different from the check at any N rate; four South Dakota corn fields on one farm ran −10.1, +3.1, +5.3 and +8.2 bu/ac, with the −10.1 and +8.2 results both significant. ISA’s 2021–22 corn sites averaged +1 bu/ac, 10 of 25 showing a gain. Independent on-farm and university strip trials in Iowa, Ohio, Delaware and South Dakota, 2021–2023, mostly single-season and single-field, plus the company’s own compilation of third-party trials. No peer-reviewed field study and no multi-state replicated small-plot program were found.4 independent sources · 1 manufacturer-authored, labelled.

**What it is.** A foliar-applied chemistry, not a living organism, that the company calls a microbiome activator: it is described as mimicking a plant signal so resident soil microbes supply nitrogen, phosphorus and micronutrients, and is marketed as supplying 25 lb of N and P from a single pass that can ride along with a herbicide or fungicide. SOURCE DC is sold for corn, soybeans, canola, potato and sugar beet and SOURCE XC for wheat, cotton, alfalfa and grass hay; the independent trials here used 0.7 fl oz/ac of DC on corn (at V4 in Delaware) and SC/DC combinations on soybean at R1–R3.

Study conditions and limitations

- Results split by field even on one farm: in South Dakota in 2023 the product lost 10.1 bu/ac in one corn field and gained 8.2 bu/ac in a low-yield zone of another, both significant at 90% confidence, while two other fields were not significant.

- In Delaware’s 2023 corn, no product (SOURCE included) out-yielded the untreated check at 100%, 80% or 50% N; at 50% N SOURCE trended higher without significance, and the authors call the 50% N rate a net economic loss against the full rate.
- Rates and timings differ by trial: 0.7 fl oz/ac DC on corn, a 0.5 fl oz SC plus 1.25 fl oz DC mix on Iowa soybean at R1–R3, and 1.24 fl oz SC on South Dakota soybean, so the record is not one product at one rate.
- The company’s third-party page reports the same 2023 Ohio State trial as a 9 bu/ac increase; the eFields report prints the two means with the same letter and calls them not statistically significant.

title: Bradyrhizobium soybean inoculant
author: FarmDeck
text:
# Bradyrhizobium soybean inoculant

**Category:** biologicals
**Sources checked:** September 26, 2026
**Cited DOIs:** 10.2135/cropsci2009.04.0185, 10.2134/agronj2016.04.0214

A live culture of Bradyrhizobium japonicum, the bacterium that forms nitrogen-fixing nodules on soybean roots, applied to the seed or in-furrow at planting.

Biologicals · Conventional + organic · Peat, liquid or on-seed · About $2.50/ac

## What the research measured

A 73-experiment Midwest study reported no average yield response on fields with recent soybean history. Other cited studies describe responses on fields without recent soybean production. Crop history, soil conditions, and existing rhizobia populations differ across these studies. A nine-author, five-state, 73-experiment peer-reviewed study plus 27 Ohio trials and 17 Nebraska on-farm trials; an industry-authored 187-trial analysis is also linked.4 independent sources · 1 manufacturer-authored, labelled.

**What it is.** A live culture of Bradyrhizobium japonicum, the bacterium that forms nitrogen-fixing nodules on soybean roots, applied to the seed or in-furrow at planting. Study conditions and limitations

- Response is near zero where soybean has been grown recently because naturalized rhizobia persist; the exceptions are new ground, more than three to five years since soybean, pH below 6.0, high sand content, or flooding for more than a week.
- Flooding advice is unsettled: Wisconsin fields flooded three weeks in 2008 showed no response to inoculant in 2009, while BASF says rhizobia can die within three to seven days under water.
- On first-time soybean ground nodulation can still fail even with correct inoculation; Ohio State notes 75 lb N/ac as urea added 8–12 bu/ac in that situation.
- Inoculants are living products: colony counts are guaranteed only to the expiry date and for a limited time on treated seed, so storage and seed-treatment compatibility matter. Read the sources · 5

1.

   Extension · Ohio State University Extension, Agronomic Crops Network (undated) · n.d. Across 27 Ohio trials (10 locations, six products) on fields already in soybean, inoculant averaged +1.5 bu/ac, reportable only at 70% confidence.

author: FarmDeck
text:
## What the research measured

The cited long-term Iowa study measured roughly half as much nitrate loss through tile drains with rye. Following-crop yield responses differed by crop and management; the linked studies report corn yield reductions under some establishment and termination practices. Two peer-reviewed meta-analyses, a 90,000-field satellite study, a four-site three-year Iowa N-rate trial, 19-year USDA-ARS drainage plots and a 70 site-year Iowa on-farm dataset.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** Winter rye drilled or broadcast after harvest to hold soil, take up leftover nitrate and suppress weeds until it is terminated ahead of the next crop. More than 85% of Iowa cover-crop acres. Study conditions and limitations

- In the Iowa State 2018–22 project, rye killed 3 days before planting made twice the biomass but cut corn yield 4.1% versus a 14-day kill.
- Broadcast rye made 3.5 times the biomass of drilled rye in the same project but 7.2% less corn yield.
- Planting green is low-risk for soybean, not corn: Iowa on-farm strips gained 3–11 bu/ac of soybean in 10 of 31 site-years, while corn lost an average 19 bu/ac in the 4 site-years that responded.
- Rye residue releases under 10 lb N/ac in the four weeks after corn planting; Nebraska and Iowa State recommend 30–50 lb/ac of starter N, and those sources do not advise a reduction in the corn N rate.
- The corn drag is worst on better soils, in cooler mid-seasons and dry springs; the nitrate benefit depends on spring growth and was absent where biomass stayed low.
- Economics: Iowa State CARD estimates net returns of −$30 to −$69 per acre for rye before corn without grazing or cost-share. Read the sources · 5

title: Crimson clover cover crop seed
author: FarmDeck
text:
## What the research measured

Published Extension measurements describe roughly 50–100 lb N/ac in crimson clover biomass in some regions. Biomass nitrogen and fertilizer-equivalent nitrogen credit are different measures. Winter survival, planting date, and termination timing affect the reported results. The meta-analyses cover legumes generally rather than crimson clover specifically, the multi-year peer-reviewed crimson-clover corn trial found is a single Ontario site, and the Midwest N-credit and winter-survival numbers come from Extension summaries.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** A winter-annual legume seeded in late summer or fall that fixes nitrogen and, where it overwinters, supplies part of the following corn crop’s N when killed in late spring. Study conditions and limitations

- Winter survival by region: dependable in Zone 8, survivable in the lower reaches of Zone 6, winter-killed in Zone 5 and colder; Michigan lists winter kill and seed cost as the main drawbacks.
- Variety matters: in a one-year Illinois trial the older Dixie survived winter 69% versus 94% for Kentucky Pride, with 14 versus 187 lb N/ac in spring biomass. That write-up is by the seed company, so treat it as company data.
- A winter-killed stand releases much of its N before corn can use it, so fall-only growth gives erosion and organic-matter benefits but little spring credit.
- Kill late: N accumulates through spring, and the 2026 meta-analysis found termination under 7 days before planting roughly doubled the unfertilized-corn benefit versus early termination.
- Ohio’s reliable establishment window is June 10 to September 28, which rules out seeding after most Corn Belt corn harvests; it needs true-clover rhizobium inoculant where clover has not been grown in three years. Read the sources · 5

# Forage radish

**Category:** cover crops
**Sources checked:** September 26, 2026

A tap-rooted brassica studied for residual nitrogen capture and spring residue effects.

Cover crops · Brassica · Conventional + organic · Brassica · Fall establishment · Winter-killed residue

## What the research measured

Maryland field research observed rapid fall nitrogen uptake and early spring nitrogen release after radish winterkill. Establishment timing and soil texture affected the outcome.

SARE project LNE03-192 · University of Maryland · Mid-Atlantic field studies, including nitrogen monitoring in 2003–2005.2 independent sources.

**What it is.** A tap-rooted brassica studied for residual nitrogen capture and spring residue effects. This profile covers the species, not a branded seed lot or a forage feeding trial.

Study conditions and limitations

- Early establishment mattered: the researchers emphasized planting before mid-September in their region.
- Rapid spring nitrogen release can precede crop demand, especially on sandy soils. Nitrogen captured in biomass is not a guaranteed fertilizer credit.
- SARE advises against placing brassica cover crops in rotations with brassica vegetables because they share diseases.
- Confirm seed treatment, organic certification, and intended use with the supplier for the specific lot.

**Category:** cover crops
**Sources checked:** September 26, 2026

A grass–legume mixture studied across different seeding proportions and growing conditions.

Cover crops · Mixture · Conventional + organic · Grass + legume · Biomass · Nitrogen accumulation

## What the research measured

A 2018 meta-analysis reported greater mixture biomass than either species alone on average. Relative responses varied with soil, preceding crop, growing degree days, and the share of vetch in the seed mix.

21 US studies · 55 site-years · Thapa et al., Agronomy Journal (2018).1 independent source.

**What it is.** A grass–legume mixture studied across different seeding proportions and growing conditions. Findings do not describe a particular commercial blend.

Study conditions and limitations

- Each bar uses a different monoculture baseline. These are relative biomass responses, not yields, nitrogen credits, or a comparison of brands.
- Pooled results do not predict the response to a specific mixture at an individual farm. No uncertainty interval is reproduced here.
- Confirm species proportions, termination requirements, and organic seed status for the actual blend.

title: Hairy vetch cover crop seed
author: FarmDeck
text:
## What the research measured

Maryland trials reported an economic nitrogen rate of about 27 lb/ac after vetch versus 179 lb/ac without a cover crop. Pennsylvania measurements averaged 164 lb N/ac in vetch biomass at termination. These are different measures; the linked studies describe their locations, management, and sampling methods. Two-site, two-year replicated Maryland kill-date trials, a two-site USDA-ARS mixture study, a 55 site-year meta-analysis and the legume-cover meta-analyses.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** A winter-hardy annual legume seeded in late summer or fall, alone or with rye, that fixes the largest spring N supply of the common winter legumes when killed at early bloom before no-till corn. Study conditions and limitations

- Kill date drives the credit: vetch added about 2 kg N/ha per day from late March to early May in Maryland; Wisconsin and Minnesota credit about 60 lb N/ac when incorporated before June 10 versus 120 for a full season.
- N release is fast, about 70 lb N/ac within four weeks of corn planting in an Illinois study, which fits corn demand but can be lost in a wet spring; mixing with rye slows release and adds cover.
- Winter survival: hardy to Zone 4 per SARE, but the Wisconsin and Minnesota bulletin says it often fails in the northern Midwest, and Nebraska stands measured only 12–29 lb N/ac.
- Stand N is not fertilizer-replacement N: Extension credits range from 75–150 lb N/ac (Maryland) to 80–100 (North Carolina); at full N rates expect the return to be the fertilizer saved, not extra bushels.
- Seeding: 15–20 lb/ac drilled or 25–30 broadcast; for maximum N in a mix the USDA-ARS study used 27 kg/ha vetch with 34 kg/ha rye. Read the sources · 5

title: Oats cover crop seed
author: FarmDeck
text:
## What the research measured

The Iowa fact sheet lists 1,000 to 4,000 lb of dry matter per acre per year for oats, and SARE lists 2,000 to 4,000 lb from late-summer or early-fall seedings. In Minnesota trials reported in 2025 an oat–radish mix measured from 425 to 540 lb/ac at Lamberton to 2,200–3,000 lb/ac at Waseca, and a 2018 Michigan variety test measured 1.07 ton/ac of fall biomass for the Jerry oat check. Penn State measured 19 lb N/ac (range 12–26) in oat biomass at termination. A joint USDA-NRCS and Iowa State fact sheet, SARE’s species chapter, a three-site Minnesota Extension seeding-rate trial, a one-site Michigan State variety test and Penn State’s cover-crop biomass-N table. No peer-reviewed multi-site study of oats alone before corn or soybean could be opened at checking time, so there is no following-crop yield chart.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** A cool-season annual grass drilled or broadcast in late summer after a small grain, silage or early soybean harvest, or in early spring ahead of a later crop. In the upper Midwest the fall stand dies over winter, so the following crop is planted into dead residue with no spring termination pass. Study conditions and limitations

- Planting date drives the stand: SARE reports oats planted August 25 had 39% fewer weed plants in spring than control plots, while oats planted two weeks later had 10% fewer; Iowa’s fall window is mid-August to mid-September and the Minnesota trials prioritized seeding before mid-September.
- Winterkill is regional: SARE lists winterkill in Hardiness Zone 6 and colder and much of Zone 7, and the Iowa sheet gives a 25°F cold-tolerance temperature.

title: Oats cover crop seed
author: FarmDeck
text:
Where oats overwinter, budget for a spring termination.
- Fall uptake is not a spring credit: SARE says late-summer plantings can absorb as much as 77 lb N/ac in eight to ten weeks, but Penn State measured 19 lb N/ac (12–26) in oat biomass at termination and the Iowa sheet lists a 33:1 carbon-to-nitrogen ratio.
- Seeding rates differ widely by source: 60 lb/ac PLS drilled, 66 broadcast and 75 aerial in Iowa; 2 to 3 bushels drilled or 3 to 4 broadcast in SARE (a bushel is 32 lb); 32 lb/ac in the Michigan test; 10 to 60 lb/ac in the Minnesota trial.
- Most Midwest trial numbers are for mixes, not oats alone: the Minnesota figures are an oat–radish mix, and in Michigan the Pratext black oat (a different species) made 2.59 ton/ac against 1.07 for Jerry oats.
- SARE advises waiting two to three weeks after killing oats before planting the next crop, and the Iowa sheet cautions that oats overseeded into soybeans can grow enough to interfere with harvest. Read the sources · 5

# Red clover frost-seeded into winter wheat

**Category:** cover crops
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026
**Cited DOIs:** 10.2134/agronj2005.0262

A short-lived perennial legume broadcast onto frozen or honeycombed soil in standing winter wheat in late winter, where freeze–thaw cycles work the seed in.

Cover crops · Legume · [Forage use ↗](https://www.sare.org/publications/managing-cover-crops-profitably/legume-cover-crops/red-clover/ "SARE: red clover uses and management") · Conventional + organic · Frost-seeded in late winter · Short-lived perennial legume · Wheat rotation

## What the research measured

Wisconsin corn N-rate trials measured nitrogen credits of 46 to 100 lb N/ac after frost-seeded red clover across four site-years, with a 16 bu/ac corn yield drag in one of them. A 12-location Ontario study reported an 82 kg/ha credit to the following corn, and a 20-year Ontario rotation experiment reported 5% higher corn yield after wheat underseeded with red clover under moldboard tillage. Penn State measured 91 lb N/ac (range 45–137) in red clover biomass at spring termination. Four Wisconsin site-years of corn N-rate trials (2010–2019), a 12-location University of Guelph wheat-management study, a 20-year Ontario tillage-by-rotation experiment, Penn State’s biomass-N table and SARE’s species chapter. No meta-analysis specific to frost-seeded red clover was found.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** A short-lived perennial legume broadcast onto frozen or honeycombed soil in standing winter wheat in late winter, where freeze–thaw cycles work the seed in. It grows under the wheat canopy, takes off after wheat harvest and is killed in fall or the next spring ahead of corn.

title: Red clover frost-seeded into winter wheat
author: FarmDeck
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- The credit moved from year to year: 46 lb N/ac at Janesville in 2010 and 57, 75 and 100 at Arlington in 2016, 2018 and 2019; SARE cites a two-year Michigan trial that logged a fertilizer replacement value of 36 lb N/ac.
- A credit does not rule out a yield drag: Arlington 2016 measured a 57 lb N/ac credit alongside a 16 bu/ac drag, 2018 showed some yield loss under no-till, and 2019 none.
- Biomass N is larger than the fertilizer credit: Wisconsin measured 80 to 110 lb N/ac in red clover top growth, and Penn State 91 (45–137), against credits of 36 to 100.
- Wheat management sets the stand: in the Guelph study conventional tillage before wheat gave 48% more red clover dry weight than no-till, and the 5% corn yield gain in the 20-year experiment was reported for the moldboard system.
- Kill date changes what is in the stand: an Ohio measurement cited by SARE found about 75 lb N/ac on May 15 rising to 130 by June 22, and SARE notes 50% of the cover-crop N was released in the first month after incorporation.
- SARE lists frost-seeding at 10 to 12 lb/ac into wheat in February, hardiness to Zone 4, a minimum pH of 6.0 and persistence of three to four years, so a stand left uncontrolled becomes a weed in the next crop. Read the sources · 5

1.

title: Corn foliar fungicide at VT/R1
author: FarmDeck
tags: Tar spot and gray leaf spot
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- Response tracks disease: the Indiana tar spot study averaged +14.6 bu/A (range 6.2 to 22.2) under high severity and −2.7 bu/A (range −11.9 to 9.3) under low severity, where the partial net return ran from a $46.5 loss to a $5.8/A loss.
- Iowa State’s 2022 trials at six research farms detected no effect of any fungicide on yield (P>0.1), even though V12 and R1 applications reduced tar spot and gray leaf spot; non-sprayed check yields ran from 178.6 to 250.5 bu/ac and tar spot reached 23.2% in the Crawfordsville check.
- At low disease (<5% severity) the 2002–09 analysis put the probability of not recovering a $40–95/ha application at 0.55–0.98 for pyraclostrobin and 0.91–0.99 for azoxystrobin at $0.12/kg corn; above 5% severity the range was 0.25–0.69 for propiconazole + trifloxystrobin and 0.37–0.98 for azoxystrobin.
- Timing matters: the 2014–15 analysis found VT (376.8 kg/ha) and V6 + VT (493.9 kg/ha) responses well above V6 alone (127.4 kg/ha), and an R5 application in Indiana gave the smallest tar spot reduction (13%).
- Mode-of-action count matters: DMI + SDHI + QoI premixes averaged 574.4 kg/ha against 180.5 kg/ha for a solo QoI, DMI alone gave no substantial response, and the tar spot trials found two- or three-MOA products suppressed disease more than one.
- The 7–18 bu/A protection in Purdue’s 2024 trial came from one northern Indiana site and was significant only at the earlier of two planting dates. Read the sources · 5

1.

# Soybean aphid foliar insecticide at the 250-aphid threshold

**Category:** crop protection
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026
**Cited DOIs:** 10.1603/0022-0493(2007)100, 10.1093/jee/tox235.full, 10.1093/jee/tox235

A foliar insecticide, most often a pyrethroid such as lambda-cyhalothrin or bifenthrin, sprayed when whole-plant counts average 250 soybean aphids per plant…

Crop protection · Conventional · 250 aphids/plant · 80% of plants infested · Through R5

## What the research measured

The cited six-state study of 19 yield-loss experiments (2003–05) calculated an economic threshold of 273 aphids per plant (95% CI 111–567) giving a 7-day lead before the economic injury level of 674 (95% CI 275–1,399); Minnesota, Iowa and South Dakota extension round this to 250 aphids on 80% of plants. The same study found populations doubled every 6.8 days and peaked at R3–R5 in 18 of 19 location-years. Iowa State reports yield losses up to 40% from aphid feeding; Minnesota and Iowa bioassays found pyrethroid mortality cut up to 39-fold in the most resistant field population. A peer-reviewed 19-location-year threshold study in six states, three state extension guides (Minnesota, Iowa, South Dakota) that apply it, and a peer-reviewed bioassay series of 27 population-years testing pyrethroid resistance in Minnesota and northern Iowa.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** A foliar insecticide, most often a pyrethroid such as lambda-cyhalothrin or bifenthrin, sprayed when whole-plant counts average 250 soybean aphids per plant on 80% of plants with numbers rising, from late vegetative stages through R5. The threshold trials used lambda-cyhalothrin (Warrior) at 16.8–28.0 g a.i./ha by ground once a target aphid density was reached.

title: Soybean aphid foliar insecticide at the 250-aphid threshold
author: FarmDeck
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- The threshold is supported through R5: aphid peaks fell at R3–R5 in 18 of 19 location-years, Iowa State says yield loss usually does not occur after R5, and Minnesota advises scouting until R6.5 because larger numbers are needed to cause loss in early R6.
- Pyrethroid resistance is documented: the most resistant Minnesota field population showed 39-fold lower mortality than a susceptible colony, and Iowa State expects every aphid in Iowa to carry at least one resistance mutation to pyrethroids such as bifenthrin and lambda-cyhalothrin.
- Spraying below threshold carries costs the study authors spell out: it treats a population growing too slowly to reach the injury level in 7 days, removes generalist predators and exposes more aphids to insecticide selection.
- South Dakota State notes the damage boundary, where yield loss becomes detectable, is about 485 aphids per plant, so injury levels below that have no practical value; the threshold range of 111–567 reflects differing control costs, prices and yields.
- The threshold needs real counts: 20 to 30 plants per field every 7 to 10 days, or speed scouting in which a plant counts as infested at 40 or more aphids and 11 plants are assessed first.

Study conditions and limitations

- The threshold is supported through R5: aphid peaks fell at R3–R5 in 18 of 19 location-years, Iowa State says yield loss usually does not occur after R5, and Minnesota advises scouting until R6.5 because larger numbers are needed to cause loss in early R6.
- Pyrethroid resistance is documented: the most resistant Minnesota field population showed 39-fold lower mortality than a susceptible colony, and Iowa State expects every aphid in Iowa to carry at least one resistance mutation to pyrethroids such as bifenthrin and lambda-cyhalothrin.
- Spraying below threshold carries costs the study authors spell out: it treats a population growing too slowly to reach the injury level in 7 days, removes generalist predators and exposes more aphids to insecticide selection.
- South Dakota State notes the damage boundary, where yield loss becomes detectable, is about 485 aphids per plant, so injury levels below that have no practical value; the threshold range of 111–567 reflects differing control costs, prices and yields.
- The threshold needs real counts: 20 to 30 plants per field every 7 to 10 days, or speed scouting in which a plant counts as infested at 40 or more aphids and 11 plants are assessed first.
- Populations can double in 2–3 days under favorable conditions (Iowa State), against the 6.8-day field average behind the 7-day lead time. Read the sources · 5

title: Foliar fungicide at R3
author: FarmDeck
text:
# Foliar fungicide at R3

**Category:** crop protection
**Sources checked:** September 26, 2026
**Cited DOIs:** 10.1094/PDIS-07-20-1578-RE, 10.1094/PDIS-02-23-0291-RE, 10.1094/PHP-RS-16-0038, 10.31274/cpn-20190620-014

A single pass of a premixed foliar fungicide, a strobilurin plus a triazole or SDHI partner, sprayed at beginning pod (R3) to protect soybean leaves from…

Crop protection · Conventional · One pass at beginning pod · Strobilurin premixes

## What the research measured

The cited 240-trial analysis reported an average soybean yield response of about 1.6 bu/ac to an R3 fungicide application. Studies with frogeye leaf spot reported different responses. Disease pressure, active ingredients, and application costs are recorded in the linked research. A 240-trial meta-analysis across nine states and Ontario (2005–18), a 66-trial eight-state frogeye analysis (2012–21), a four-state economic analysis and annual university trial programs.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** A single pass of a premixed foliar fungicide, a strobilurin plus a triazole or SDHI partner, sprayed at beginning pod (R3) to protect soybean leaves from frogeye leaf spot, Septoria brown spot and other late-season diseases. Study conditions and limitations

- Iowa State’s statewide R3 trials found no significant gain in 2021, 2022 or 2024, but +2.6 to +3.7 bu/ac for several premixes in 2025 even with low brown spot.
- Strobilurin resistance in frogeye, brown spot, target spot and Cercospora is present; the Crop Protection Network rates solo strobilurins Poor on frogeye, and pyraclostrobin efficacy fell 18 points over ten years. The source provides efficacy ratings by active ingredient.
- Purdue’s 2019 central-Indiana trials cut disease severity with seven premixes but found no significant yield difference in any of five trials.
- Timing is disease-specific: R3 is standard for frogeye and brown spot, white mold needs R1–R2, and R3 may not control Cercospora leaf blight.
- Response is larger with early planting and wet weather between planting and R3, and in average-yield fields; it shrinks as base yield rises. Read the sources · 5

author: FarmDeck
text:
[Meta-analysis of soybean yield response to foliar fungicides evaluated from 2005 to 2018 in the United States and Canada ↗](https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/meta-analysis-of-soybean-yield-response-to-foliar-fungicides-eval/)

   Meta-analysis · Kandel, Hunt, Ames, Arneson, Bradley et al. · Plant Disease 105(5) · 2021 · [doi:10.1094/PDIS-07-20-1578-RE](https://doi.org/10.1094/PDIS-07-20-1578-RE)

   240 field trials across nine US states and Ontario, all sprayed at R3: mean yield response 2.7% (110 kg/ha, about 1.6 bu/ac). Premixes of multiple fungicide groups gave 3.0%; the response was 4.7% in average-yield fields and fell as base yield rose. Less likely to be profitable when foliar diseases are absent or low. 2. [Efficacy and Profitability of Fungicides for Managing Frogeye Leaf Spot on Soybean in the United States: A 10-Year Quantitative Summary ↗](https://repository.lsu.edu/plantcrop_pubs/337/)

   Meta-analysis · Barro, Del Ponte, Allen, Bond, Faske et al. · Plant Disease 107(11) · 2023 · [doi:10.1094/PDIS-02-23-0291-RE](https://doi.org/10.1094/PDIS-02-23-0291-RE)

   Network meta-analysis of 66 uniform trials (2012–21) in eight states with frogeye leaf spot: pyraclostrobin alone cut severity 11% and returned 136 kg/ha, while difenoconazole + pydiflumetofen cut severity 57% and returned 441 kg/ha, breaking even more than 65% of the time. Efficacy declined over time for several products. 3.

# Preemergence residual herbicide for waterhemp in soybean

**Category:** crop protection
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026

A soil-applied residual herbicide, a Group 14 (flumioxazin, sulfentrazone), Group 15 (S-metolachlor, acetochlor, dimethenamid, pyroxasulfone) or Group 5…

Crop protection · Conventional · PRE at planting · Layered residual · Groups 5, 14, 15

## What the research measured

The cited Iowa State summary of 2015–19 trials reported that pyroxasulfone alone never fell below 88% waterhemp control at three weeks, while S-metolachlor, dimethenamid-P and acetochlor gave 82% or more half the time but fell below 50% at worst and flumioxazin fell below 60% in one of five years. Purdue’s multi-year screening put Spartan, Valor, Outlook, Zidua and Warrant at 90% or greater at 28 days and metribuzin or Prowl in the mid-70s. In Minnesota’s 2015 trial a single PRE held 62 to 81% control by late September against 90 to 95% for a layered program, with a 10-bushel average yield difference. Iowa State’s five-year PRE screening summary and 2021 program comparison, Purdue’s multi-year residual screening at 28 days, one replicated Minnesota layered-residual trial (2015) and one Ohio on-farm trial (2017). All are percent-control ratings; only Minnesota reports yield.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** A soil-applied residual herbicide, a Group 14 (flumioxazin, sulfentrazone), Group 15 (S-metolachlor, acetochlor, dimethenamid, pyroxasulfone) or Group 5 (metribuzin) active or a premix, sprayed at or just before soybean planting so waterhemp seedlings die as they germinate. Because waterhemp emerges from May into August, the PRE is usually followed by a postemergence pass that adds a second residual, the “layered” program.

title: Preemergence residual herbicide for waterhemp in soybean
author: FarmDeck
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- Residual length is short for some actives: Purdue found metribuzin very active for two to three weeks, Prowl at 70 to 80% for four to six weeks and Sharpen at 1 oz/A good for about 10–14 days, and lists minimum rates for 4–5 weeks of control (at least 2 oz Valor SX, 6 oz Authority/Spartan 4F, 2 oz Zidua WG, 5–6 oz metribuzin 75 DF).
- Emergence outlasts any PRE: Iowa State reports waterhemp emerging May through August at up to 1 to 1¼ inches a day, and in Ohio no soil-applied herbicide gave season-long control, so a postemergence pass was necessary.
- Weather breaks residuals: in the Iowa 2015–19 data flumioxazin fell below 60% in one of five years and the Group 15 actives fell below 50% at their worst, with early breakdown in the wet spring of 2019.
- Resistance narrows the options: almost 25% of 75 Iowa waterhemp populations collected in 2019 carried four-way resistance, and the Purdue screening population was ALS- and glyphosate-resistant with PPO resistance below 15%.
- The yield evidence is one trial: Minnesota 2015 layered treatments yielded 46 to 51 bu/ac against 32 to 43 for PRE-only and 14 for the weedy check, under 51 waterhemp per square foot on June 8.
- The Ohio trial was a single year, was not harvested, and planted June 2 after a May 16 PRE; its 70% to 99% August ratings include a Liberty pass in every treatment. Read the sources · 5

1.

title: Wheat fungicide at flowering for Fusarium head blight
author: FarmDeck
text:
# Wheat fungicide at flowering for Fusarium head blight

**Category:** crop protection
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026
**Cited DOIs:** 10.1094/PHYTO-98-9-0999, 10.1094/PDIS-02-18-0211-RE

A triazole (DMI) fungicide such as prothioconazole + tebuconazole, metconazole or a pydiflumetofen + propiconazole premix, sprayed at early anthesis (Feekes…

Crop protection · Conventional · Feekes 10.5.1 timing · DON suppression · Triazole or SDHI + triazole

## What the research measured

The cited meta-analysis of more than 100 uniform trials reported head blight index reductions of 32% to 52% and DON reductions of 12% to 45% by triazole, with prothioconazole + tebuconazole highest for index (52%) and metconazole highest for DON (45%). The 2022–25 uniform trials across 21 states reported 49% to 75% index control and 31% to 60% DON control across programs, with Miravis Ace at anthesis the most effective single application (66% index, 44% DON). Pennsylvania on-farm fields in 2023–25 yielded 4% to 24% more where treated. A 14-state meta-analysis of uniform fungicide trials over 11 years, a 17-state network meta-analysis of strobilurin and triazole programs, the 2022–25 USWBSI uniform fungicide trials in 21 states and an 11-field Pennsylvania on-farm series.4 independent sources.

**What it is.** A triazole (DMI) fungicide such as prothioconazole + tebuconazole, metconazole or a pydiflumetofen + propiconazole premix, sprayed at early anthesis (Feekes 10.5.1, about 50% of tillers with fresh anthers) to suppress Fusarium head blight and the mycotoxin deoxynivalenol (DON) in grain. Trial rates were 6.5 fl oz/A Prosaro, 13.5 Caramba, 13.7 Miravis Ace, 10.3 Prosaro Pro and 7.3 Sphaerex, each with a nonionic surfactant.

title: Wheat fungicide at flowering for Fusarium head blight
author: FarmDeck
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- Strobilurin (QoI) programs alone raised DON relative to the untreated check in the 17-state analysis, most of all when applied at Feekes 10.5; a Feekes 9 QoI followed by a Feekes 10.5.1 DMI only partly offset that and did not match DMI-alone efficacy.
- Two-pass programs did more: Miravis Ace at anthesis followed by Prosaro Pro or Sphaerex 4–6 days later cut index and DON a further 24 to 29% against Miravis Ace alone, and were the most effective programs tested; the trials do not report the cost of the second pass.
- The uniform trials used a susceptible cultivar, artificial inoculation and often mist irrigation; untreated plots ran from 0 to 50.2% index and 0 to 40.6 ppm DON, so percent control under natural infection can differ.
- Efficacy was 5 to 20% higher for index and 7 to 16% higher for DON in spring wheat than in soft winter wheat studies, depending on the fungicide.
- The newer premixes Prosaro Pro and Sphaerex performed about the same as Prosaro (2 to 4% more index control relative to Prosaro), and Caramba was the least effective single application relative to Prosaro in 2022–25.
- In the Pennsylvania on-farm fields the head blight index fell 4 to 19% and foliar disease 2 to 34%, but one low-disease farm (under 9% foliar severity) saw a negative disease reduction. Read the sources · 4

   University trial · Kikway, Bish, Bradley, Chilvers, Collins, Cowger et al., Paul (corresponding) · U.S.

title: Sulfur for corn (ammonium sulfate)
author: FarmDeck
text:
# Sulfur for corn (ammonium sulfate)

**Category:** fertility
**Sources checked:** September 26, 2026
**Cited DOIs:** 10.1002/agj2.70169, 10.1016/j.fcr.2025.109990

Ammonium sulfate, ammonium thiosulfate and gypsum supply plant-available sulfate to corn, a nutrient that used to arrive free from the air in power-plant…

Fertility · Conventional · 15–25 lb S/ac · Gypsum for organic

## What the research measured

The cited Iowa and Indiana studies reported sulfur responses in roughly half of tested corn fields, compared with about 5% of sites in the cited Illinois research. Soil properties, manure history, and trial design differ across these datasets; the percentages describe the studies, not all fields in each state. About 150 Iowa trials, 55 Indiana field-scale trials and 40 (plus 81 historical) Illinois trials, two sets published in peer-reviewed journals in 2025,.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** Ammonium sulfate, ammonium thiosulfate and gypsum supply plant-available sulfate to corn, a nutrient that used to arrive free from the air in power-plant fallout and now largely does not: Midwest wet sulfate deposition fell 72% between 2000–02 and 2020–22. Study conditions and limitations

- Response concentrates on coarse, low-organic-matter, eroded or side-slope soils and fields without manure; Minnesota rates the probability high at 0–2% organic matter, moderate at 2–4%, low above 4%.
- Rates: about 15 lb S/ac on fine-textured and 25 lb S/ac on coarse soils (Iowa State, Purdue); sandy soils usually need S every year.
- Starter-only S at 5 lb or less paid in just 1 of 9 Indiana trials; the lowest sidedress rate tested (5–30 lb S/ac) captured the full response.
- Soil sulfate tests and ear-leaf S were unreliable predictors in the Illinois trials; Purdue uses tissue S below 0.15% with an N:S ratio above 20:1 as the deficiency signal.
- Elemental S reduced yield at 1 of 18 Illinois sites; sulfate sources are needed for current-season supply, and ammonium sulfate’s 21% N belongs in the N budget. Read the sources · 5

title: Starter fertilizer for corn
author: FarmDeck
text:
# Starter fertilizer for corn

**Category:** fertility
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026
**Cited DOIs:** 10.2134/jpa1999.0664, 10.2134/agronj2002.1024, 10.2134/agronj2005.0620

A small dose of liquid or dry N-P-K fertilizer placed by the planter, either in the seed furrow or in a band about 2 inches beside and 2 inches below the…

Fertility · Conventional · In-furrow or 2×2 band · Small N-P-K rates at planting · Response tied to soil-test P

## What the research measured

Starter raised early corn growth far more often than grain yield. Across 100 Wisconsin on-farm sites, most testing excessively high in P and K, starter raised yield by about 4 bu/ac statewide each year, individual responses ranged from −10 to +42 bu/ac, and 40% of sites showed a positive economic response. In Iowa, in-furrow starter raised no-till yield in 7 of 11 fields and lowered it in one; in 13 on-farm trials P-K fertilization raised yield at 5 sites; and in 16 further trials, starter added on top of broadcast P-K did not raise yield at any site. Four Iowa State and University of Wisconsin field programs in farmers’ fields (11, 13, 16 and 100 sites), published 1999–2005 in Agronomy Journal, Journal of Production Agriculture and a regional conference, plus a 2022 Iowa State extension summary covering 31 Iowa trials.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** A small dose of liquid or dry N-P-K fertilizer placed by the planter, either in the seed furrow or in a band about 2 inches beside and 2 inches below the seed, so seedling roots meet concentrated nutrients in cold spring soil. The trials here used in-furrow 3-18-18 at 10 to 14 lb P2O5 and K2O/ac in Iowa and a 2×2 band averaging 15+26+32 lb N+P2O5+K2O/ac in Wisconsin.

title: Starter fertilizer for corn
author: FarmDeck
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- Soil-test P is the main switch: Iowa no-till yield gains were large (200–671 kg/ha, about 3–11 bu/ac) where Bray-1 P was below 16 mg/kg and small (80–194 kg/ha, about 1–3 bu/ac) with in-furrow starter on high-P soils; Iowa State says yield responses to starter P are seldom observed when the recommended pre-plant P rate is broadcast.
- Early growth is not yield: early growth response averaged 32% against a 2.4% yield response in the no-till study (r = 0.44), and early growth rose in 9 of 11 sampled sites in the 13-trial study while yield rose at 5.
- In-furrow rates are capped by salt: Iowa State’s rule of thumb is less than 10 to 12 lb of N plus K2O per acre in the furrow, and urea, ammonium sulfate and ammonium or potassium thiosulfate are not recommended in-furrow in the north-central region.
- Wisconsin responses were more frequent with soil K below 140 ppm and with later planting dates and longer-maturity hybrids (planting date plus RM above 235), not with early planting as often assumed.
- Starter in addition to a 2-year broadcast P-K rate did not raise yield at any of 16 Iowa sites, and in-furrow starter alone yielded less than broadcast P-K at 5 sites, 4 of them testing low in P (15 mg/kg or less).
- In high-testing soils, Iowa State attributes the infrequent yield responses to N-P-K starter mostly to the N, under no-till, corn after corn, or when the main N rate is not applied pre-plant in spring. Read the sources · 5

title: ESN polymer-coated urea
author: FarmDeck
text:
# ESN polymer-coated urea

**Category:** fertility
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026

Urea granules sealed in a flexible polymer coating: water diffuses in, dissolves the urea, and the N solution diffuses back out at a rate set by soil…

Fertility · Conventional · Pre-plant or at planting · Temperature-controlled release · 44% N

## What the research measured

In 35 Minnesota locations from 2014 to 2018, polymer-coated urea yielded more than urea 26% of the time for corn following corn and 28% for corn following soybean, and never reduced yield relative to urea; fall-applied ESN beat fall urea about 25% of the time. On a sandy loam near Becker, Minnesota (2014–15) the advantage was 39 bu/ac at 120 lb N/ac, while the same treatments on fine-textured southern Minnesota soils showed no difference. A three-year Iowa study found an ESN advantage in one of nine site-years, and a four-year Wisconsin irrigated-sand study averaged 185 bu/ac for pre-plant ESN against 159 for pre-plant urea and 189 for split-sidedressed ammonium sulfate. Minnesota land-grant trials at 35 locations over five years plus the Becker sandy-loam site, a four-year University of Wisconsin irrigated-sand study (2003–06), and NDSU’s regional summary of Iowa, Nebraska and Michigan trials. The manufacturer’s pages returned 403 and 404 and are not cited.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** Urea granules sealed in a flexible polymer coating: water diffuses in, dissolves the urea, and the N solution diffuses back out at a rate set by soil temperature and moisture. It carries 44% N against 46% for urea, is broadcast alone or blended with urea before or at planting, and the Wisconsin authors describe release as typically complete about 6 weeks after application.

title: ESN polymer-coated urea
author: FarmDeck
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- Soil texture decides much of the response: the 39 bu/ac Becker advantage was on sandy loam, and the same treatments on fine-textured soils in southern Minnesota in 2014 and 2015 showed no yield difference between ESN and urea.
- Timing matters: Minnesota found a consistent corn yield increase and reduced N loss only with ESN in the pre-plant application; fall ESN out-yielded fall urea about 25% of the time and, averaged over the study, yielded less than spring pre-plant urea.
- Release is temperature-driven: ESN held at a constant 59°F for 40 days released only 29% of its N.
- In Wisconsin’s heavy-leaching 2004 season, split-sidedressed ammonium sulfate yielded 196 bu/ac against 167 for pre-plant ESN; the authors conclude that relying on pre-plant ESN as a general practice carries risk of reduced performance in wet years.
- Other Iowa work (2013–14, two locations) found no agronomic or N-use-efficiency benefit from ESN compared with urea, and Michigan blend-ratio trials showed few corn yield differences among ESN:urea ratios.
- With low loss potential there is little to protect: the first year of Minnesota’s new study (the 2021 drought) showed little or no difference between treatments. Damaged coatings release immediately; Minnesota suggests soaking 100 granules in room-temperature water for 24 hours, and if five dissolve roughly 5% of the product is damaged. Read the sources · 5

title: NBPT urease inhibitor
author: FarmDeck
text:
# NBPT urease inhibitor

**Category:** fertility
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026
**Cited DOIs:** 10.2134/agronj2016.04.0200

N-(n-butyl) thiophosphoric triamide, a liquid or dry additive coated onto urea (2.0 quarts per ton in the AGROTAIN Advanced formulation, 1.0 quart per ton…

Fertility · Conventional · Surface-applied urea or UAN · About 10 days of protection · Urease inhibitor

## What the research measured

A meta-analysis of published trials found cumulative ammonia loss of 31.0% of applied N for urea and 14.8% for NBPT-treated urea, a 52% reduction, and an average crop yield increase of 5.3% that was limited in coarse-textured soils. In US corn, a 17-state summary of 78 experiments reported average gains of 4.3 bu/ac with surface-applied urea and 1.6 bu/ac with UAN, rising to 6.6 bu/ac at the 59 sites with significant ammonia loss, while yield fell 10 bu/ac or more at 7% of sites. A 14-year southern Illinois comparison showed a 3 bu/ac advantage with conventional tillage and 11 bu/ac over four no-till years. An international meta-analysis, a 17-state five-year summary of 78 US corn experiments as reported by Wisconsin Extension, NDSU’s regional summary of Illinois and other trials, 1989 Indiana trials at four Purdue locations, and the manufacturer’s claims page.4 independent sources · 1 manufacturer-authored, labelled.

**What it is.** N-(n-butyl) thiophosphoric triamide, a liquid or dry additive coated onto urea (2.0 quarts per ton in the AGROTAIN Advanced formulation, 1.0 quart per ton of UAN) that temporarily blocks the soil enzyme urease, so surface-applied urea stays as urea instead of converting to ammonia gas before rain or tillage moves it into the soil. NDSU describes the delay as about 10 days; the 2006 Wisconsin cost analysis assumed 14 days.

title: NBPT urease inhibitor
author: FarmDeck
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- The product only matters when urea sits on the surface: Wisconsin notes urea breaks down within 2 to 3 days and up to 20% of applied N can volatilize if it is not incorporated mechanically or by 0.5 to 0.75 inches of rain; the manufacturer defines adequate incorporation as more than 0.5 inch of rain or irrigation or mechanical incorporation deeper than 2 inches.
- Yield responses are not every year: the Wisconsin summary expects benefits 30 to 40% of the time and negative yield effects 5 to 10% of the time, and at Arlington, Wisconsin there was no benefit because 30 to 40 lb N/ac already maximized yield.
- N rate interacts: at Hancock, Wisconsin (1988) NBPT added 8 bu/ac at 70 lb N/ac (135 vs 127) and nothing at 140 lb N/ac (132 vs 134), because the higher rate covered the loss.
- In the meta-analysis the yield benefit was limited in coarse-textured soils and at NBPT rates above 1,060 mg/kg, and the volatilization benefit shrank under high N rates.
- UAN responds less than urea because only 50% of the N in UAN is urea: 1.6 bu/ac against 4.3 bu/ac across the 78 experiments.
- Protection is temporary (about 10 days per NDSU). The manufacturer’s +20 bu/ac average corn figure and its 40% maximum-loss figure are company marketing numbers without a trial list on the page. Read the sources · 5

title: Nitrapyrin nitrification inhibitor
author: FarmDeck
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- In a comparison with fall-applied anhydrous ammonia: Minnesota’s seven study years showed +15 bu/ac for fall anhydrous with N-Serve over fall anhydrous alone, but spring anhydrous beat fall anhydrous alone by 27 bu/ac, in that study.
- Apply fall ammonia only after soils drop below 50°F and keep cooling; nitrapyrin breaks down faster in warm soil.
- With spring or sidedress N, three Indiana site-years showed no yield effect, and the NDSU summary reports no yield increase from the encapsulated Instinct product in Illinois, Iowa, Minnesota or Nebraska (2008–09).
- With liquid swine manure, 11 Iowa on-farm trials responded only in an extremely wet year; profit required spring–summer rain more than 40% above the long-term average.
- In 16 Illinois paired trials, fall anhydrous with N-Serve matched spring N yield (235 vs 236 bu/ac) but needed about 12 lb/ac more N at the optimum, a $9/ac edge for spring application.

text:
# Potash (potassium chloride) for soybean

**Category:** fertility
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026

Granular potassium chloride (0-0-62), broadcast and usually incorporated once for the two-year corn–soybean rotation, with fluid K sidedress tested as a…

Fertility · Conventional · Broadcast before corn or soybean · Soil-test K driven · About $516/ton (Illinois, Oct 2026)

## What the research measured

Iowa State’s published probability of a yield response to K is 80% at Very Low soil-test K, 65% at Low, 25% at Optimum, 5% at High and about 1% at Very High. In 18 Iowa trials (2003–05) K raised yield at 7 sites, all testing Optimum, and responsive soybean sites gained linearly up to 106 lb K2O/ac. In 12 Iowa soybean trials (2018–19) a 45 lb K2O/ac fluid sidedress added 4–6 bu/ac where no K had gone on before the prior corn, 2–3 bu/ac after a 90-lb rate, and nothing significant after 135 lb or on high-testing plots. A 40-year northeast Iowa study found 144 lb K2O/ac per year began lowering soybean yield once soil-test K reached about 300 ppm. Iowa State field programs: 18 one-year rate trials (2003–05), 12 soybean sidedress trials (2018–19, industry-funded) and a 40-year rate study (1979–2018), plus the Tri-State (Michigan State, Ohio State, Purdue) and Minnesota extension guidelines that set critical levels and rates.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** Granular potassium chloride (0-0-62), broadcast and usually incorporated once for the two-year corn–soybean rotation, with fluid K sidedress tested as a rescue option. Iowa State interprets dry ammonium-acetate soil-test K as Very Low 0–125, Low 126–170 and Optimum 171–220 ppm; the Tri-State (Michigan, Ohio, Indiana) critical level is 75 + 2.5 × CEC ppm.

A 40-year northeast Iowa study found 144 lb K2O/ac per year began lowering soybean yield once soil-test K reached about 300 ppm. Iowa State field programs: 18 one-year rate trials (2003–05), 12 soybean sidedress trials (2018–19, industry-funded) and a 40-year rate study (1979–2018), plus the Tri-State (Michigan State, Ohio State, Purdue) and Minnesota extension guidelines that set critical levels and rates.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** Granular potassium chloride (0-0-62), broadcast and usually incorporated once for the two-year corn–soybean rotation, with fluid K sidedress tested as a rescue option. Iowa State interprets dry ammonium-acetate soil-test K as Very Low 0–125, Low 126–170 and Optimum 171–220 ppm; the Tri-State (Michigan, Ohio, Indiana) critical level is 75 + 2.5 × CEC ppm.

title: Potash (potassium chloride) for soybean
author: FarmDeck
text:
Study conditions and limitations

- Category matters more than product: no Iowa site testing High or Very High responded in 2003–05, and Iowa State recommends only removal-based maintenance K in the Optimum range.
- Residual K from the corn year carries over: without sidedress, 2019 soybean yield plateaued at 67.5 bu/ac with an estimated 126 lb K2O/ac broadcast before the prior corn, and sidedress added nothing significant on top of a 135-lb rate or on high-testing plots.
- More is not neutral for soybean: in the 40-year study, 144 lb K2O/ac per year lowered soybean yield relative to 72 lb since about 2004, which the authors attribute to salt and chloride sensitivity at about 300 ppm soil-test K or higher; corn was unaffected. Minnesota advises no more than 100 lb of KCl per acre applied directly to the soybean crop.
- Leaf K is not a yield signal: K raised leaf K concentration at 17 of 18 Iowa sites regardless of yield response, and 2018–19 leaf K kept rising at rates above those that maximized yield.
- Soil-test numbers are not interchangeable: Iowa’s Optimum range was 90–130 ppm in the 2007 paper and is 171–220 ppm on the dry test in the 2023 report (moist test 101–150 ppm), and the Tri-State critical level rises from 88 ppm at CEC 5 to 150 ppm at CEC 30.
- Soybean removes 1.40 lb K2O per bushel against 0.27 for corn grain (Tri-State), so the rotation’s K draw is concentrated in the soybean year. Read the sources · 5

# ILeVO (fluopyram)

**Category:** seed treatments
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026
**Cited DOIs:** 10.1094/PDIS-10-17-1540-RE

A fungicide seed treatment whose active ingredient is fluopyram (48.4% of the formulation), applied at a seed-treating facility on top of a standard…

Seed treatments · Conventional · Fluopyram · Added to a base seed treatment · SDS and SCN label

## What the research measured

The cited meta-analysis of more than 200 trials in 12 states and Ontario reported a 35% reduction in SDS foliar disease and a 295 kg/ha (7.6%, or 4.4 bu/ac) average yield increase from adding fluopyram to a commercial base seed treatment, with the probability of a yield gain above 80% where disease was high and very low where no foliar symptoms appeared. Missouri strip trials reported a 50% chance of at least 3.5 bu/ac where SDS was confirmed and about 1 bu/ac where it was not; Iowa data in the same report showed no evidence of a gain on SDS fields. Nebraska on-farm trials reported +3 bu/ac on one SDS-history field in 2020 and no difference on a field where SDS did not appear in 2017. A peer-reviewed meta-analysis of over 200 field trials (12 US states and Ontario, 2013–15), a two-year university product evaluation combining 14 locations in six states (2015–16), 20 Missouri and 23 Iowa on-farm strip trials (2015–18), and two University of Nebraska on-farm trials (2017 and 2020).5 independent sources.

**What it is.** A fungicide seed treatment whose active ingredient is fluopyram (48.4% of the formulation), applied at a seed-treating facility on top of a standard fungicide-and-insecticide base package at 1.18 to 1.97 ounces per 140,000 soybean seeds, with the high end of that range labelled for both sudden death syndrome and soybean cyst nematode. It reached Missouri farmers in 2015 as the first commercial seed treatment marketed for SDS. Study conditions and limitations

- Response tracks disease.

title: ILeVO (fluopyram)
author: FarmDeck
tags: Added to a base seed treatment
text:
The meta-analysis found yield gains very unlikely without foliar SDS symptoms, and disease severity explained 19% of the yield variation against 8% for region and 10% for sowing date; cultivar resistance level did not explain it.
- Results differed between neighbouring states: Iowa Soybean Association data from 23 trials (2015–16) showed no evidence that ILeVO raised yield on Iowa fields with SDS, while Missouri farms with confirmed SDS (4 of 20) had a 50% chance of 3.5 bu/ac or more.
- A 17-replicate Nebraska field chosen for its 2014 SDS history showed no disease in 2017 and no yield difference (66 vs 65 bu/ac in the SDS zone, 65 vs 65 in the rest), so the $15.17/ac treatment returned less than the standard package.
- Trial rates vary: 1.18 fl oz per 140,000 seeds (Nebraska 2017), 2.14 oz per 100 lb of seed (Nebraska 2020), 1.98 oz per 140,000 seeds (Missouri), and 0.15 mg active ingredient per seed in the multi-state evaluation; the Missouri report says only the high rate is labelled for SCN.
- SCN effects were variable: Missouri found the high rate reduced the SCN reproductive factor by more than 50% using all data and about 20% where Rf was under 10, with highly variable egg counts; the Nebraska 2020 trial found no difference in SCN reproduction (Rf 4.2 with ILeVO vs 3.6 without).
- Break-even depends on how often SDS shows up: the Missouri analysis at $14/ac and SDS in 20% of years put the best-case break-even soybean price near $6.50/bu; the multi-state analysis gave an 89% chance of a positive return at $13/ac and $10 beans only where SDS was severe. Read the sources · 5

title: Corn neonicotinoid seed treatment
author: FarmDeck
tags: On nearly all conventional corn seed
text:
## What the research measured

Results in the cited studies divide by pest pressure. In 91 Mid-South trials over 14 years, neonicotinoid-treated seed yielded 700 kg/ha more than fungicide-only seed on average, significant in two of four states and with higher net return in 8 of 14 years. In Indiana, a meta-analysis of 15 years of trials run under deliberately high rootworm pressure found an 8.7% yield increase associated with the seed treatment, while three-location Indiana trials in 2012–14, 84 Quebec fields in 2012–16 and a 2022 Iowa on-farm trial reported no yield difference between treated and untreated or fungicide-only seed. Four peer-reviewed analyses (an Indiana 2000–15 meta-analysis of 69 efficacy trials; Indiana field trials at three locations 2012–14; 91 Mid-South trials in four states over 14 years; 84 Quebec corn and soybean fields 2012–16) and one five-replicate Iowa on-farm strip trial (2022). All test the neonicotinoid component on conventional corn.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** A factory-applied insecticide coating, clothianidin or thiamethoxam at 0.25 mg per kernel (the base seed-protection rate) or 1.25 mg (the corn rootworm rate), bundled with seedling fungicides on virtually all conventionally produced corn seed; by 2011 preemptive insecticide use covered 79–100% of US maize. It protects seedlings from wireworms, seedcorn maggots, white grubs and rootworm larvae for the first weeks after planting. Study conditions and limitations

- Pest pressure decides the result: 92.6% of Quebec corn fields had under 1 wireworm per bait trap and the authors judged the treatment useful in under 5% of cases, while the Indiana meta-analysis trials mostly followed a late-planted corn trap crop to maximize rootworm egg-laying.
- Rate matters: 0.25 mg per kernel is the seed-protection rate and 1.25 mg the rootworm rate.

title: Corn neonicotinoid seed treatment
author: FarmDeck
tags: On nearly all conventional corn seed
text:
The Indiana 2012–14 trials found no yield benefit from either rate over naked seed at any of eight location-years.
- The insecticide effect is hard to separate from the fungicide: the Indiana meta-analysis notes seed treatments were paired with fungicides in most site-years, calling that “an important confounding factor”, and the Quebec corn comparison measured stand at 5.80 vs 5.73 plants per metre.
- Regional: the Mid-South gain was significant only in Louisiana (1,093 kg/ha) and Mississippi (416 kg/ha); Arkansas (111) and Tennessee (140) were not, and the net-return advantage by state was significant only in Louisiana.
- The treatment cost is bundled into the seed price and not disclosed; published estimates in the Indiana meta-analysis ran from about $17/ha to $52.36/ha, and the Iowa on-farm insecticide package cost $3.68/ac more than fungicide-only seed.
- Off-target exposure: the Indiana study estimated that over 94% of the state’s honey bee foragers and over 42% of its land area encounter neonicotinoid planter dust during corn sowing. Read the sources · 5

1.

[A Meta-Analysis and Economic Evaluation of Neonicotinoid Seed Treatments and Other Prophylactic Insecticides in Indiana Maize From 2000–2015 With IPM Recommendations ↗](https://ag.purdue.edu/entm/extension/field-crops-ipm/_docs/pubs/12_meta-analysis.pdf)

   Peer-reviewed · Alford & Krupke (Purdue University) · Journal of Economic Entomology 111(2), 689–699 (copy hosted by Purdue Extension) · 2018 · [doi:10.1093/jee/tox379](https://doi.org/10.1093/jee/tox379)

   Fifteen years (2000–15) of Purdue insecticide efficacy trials in Indiana corn, 69 trials, only 8 of them following soybean and the rest following corn (21) or a late-planted corn trap crop (40) to build rootworm pressure: all rootworm-rate insecticides including the 1.25 mg clothianidin seed treatment raised yield over untreated checks (Hedge’s g 0.82 across 31 site-years), the seed-treatment-associated yield increase was 8.7%, and every compound had over an 80% probability of recovering its cost. Only the neonicotinoid seed treatments raised early stand. The authors suggest the treatments be optional and rotated. 2.

title: Neonicotinoid + fungicide seed treatment
author: FarmDeck
text:
## What the research measured

Across 194 trials in 14 states, the cited analysis reported up to 0.04 Mg/ha additional soybean yield from adding a neonicotinoid to a fungicide seed treatment. The sources discuss insecticide and fungicide components separately, with responses depending on pest, disease, and establishment conditions. Two peer-reviewed multi-state meta-analyses (194 studies in 14 states; 143 studies in 12 states plus 3,614 grower fields), an EPA benefits assessment and Extension syntheses.5 independent sources.

**What it is.** A factory-applied seed coating pairing a neonicotinoid insecticide with two or more seedling-disease fungicides, protecting the seedling for its first few weeks after planting. Neonicotinoid-treated seed covered a third to nearly half of US soybean acres in the study years. Study conditions and limitations

- Sources describe the following risk factors for seedling disease: soils below 60°F at planting, compacted, no-till or flood-prone fields, continuous soybean, seeding rates under 140,000, or a history of seedling disease, SDS or red crown rot.
- The insecticide is more likely to matter after pasture, grassland or CRP, with heavy decomposing residue, in double-crop soybean, or where bean pod mottle virus is a risk; it is bioactive only 3–4 weeks after planting.
- Single seasons can show large responses that multi-year averages do not: Iowa State’s 2011 trials found effects at all four sites, for example 71.6 vs 63.3 bu/ac at Crawfordsville.
- SDS products (ILEVO, Saltro) are separate actives added to the base package and only return money where SDS shows up: an 89% chance of a positive return with severe SDS at $13/ac, very low without symptoms.
- Economics swing on price: Esker et al. 2026 found a net benefit only at $5.10–8.52 per unit with soybean prices near 20-year highs; a conservative scenario lost $5.89–10.18 per acre.

text:
# Saltro (pydiflumetofen)

**Category:** seed treatments
**Sources checked:** October 12, 2026
**Cited DOIs:** 10.4148/2378-5977.7932, 10.3390/pathogens12070913

A fungicide seed treatment with the SDHI active ingredient pydiflumetofen (Syngenta’s Adepidyn technology), applied at a treating facility over a standard…

Seed treatments · Conventional · Pydiflumetofen (Adepidyn) · Added to a base seed treatment · On the market since 2020

## What the research measured

In one Kansas trial with severe, late-onset SDS, plots treated with Saltro yielded 71.8 bu/ac against 59.5 for the base treatment alone and 66.2 with ILeVO, and SDS severity fell from 46.2% to 12.6%. Where SDS was light or absent, Nebraska (83 vs 83 bu/ac), Indiana (3,882 vs 3,879 kg/ha) and North Dakota trials reported no significant yield difference from adding Saltro, although it reduced the SDS index in Nebraska and root pathogen DNA by 64% in Indiana. The manufacturer’s own trial summaries report about 3 bu/ac more than ILeVO under SDS pressure. Four independent trials or trial sets from 2019–25 (Kansas State, University of Nebraska on-farm, Purdue and Iowa State in Indiana, North Dakota State), each one to three sites, plus the manufacturer’s multi-year summaries. No independent multi-state meta-analysis for pydiflumetofen was found; the product has only been sold since 2020.4 independent sources · 1 manufacturer-authored, labelled.

**What it is.** A fungicide seed treatment with the SDHI active ingredient pydiflumetofen (Syngenta’s Adepidyn technology), applied at a treating facility over a standard fungicide-and-insecticide base at about 0.075 mg active ingredient per seed, which the university trials below ran at 1.29 to 1.52 fl oz per 100 lb of seed. It is marketed for sudden death syndrome with soybean cyst nematode activity and became available to farmers in 2020. Study conditions and limitations

- Only one independent trial had heavy SDS: Kansas 2019, where severity reached 46.2% in the control and individual plots were at 40% by Aug. 22 after 11.28 inches of May rain.

title: Saltro (pydiflumetofen)
author: FarmDeck
tags: Added to a base seed treatment
text:
The Nebraska field peaked at an SDS index of 9.5, Indiana foliar index stayed under 1.0, and the North Dakota plots never exceeded 1.83%.
- Indiana 2019–20: pydiflumetofen cut Fusarium virguliforme root DNA 64% but root rot (27.2% vs 28.3%) and yield were not different from the control, and net return was not affected by seed treatment (p = 0.1039) with pydiflumetofen costed at $14 per 140,000-seed unit.
- North Dakota 2025 (La Mars, SDS-history field): a hail and wind storm hit during vegetative growth, stand counts fell in every treatment between June 3 and June 30, and no treatment differed in stand, SDS index or yield (P = 0.5572).
- Head-to-head with ILeVO went both ways in independent trials: Kansas 2019 favoured Saltro (71.8 vs 66.2 bu/ac), Nebraska 2020 favoured ILeVO (86 vs 83 bu/ac, P = 0.006). The manufacturer’s 48-trial comparison (2015–2023) claims about 3 bu/ac for Saltro.
- Adding the nematicides Avicta or Clariva Elite Beans to Saltro did not change SDS or yield in Kansas 2019, where SCN was very low at 43 eggs per 100 cc of soil.
- Trial rates vary: 1.52 fl oz/cwt (Kansas), 1.29 oz per 100 lb seed (Nebraska), 1.45 fl oz/cwt (North Dakota) and 0.075 mg active ingredient per seed (Indiana). Confirm which rate your treater applies. Read the sources · 5
